reviews.title: supergirl can't save this weak script.
reviews.review:
I went into this movie excited to watch Supergirl, but somehow the film seemed far more interested in another character that was constantly pushed to the forefront. By the end, it felt like she was the actual protagonist while Supergirl had been reduced to a supporting role in her own movie.

This character is easily the most frustrating part of the film. Her dialogue is annoying, her performance never clicked with me, and the camera keeps returning to her so often that it becomes distracting. What's worse is that she doesn't have any meaningful character arc that justifies the amount of screen time she receives.

The screenplay is shockingly weak. Considering the budget and the talent involved, this should have been a far more entertaining and engaging film. Instead, it somehow manages to be dull, poorly paced, and emotionally flat. It's genuinely surprising that a movie with so many resources ended up feeling this underdeveloped.

As for Supergirl herself, she's actually one of the few bright spots. She has charisma, presence, and looks every bit the hero the movie should have focused on.

Unfortunately, the lack of chemistry between the two leads drags the entire film down, and she simply isn't given enough material to carry the story by herself.

This is one of the most disappointing superhero movies I've seen in recent years. A strong lead performance can't save a film when the script is this weak and the focus is placed on all the wrong characters.
reviews.author: hyde_20

reviews.title: Why
reviews.review:
They poisoned the dog. Except instead of John Wick, we got a nerfed Supergirl running errands.

You know how John Wick starts with someone killing a dog and unleashing the most unstoppable force of nature in cinema? Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow has a similar inciting incident, someone poisons Krypto, except instead of an unstoppable rampage, what follows is a rescue mission featuring a Supergirl who spends most of the movie barely functional. Same energy as John Wick, if John Wick had been quietly slipped something in his drink before the movie started and spent three acts trying to walk it off.

To be fair, Krypto getting poisoned on a red sun planet technically makes sense, no yellow sun, no powers, Kryptonian biology is basically human. Fine. The writers did their homework there. What they apparently skipped is the chapter where Supergirl herself gets poisoned under a yellow sun, full powers and all, and the movie just quietly hopes you're too distracted to notice. If Kryptonian poison works under a yellow sun, Lex Luthor deserves a full refund on every Kryptonite purchase he ever made.

The villain is forgettable in the very specific way that takes genuine effort - not Deadpool1-villain forgettable where there's at least some charisma, more like Guardians of the Galaxy goon #4 who got promoted to the poster without earning it.

A young girl seeking revenge for her murdered family has a compelling enough setup, but the film is too busy managing Supergirl's hot mess schedule to let her arc breathe.

The one genuine bright spot is Lobo, who walks in, owns every frame he's in, and exits leaving you wanting a spinoff series that will almost certainly never get made.

This is what happens when a studio orders a feel-good action movie and the writers treat it as a Netflix checklist. Star Wars world-building aesthetics. Guardians of the Galaxy ensemble energy. Discount rack execution.

I went in with low expectations. The movie limbo-danced under them.

No one will remember the plot by next Thursday. I'm barely holding onto it now.
reviews.author: syedhaye

reviews.title: It was a let down
reviews.review:
I had high expectations for Supergirl (2026), especially after how much I enjoyed Superman (2026). Unfortunately, this one was a bit of a letdown for me.

First, Milly Alcock did a great job as Supergirl. She brought heart and emotion to the character, and I think she has a bright future in the DC Universe.

However, I wish the filmmakers had stayed closer to the visual style of Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow. The comic is filled with vibrant, colorful, and breathtaking worlds that could have translated beautifully to the big screen. Instead, the movie leaned into a gritty, Mad Max-style aesthetic, which didn't quite capture the same magic for me.

Krem was also disappointing as the main villain. He never felt truly intimidating, and some of his odd antics made him difficult to take seriously. In the comics, Krem is much more ruthless, making Supergirl's journey feel more emotional and personal. I think the movie missed an opportunity to show just how evil he really was.

I was also hoping to see more of Lobo. Instead of being a meaningful ally or rival, he felt more like an extra with very little impact on the story.

Another issue was the overuse of slow-motion scenes. Rather than making moments feel epic, some of them came across as unnecessary and a bit cringey.

Overall, I left the theater disappointed. It wasn't a terrible movie, but considering how strong Superman (2026) was, I expected much more. I'd give it a 6.5/10.
reviews.author: EnriqueE-14

reviews.title: Weak Script, CGI dog distracting
reviews.review:
I am not a DC Universe nerd, although two of the six people in the entire theater were. Instead of the movie using the plot to let the story line breathe, too frequently the characters had to explain to each other who the other characters were (Lobo) and where their motivation lie. When the Brigands arrive to steal the swords the father says (paraphrasing) 'they are here to steal my swords, they are the best in the galaxy, I'll just give him my life's work if they let us live.' Well surprise, they don't. At the end of the movie the subtagonist says she will return to her home planet and carry on making swords like her father. There was nothing in the movie showing she knew how to make the swords, or how legendary they supposedly were.

The dog, Krypto, was entirely CGI and the animated version of 101 Dalmations had more emotional animals. The movie Stuart Little was fantastic at using cartoonish characters interacting with live action models. Not so for Krypto. He flies, literally, through the apartment at the end but in other scenes he walks on the ground. If it wasn't for the poisoned arrows he didn't need to be in the movie.

Red Sun, Yellow Sun, Green Sun. Supergirl is humanesque under a Red Sun, nearly immortal under the Yellow Sun, and near death under a Green Sun. So should be the dog, yet despite appearing to have immortal powers in flying toward the Brigands he gets hit with poisoned arrows, the same type Supergirl is struck by and auto cleansed under the Yellow Sun. Krypto should have been able to clear the toxins himself. Why wouldn't the Brigands park their ship on a Green Sun planet instead of a Green Sun Yellow Sun duos star system if they were simply trying to hide from Supergirl?

A pocket watch with three moon rises, which is stated to be 72 hours, yet there is no moon in any of the scenes, and the time references are only applicable on Earth.

This movie suffers from the story being told to the audience by the actors, instead of letting the story line play out and letting the audience pick up the clues to fill in the blanks.

I was initially puzzled how a character (Lobo) deemed immortal, could be captured and jailed, except it was part of his plan to get close to his targets.

The main villain proves his near invincibility in a scuffle with Supergirl, yet a sword to the ribs through his armor swiftly fells him.

The movie contains a surplusage of action, an unnecessary insertion of dialog to explain character motivation, and a subtagonist whose primary edict was to stand there and don't move as she follows Supergirl from scene to scene waiting to Supergirl to kill the antagonist so she can get the antidote to the poison slowly killing her CGI dog.

Unless you are into the DC Universe this movie is a must NOT see.

reviews.author: neffy2005

reviews.title: script was very fragmented
reviews.review:
I walked into the theater with high expectations, but I quickly found myself struggling to stay engaged with the story. Surprisingly, the film never seems fully committed to Supergirl as its central focus, nor does it establish any other character strongly enough to carry the narrative. While the principal cast receives a relatively even share of screen time, that balance comes at the expense of meaningful character development. The characters simply exist within the story, with little effort made to explain their motivations, relationships, or growth.

The screenplay is equally disappointing. Much of the dialogue feels awkward and derivative, as though it borrows familiar one-liners from more successful superhero films without understanding what made those moments work. Instead of feeling natural or memorable, the exchanges come across as forced and often unintentionally corny. Combined with an unfocused narrative, the writing struggles to establish a compelling emotional or dramatic foundation.

That said, if this film is merely one chapter in James Gunn's larger vision for the DC Universe, I remain genuinely excited to see where it leads. I want to believe this is laying the groundwork for something much stronger. I'm eager to see a carefully crafted overarching story that brings DC's greatest heroes together with the depth and ambition they deserve. Future installments need scripts that reflect the scale and potential of these iconic characters, rather than feeling rushed or underdeveloped. The visual spectacle alone isn't enough-strong storytelling and thoughtful writing are what will ultimately determine the success of this new era for DC.
reviews.author: fcai168

reviews.title: A major setback for James Gunn and his universe...
reviews.review:
We have to accept once and for all that the superhero movie genre is going through a rough patch. We're far from the days of the MCU when every film was a blockbuster, easily grossing over $1 billion. Even the DCU had some very good box office returns, though never at the level of its competitor.

Since James Gunn took over producing this whole universe, we've seen highs and lows, but always with a clear vision and without any major failures until now... until now, because "Supergirl" will definitely be the flop of the year, with the exception of "He-Man," which is also having a major failure.

Is this movie bad? I don't think so. It actually has some very good points and some not so good ones. But it suffers from what I mentioned before: it doesn't bring anything new to the genre and ends up being just another run-of-the-mill movie, like "Black Adam" or "Shazam," among others.

The idea was to present a dark and vengeful story based on the excellent and classic comic "Woman of Tomorrow." But, as is often the case, the film doesn't live up to the source material.

Let's talk about the good things: Millie Alcock's performance. Her portrayal of a rebellious and traumatized Kara Zor-El is truly excellent, showing great depth and a different attitude from the classic Superman.

The film explores very well how Kara's past (remembering the destruction of her planet) makes her harder and angrier than her cousin Clark, and it's a major turning point for understanding her motivations and why she is the way she is.

The space landscapes and the appearance of the aliens are very striking, expanding the DC universe in an interesting way, but with one fundamental flaw: at times, it looks very bad.

The action is entertaining and features dynamic action scenes and a good overall pace, but again, at times, the CGI looks bad, unfortunately. It also has other flaws worth highlighting: the script is superficial, and it shows. It feels like it fails to develop the characters' full potential or the chemistry between them, especially considering we have characters like Lobo who seems to be there simply for show, to give off a tough-guy image.

It has a similar tone to other films we've seen countless times in the last 15 years. The direction shamelessly tries to imitate the comedic and musical style of Guardians of the Galaxy, which doesn't always mesh with the dark revenge story.

The main antagonist and other secondary characters feel underdeveloped or not very threatening to the viewer; although they have some good moments, they're just bad for the sake of being bad.

The ending, with Kara killing Krem, is somewhat anticlimactic, I won't deny it. After everything she says to Ruthye, does she just end up committing an act of revenge? It's hard to believe... Generally speaking, the film has its good and bad points, obviously. It's not the garbage some people say it is, but it is a major blow to this universe that doesn't quite know what it wants to be or what it wants to do... We'll have to wait and see what the next projects are; this one, for now, is a huge box office flop.
reviews.author: LeonardoOliva69

reviews.title: Just another forgettable superhero movie
reviews.review:
First of all, I'm reviewing this movie from the perspective of someone who has never read the comic source material.

The movie begins with Kara living the life of a reckless party girl, constantly drowning herself in alcohol because of her troubled past and her inability to truly fit in on Earth. Unfortunately, this characterization makes her difficult to connect with. Throughout most of the film, she lacks the charisma and presence you would expect from Supergirl, making her a rather unlikeable protagonist.

The turning point comes when her dog is shot by the villain. Suddenly, she abandons her self-destructive behaviour and decides to take her life seriously. However, this character development feels abrupt and unearned, as there is little buildup leading to such a dramatic change.

Then there is Rutheye, a character who adds very little to the story. Instead of enhancing the narrative, she often feels like a distraction. There are several moments where Kara and Rutheye argue or fight, but rather than creating meaningful tension, these scenes resemble petty high school conflicts. Despite Kara being 23 years old, she comes across as emotionally immature and mentally stunted. The chemistry between the two characters is also weak, making it difficult to become invested in their relationship.

The main villain is generic and lacks any real presence or depth. The same can be said for Lobo. I was genuinely excited to see more of this character, but he ended up being severely underutilized. Considering his popularity and potential, his limited role was disappointing.

For the most part, the movie is simply boring. The pacing drags, and there are long stretches where very little of interest happens. While watching in the cinema, I noticed many people around me becoming visibly disengaged, with some yawning and others appearing restless.

Overall, the film struggles with weak character development, underwhelming villains, and a lack of engaging storytelling. While it may appeal to some fans, I found it difficult to stay invested and left the cinema feeling disappointed.

reviews.author: Marijnvb

reviews.title: ABSOLUTE TRASH
reviews.review:
DC's Supergirl (2026) tries very hard to convince you it's the emotional, cosmic backbone of a new cinematic universe. Instead, it ends up feeling like a confused draft of three different movies fighting for control of the same script.

The biggest issue is how desperately the film wants to be "deep." Kara Zor-El's trauma, isolation, and identity crisis are all there on paper, but none of it lands emotionally because the movie keeps interrupting itself. Every time it starts to build something meaningful, it undercuts it with forced humor, random action, or another "cool" needle drop that kills the mood instantly.

Milly Alcock does what she can, but she's basically acting inside a story that refuses to support her. Kara's arc repeats the same cycle over and over: emotional breakdown, quick action sequence, reset, repeat. After a while, even the supposed character growth feels like déjà vu.

The supporting cast doesn't help much either. Most characters feel like they were introduced because the universe needed "more pieces," not because the story actually needed them. The antagonist is especially weak-generic motivation, predictable presence, and zero real tension.

Visually, the film has moments where it almost works. Some space imagery and action beats look decent on their own. But the editing is so fragmented that none of it builds momentum. Big moments feel small, and emotional moments feel rushed.

In the end, Supergirl (2026) feels less like a bold new direction and more like a studio checklist: establish universe, tease lore, set up future projects-story comes last. It's not a disaster, but it's frustrating in a way that's almost worse: it could have been something, but it constantly chooses not to be.
reviews.author: mimayvsc

reviews.title: A cosmic Supergirl with heart, humor and great energy
reviews.review:
I had a really good time with Supergirl. The story is simple, but that works in its favor: it keeps the movie focused on Kara's journey, her relationships, and the emotional weight behind the adventure.

What I liked most is how the film feels like a mix between James Gunn's Superman and the cosmic energy of Guardians of the Galaxy. It has action, humor, colorful worlds, and a strong soundtrack that fits very well with both the fun moments and the more emotional scenes.

Milly Alcock brings a more vulnerable and impulsive side to Supergirl, which makes Kara feel different from Superman while still belonging to the same universe. The movie doesn't try to be overly complex, but it has charm, personality, and a great sense of adventure.

For me, it was a very enjoyable superhero film: simple, emotional, funny when it needs to be, and with enough heart to make the journey worth it.

reviews.author: exitdust

reviews.title: Supergirl Takes the Scenic Route to Nowhere
reviews.review:
"Supergirl" tries to deliver a different kind of origin story through a road-movie-style adventure, but the result is dull, messy, and surprisingly forgettable. Aside from Milly Alcock's performance, there is very little here that leaves a strong impression.

The film clearly does not want Kara to be a traditional, lovable heroine. That could have been interesting, even refreshing. Unfortunately, instead of becoming a compelling antihero story, it ends up feeling confused. The relationship between Supergirl and the revenge-driven girl she travels with lacks chemistry, and their journey never creates the emotional growth or connection the movie seems to be aiming for.

Milly Alcock is easily the best part of the film. Her tired, cynical, slightly half-drunk energy gives Kara more personality than the script does. Her trauma over the destruction of her home planet also provides one of the few emotional moments, though even that scene is placed awkwardly and loses some of its impact.

The story itself feels scattered. The villain appears whenever convenient, Lobo feels more like a teaser than a meaningful character, and the many alien creatures and side plots never become memorable. The main plot basically comes down to Supergirl saving her dog while another girl seeks revenge, but neither storyline creates much urgency. The revenge subplot is especially thin, making it hard to care about the girl's anger or her role in Kara's journey.

For a superhero movie, the action is also disappointing. The set pieces are either overdone or bland, with a cheap TV-like quality at times. Compared with more visually exciting superhero films, "Supergirl" feels surprisingly small and forgettable. Even weaker comic-book movies usually offer some spectacle, but this one struggles to deliver even that.

In the end, "Supergirl" does not fail because of casting or political controversy. It fails because the story, action, pacing, and character relationships are all underwhelming. The biggest surprise is that Milly Alcock, who received plenty of criticism before release, turns out to be the movie's strongest asset.

She deserved a better film. Honestly, the dog probably did too.

reviews.author: ILuvNujabes

reviews.title: Who Is This Supposed To Be For?
reviews.review: When one watches a movie and leaves the theater wondering who the picture was supposed to be made for, it doesn't bode well for the film. Unfortunately, that's very much the case for one of this summer's most anticipated blockbusters, the latest effort from director Craig Gillespie. So why the confusion over the target audience? It's simple: this action-adventure superhero release is all over the map, an offering that decidedly feels like it was put together by committee (and probably a marketing/product development committee at that). The picture includes a little of this, a little of that, and, ultimately, a whole lot of nothing. "Supergirl" plays like yet another cookie-cutter release in this genre, except that it also can't really decide what it wants to be. From what I could tell, this is supposed to be an introduction/origin story (told in flashbacks) about Kara Zor-El (better known as the film's title character) (Milly Alcock), a refugee from the doomed planet Krypton. She makes her way to Earth with her beloved pooch, Krypto, where she reunites with her cousin, Kal-El (aka Clark Kent), better known to the residents of his adopted world as Superman (David Corenswet), subject of a 2025 release by the same name. However, despite the reunion with her cousin and living on a planet whose yellow sun has imbued her with an array of fantastic superpowers, our heroine laments the loss of her home world and subsequently leaves Earth to roam the galaxy with her unruly canine sidekick in search of a new home, answers and herself. She spends much of her time hanging out in dive bars, usually three sheets to the solar wind, and in the company of unsavory characters when not cleaning up the messes created by her dog. Her odyssey eventually leads to a chance off-world encounter with a zealous, articulate would-be teenage warrior, Ruthye Knoll (Eve Ridley), who seeks revenge against the evil Krem (Matthias Schoenaerts), a marauding villain who murdered her family in cold blood. But, given Ruthye's limited combat experience, she needs help in taking him on, so Kara comes to her rescue but pays a big price for doing so - Krypto is shot with a poison arrow and only has three days to live. Consequently, Kara and Ruthye team up to exact revenge against Krem and to procure from him an antidote to save the pup's life. Sadly, though, the execution of this adventure leaves much to be desired. For starters, the narrative is simplistic and not particularly compelling, meandering from fight scene to fight scene with action that's pretty generic, punctuated with some incredibly cheesy special effects and trite cinematography. The story is often derivative, too, tapping many other movie franchises to move the picture forward, including elements reminiscent of the "Star Wars," "Road Warrior" and "John Wick" films. Furthermore, several brief appearances by Superman and by Jason Momoa as Lobo, one of Kara's colorful brawling allies, serve as little more than shameless visual marketing plugs for the respective existing and upcoming cinematic franchises of these characters. But perhaps the biggest problem is the character development, especially that of Supergirl herself. She's definitely not someone made for kids, what with her frequently inebriated behavior, salty language, repeated graphically violent encounters and questionable cohorts, but she's also not someone who's going to appeal much to adults, either (and it doesn't help that Alcock seems wrong for the part and that her character development is wildly uneven at times). And all of this leads back to the question I rhetorically asked at the beginning: Who is this movie supposed to be made for? I'll admit I found Schoenaerts to be a surprisingly convincing villain. I also thought the idea of taking Supergirl's character in an unexpectedly dark direction to be an inspired (albeit risky) choice. But the clumsy handling of this decision (among many others) undermines whatever value it may have otherwise added. In short, there's nothing especially "super" about this release, something that the creators should have more consciously borne in mind when bringing this project to life in light of its title.

The performances of the leads are a bright spot about the film. Milly Alcock delivers a charismatic, fierce performance as Kara Zor-El, bringing fresh energy and heart to the role. His character feels disappointingly one-dimensional and forgettable, more plot device than compelling threat.

Overall a promising DCU entry but room for tighter execution. Expected a much better movie than this.

reviews.title: Not as bad as the reviews were saying
reviews.review:
I enjoyed this movie, it was a fun watch. Yes there are some issue of course however people are painting it way worse then it actually is. It gives off early MCU vibes.

Before starting this I want to say I had read Supergirl woman of tomorrow which the comic is based off.

I don't want to get into any many spoilers but Milly Alcock was great at playing Supergirl, how she portrayed her sadness and loneliness being one of the last of her species(besides clark of course) and then at the end going back to earth.

Ruthye and Krem could have had a little bit more in my opinion with some moments I didn't care a little about them however I believe Ruthye got a decent to good conclusion and Krem was a entertaining villain(his death was a not something I expected as it doesn't happen in the comic).

Lobo was also a fun inclusion in the movie despite not being in the comic Jason Momoa looks like he is having so much fun and we are having fun watching it in the screen.

Overall a 7.5/10 leaning more on a 7 if I had to round, its a good movie and fun watch.

reviews.author: HarryS-7353

reviews.title: Supergirl: Milly Alcock Shines in a Mixed Bag of a Movie
reviews.review:
I am still warming up to James Gunn's version of the DC Universe as a movie franchise. I had some problems with regards to Superman starring David Corenswet but was still warming up to what else would be in store. And so, with Supergirl, featuring Milly Alcock as the titular protagonist, I was hoping it could be somewhat better than the first DCU movie. And well, the best way I could describe it after watching it is me feeling conflicted. Despite Milly Alcock's committed performance and decent technical aspects, Supergirl struggles to tell a compelling journey of a broken hero through its story and dialogue.

Just to say it right off the bat, I dig Milly Alcock as Supergirl while everyone else in the cast felt underused or underdeveloped. I know for some people they don't like the drunk and comedic version of the character but honestly, I liked it. It shows a real contrast between her and Superman and how they view the world - with him being optimistic while she has a tragic backstory. In terms of supporting performances, Jason Momoa as Lobo was the clear standout in the movie. It literally feels like he was enjoying his role as this goofy yet badass character on a motorcycle. But the problem that I have with him is that he barely contributed anything significant to the plot other than cool action moments and some funny lines. Other characters as Eve Ridley and Matthias Schoenaerts playing Ruthye Marye Knoll and Krem. The former's quest for revenge could have been more than just that while the latter felt nothing much of a threat other than just hurting Krypto.

Nothing much can be said, at least for me, when it comes to the technical craftsmanship other than its decent. For the most part, the cinematography was better than Superman in that it didn't have much of the close-up shots of the faces. Instead, it featured somewhat cool panning shots when it comes to the action sequences whether its in a circle or from left to right. I also have to give props to the makeup and hairstyling, specifically for the people behind Lobo. It gave off that punk rock vibe just from looking at his mix of dark and white makeup on him. The visual effects can be noticeable at times but it never bothered me nor did it take me out of the movie at times. The production design was really good at giving you a compare and contrast of the different planets that Kara and Ruthye visit. Overall, it is really hard to pinpoint anything that stood out from the craftsmanship of the movie, not even the editing or the score too.

The story felt like it lost its way throughout the movie. For instance, I was already hooked in the first act in which it gives us snippets of who Supergirl is alongside the conflict that puts the story in motion. Unfortunately, after the setup, despite some cool action sequences here and there, the journey struggles to find its pacing as it gets lost in a mix of adventures with little impact. I get the whole idea about the theme of revenge through the lens of Supergirl and Ruthye. However, there could have been a more emotional depth for me beyond mentioning what they went through and instead how they could have learned from their pain and grief. The film did not need to have some exposition to tell the audience what they needed to know. For instance, there are moments in the movie where a character has to explain the motivations of villains or how something works. Throughout the movie, I see what the thematic emotions and compelling story could have been delivered by Supergirl - it all just felt undercooked.

Overall, Supergirl was a mixed bag for me because while I did not hate the movie, I wouldn't go as far and say that it was decent either. Comparing this to Superman, this movie is a bit of a step down despite my own criticisms of that first movie. If you are someone like me who is just a casual fan, I don't see anything wrong if you skip this one as it fails to deliver something that was worth watching. Still curious to see how the DCU will continue, especially Milly Alcock's Supergirl, but I now have reservations for the franchise moving forward.

reviews.title: Not Bad as Others say
reviews.review:
I went in after hearing that the movie is complete trash, with bad VFX, poor plot, etc.

Genre: But contrary to that, the movie actually wasn't bad. It's not a traditional superhero movie; rather, it's a John Wick/Nobody-style action movie.

Lobo & Milly nailed it: She has her own way of being a superhero, completely different from Clark Kent, and an amazing fight style.

Others say that Jason must have been given more screen time, but he fulfills the supporting actor role as much as required. And yes, I just can't wait to see him more in future movies. Hands down, there's no better Lobo than Momoa.

Final verdict: If you like superheroes, if you like action, this movie is for you. Don't expect this movie to be like Marvel, playing a part in a bigger phase. Just enjoy.

reviews.title: Girlboss in Space that Crashed Harder than Krypton
reviews.review:
Oh sweet Rao, what fresh cosmic hell is this? I walked into Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow expecting the gritty, vengeful space opera teased in the trailers: Tom King's comic brought to life with Milly Alcock serving fierce Kryptonian rage. Instead, I got two hours of a confused YA novel that wandered into a Marvel Studios reject pile, got mugged for its personality, and then tried to fly home with one broken wing and a bad attitude. This isn't a movie; it's a $180 million therapy session for an entire franchise that still hasn't recovered from The Flash.

The plot? Kara Zor-El (Milly Alcock) watches her mom die from space cancer or whatever, gets yeeted to Earth, and immediately pivots to a "murderous quest for revenge" across the galaxy with a plucky sidekick (Eve Ridley) and the galaxy's favorite Czarnian bounty hunter, Lobo (Jason Momoa, collecting another fat check while phoning it in from the next solar system). There's vengeance, justice, and whatever. Mostly "whatever." The story meanders like a drunk tourist on a budget airline, hitting every cliché: reluctant hero, quirky found family, big bad who's basically "space incel with a grudge," and enough needle drops to make your ears file for emancipation.

Milly Alcock has the cheekbones and the stare that could melt steel beams, and she clearly showed up ready to cook. Too bad the script serves her raw tofu and kale. She spends half the movie doing intense brooding faces while the CGI around her looks like it was rendered on a 2012 MacBook during a power outage. The other half she's quipping in that modern MCU-lite patter that feels contractually obligated. "I'm Supergirl. I don't do sidekicks... unless they're emotionally available and have good WiFi." Girl, pick a lane: angsty anti-hero or snarky Disney Channel alum.

Jason Momoa as Lobo is the one bit of chaotic fun, mainly because he seems to have ignored all direction and just showed up as Aquaman with a mullet and worse impulse control. Every scene with him is like the movie briefly remembers it was allowed to be stupid and fun, then immediately apologises and goes back to brooding montages set to indie singer-songwriters covering '80s hits. Matthias Schoenaerts as the villain looks perpetually confused about why he's in a cape movie instead of a prestige drama about French coal miners.

The visual effects are what happens when you give the Cruella guy (Craig Gillespie) a blank check and tell him "make it epic." Spaceships look like they were designed by someone who only watched Guardians of the Galaxy once on a flip phone. Planetary destruction? More like planetary mild inconvenience. The action set pieces have all the weight and excitement of a Fortnite lobby dance-off. And Krypto the Superdog? Reduced to a glorified emotional support animal who contributes exactly one (1) cute bark before vanishing into the plot void.

This is peak 2026 DCU "we're different, we swear" energy: dark enough to alienate kids, jokey enough to alienate adults, and competently mediocre enough to bore everyone. It has the production values of a mid-tier streaming series stretched across an IMAX screen and the emotional depth of a motivational poster in a dentist's office. James Gunn and Peter Safran promised a bold new universe. What we got was a $170M+ intergalactic Uber ride that ended with everyone politely clapping while the driver missed the destination by three galaxies.

By the time the credits rolled (with the inevitable post-credits tease for the next thing no one asked for), I felt the same way Kara must have watching Argo City slowly poison itself: mildly nauseous, slightly radioactive, and wondering why no one just called Superman to handle it.

DC, please. Stop sending your girls to space until you remember how to land a movie.
reviews.author: kieron-rowe

reviews.title: Not So Super, Girl.
reviews.review:
"Supergirl," 2026 Directed by: Craig Gillespie Screeplay by: Ana Nogueira, from characters created by Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster.

Starring: Milly Alcock, David Corenswet, Jason Momoa, Matthias Schoenaerts

---

Derived from the acclaimed "Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow" comic book written by Tom King and illustrated by Bilquis Evely, "Supergirl" is the second film in the rebooted DC Universe spearheaded by James Gunn.

It was...fine, I guess.

Not the total spaceshipwreck early reviews said, but nothing special, really.

Audiences had an exciting glimpse of the DCU Supergirl in last year's "Superman," as Clark's surprisingly boozy, slightly brash cousin - a far cry from the wholesome blonde ingenue embodied by actresses from Helen Slater to Melissa Benoist.

Milly Alcock ( "House of the Dragon" ) reprises Kara Zor-El and fleshes out her story as a survivor trying to blot out her trauma by wandering the galaxies on a spaceship and getting wasted on planets with no yellow suns.

Well, she tries, anyway.

A messier, more complicated Supergirl is a great counterpoint to the wholesome perfection of the Big Blue Boy Scout, and Alcock was cast by DCU Creative Head James Gunn for her edginess. Alcock gamely tries to expand a two-note role and almost succeeds, but concessions to a GP rating neuter her character into little more than a bar hopping lush who doesn't really have enough of a chip on her shoulder to be actually interesting.

A shame, really, since DC has never been afraid of going dark, and it was the one thing that set it apart from the tiresome vacuousness of the MCU.

The film makes noises about how vengeance isn't really worth it, primarily aimed at young Ruthye Marye Knoll ( Eve Ridley ), daughter of a famed swordmaker, who witnessed her family slain by head villain Krem ( a metal-studded, smirking Matthias Schoenaerts ), and vows revenge.

Ho.

Ruthye encounters Kara and her destructive dog, Krypto, at some Star Wars-style cantina, sees her powers after a brawl, and tries to enlist her on her noble quest before getting repeatedly turned down.

Hum.

Kara is finally persuaded to accompany Ruthye on her vengeance quest, but only after Krypto ( extra-annoying especially without superpowers) is lanced with a poison dart by Krem. Kara only has three days to get the antidote ( which Krem oddly carries around his neck - why? ) before doggo dies.

Hrmhhhhh.

The unlikely pair get into scrapes and misadventures on various planets, all the while as Kara continuously lectures Ruthye on the uselessness of revenge. We get the backstory of young Kara, who was born after the destruction of Krypton. She grows up in Argo, the shard of floating city created by her father, Zor-El ( David Krumholz ), the Yiddish younger brother of proud Jor-El, who had sent his infant son Kal-El to the planet Earth to be its god-king.

Zor-el wanted no such fate for his daughter, but is forced to send her off to her cousin anyway when it becomes clear that Argo and its inhabitants are all dying due to the Kryptonite layers uncovered by their life-sustaining force field.

Fine.

The story plods along until the girls encounter space bounty hunter Lobo ( Jason Momoa ), who enlivens the proceedings like a drunken uncle at a wake.

Some boring and repetitive fight scenes break out until some characters get their comeuppance, and then it mercifully ends.

The film runs longer than it deserves, and gets dragged down in parts by repetitiveness. Kara's adventures in outer space do give off "Star Wars Meets Guardians of the Galaxy" vibes, but there's one self-conscious needle drop too many - ironically, not one memorable song among them. And Blondie's "Call Me," which was used to great effect in the otherwise-nondescript trailers, isn't even in the film.

Milly Alcock was fine as Supergirl but Jason Momoa's Lobo had all the fun and easily stole the show. I hope he gets his own spinoff movie.

Ruthye is presented as a sword-wielding badass but is actually about as useful as a third nip, but nowhere near as interesting. She does manage to carry her weight eventually and help the heroes out, but she is little more than a plot device to try and help Kara work out her own shiz.

They say a film is only as good as its villains, and Krem and his crew are supposed to be a males-only race that abduct brides and also engage in interplanetary woman trafficking. In a more daring film they would've been horrifically evil, but here they just look like a bunch of snarling space Mad Max rejects - almost cosplayers, really. I'm aware that sometimes, evil characters aren't nuanced and exist just to be evil, and done well, that s fine. But Schoenaerts' Krem is nowhere near as interesting nor compelling as, say, Chris Hemsworth's Warlord Dementus in "Furiosa," to earn the right to coast on evil alone.

Despite the two female protagonists, the film doesn't lean into the tiresome "girlboss" trope. Kara is an aimless individual who isn't overpowered; she still needs a yellow sun to become super, and is vulnerably mortal otherwise. Ruthye is driven by honor and vengeance but is full of the piss and pigheadedness of youth.

Both girls are imperfect characters set against a band of galactic i n c e l s, and in lesser hands this would've been intolerably preachy. Director Craig Gillespie ( "I, Tonya," "Cruella" ) manages to avoid being too on-the-nose, but still fails to stick the landing. Ruthye's and Kara's character arcs are clear, but land with a thud, with all the heft of Erika Kirk trying to summon tears.

The film is emotionally inert. It tries for pathos, and while it never descends into bathos like an MCU flick, it just fails to make a connection like "Superman" did. Considering that a dog gets hurt and is in mortal danger in this film, I never got concerned nor teary-eyed for Krypto as I did for him in "Superman." Dogs in danger is a guaranteed emotional pull in films, and it's damning that this movie fails in that simple task.

Visually, the movie looks both grimy and nondescript, overall. Another wasted opportunity, since Kara's cosmic bar-hopping could've been an amazing visual spectacle; something that was presented in beautiful detail in the comic book. Instead, there isn't a single cinematic moment in the entire 1hr 48 min runtime.

It was just...there.

Not even IMAX could save this film from being visually underwhelming.

The film does contain a couple of surprising kills, which were more satisfying than the movie itself.

The promotional poster for "Supergirl" tried to be clever and subvert the Superman slogan to "Truth. Justice. Whatever."

It's too bad it just settled for "whatever."

reviews.title: Kryptonshite.
reviews.review:
As soon as I clapped eyes on the dreadful CGI dog in the opening scene of Supergirl, I knew I would be in for a rough time, but I had no idea just how terrible the film would be. People have been cruel about star Millie Alcock, saying that she looks more like the feral kid from Mad Max 2 than she does DC's gorgeous comic book character Kara Zor-El, but perhaps their focus should be on writer Ana Nogueira and director Craig Gillespie, who are clearly not suited for such fare. Nogueira's script is sloppy and Gillespie's direction is weak, the vast majority of the film committing that cardinal sin for a superhero summer blockbuster: being boring. Watching Supergirl being not very super for most of the movie made me feel like a Kryptonian under a green sun: I felt the energy and enthusiasm being sapped from my body, leaving me struggling to stay conscious.

The story goes like this: 13-year-old Ruthye (Eve Ridley) teams up with Supergirl to find a ruthless band of intergalactic marauders, the teenager seeking revenge for the murder of her parents, and Supergirl looking for the antidote needed to save the life of her digital doggie Krypto. The terrible script see Kara Zor-El attempting to convince Ruthye not to kill head villain Krem (Matthias Schoenaerts), because doing so will lead her down a dark path. With hoary old clichés like that, and a whole load of ridiculous plot holes and contrivances (Supergirl is shot with arrows that pierce her skin; she displays zero smarts by accepting a drink from a very dubious couple; a spaceship plummets to earth in a fireball, yet the female sex slaves on board miraculously survive the crash), I do wonder how Nogueira got this gig. Even the 1984 Helen Slater dud was better than this -- at least Slater looked the part.

reviews.title: Nothing Super
reviews.review:
By Ian Chandler - July 2, 2026

Supergirl, directed by Craig Gillespie and written by Ana Nogueira, is the second entry of the new DC Universe following last year's Superman. Starring Milly Alcock, this superhero movie tries to distinguish itself from its predecessor by possessing more edge and cynicism. However, while it manages to be a different flavor than Superman, it does not do a stellar job at differentiating itself from other blockbuster fare. Worse yet, Nogueira's writing is uneven, while Gillespie's direction and muddy editing make for an ugly visual presentation. So, unfortunately, the DC Universe's sophomore offering is super mediocre, leaving me with less excitement for the franchise moving forward.

The highlights of the film are its two noteworthy stars: Milly Alcock and Jason Momoa. Unfortunately, while it is obvious both had fun on set and give the film much needed energy, the script gives them disappointingly flat lines and fails to give them bigger personalities. For a film called Supergirl, there is not as much screentime of its titular character as you would expect. Most fatally, the character is stifled by benign story beats and uninspired dialogue, rendering a historic hero completely uncompelling. Momoa's role as Lobo equally disappoints, given that he has little reason to be in the plot and because he has no nuance beyond his thirst for blood. So, despite both performances being strong, Alcock and Momoa's characters remain uninteresting. Other roles are both flatly acted and written, making them entirely forgettable.

Many comic book movie fans usually come for one reason: thrilling action. And, sadly, Supergirl underwhelms on that front too. If kryptonite is nearby, the lead struggles. If not, she effortlessly knocks everyone out. There is little to no other elements introduced to raise stakes or enhance tension. It is a matter of checking your watch, waiting for the sun to power Supergirl up. The action itself is quick, but repetitive and the green screen effects are outright poor. The cinematography is admirable during the first third of the film; but once the colorful, but moody bar scenes are behind us, so is the dazzle. Supergirl has many powers, aside from masking the cracks both on and off screen in her own feature film.

The direction is perhaps the most annoying aspect of the movie. Without covering spoilers, the story has some admittedly bold and dark ideas that potentially imply a more gripping narrative. But the direction is tone deaf and fails to capitalize on those elements. For example, two characters witness something truly awful and it will shock many viewers. Unfortunately, instead of dwelling on that misery and giving the audience time to process it, one character flees the scene, and we follow them being upset about something entirely different. It feels self-centered and ignorant, which is fine for writing in a vacuum; but the direction should have focused on the other character's reaction, which would have been more moving, relevant, and impactful. That moment is no outlier, as a great number of decisions feel purposeful in avoiding potentially enriching ideas and memorable storytelling.

Though the film violently crashes on delivering a well-rounded superhero feature, not all is dreary. Supergirl's first 30 minutes is decently entertaining, full of comical sequences and a harmless opening. The editing is sleek and the cinematography is gorgeous, despite the narrative familiarity of the scenes. It initially took itself less seriously too, hiding the muddled writing that eventually emerged. With its derivative, but admittedly fun beginning, it could be argued that even a safer route would have been a better idea--if proper direction was off the table.

So, thanks to the flimsy direction and half-baked writing, Supergirl leaves a lot to be desired. The fierce, rebellious tone has nothing to grapple onto, rendering it as a gimmick more than anything else. Momoa's infectious energy is wasted on a one-dimensional character and Alcock's Supergirl is stuck with a screenplay that does not know what to do with her. Even worse, the movie takes some dark turns without earning them or exploring their severity, crumbling the story as a result. One bad feature will not kill the DC Universe, but it certainly puts kryptonite alarmingly close to any optimism I had with it.

Score: 40/100

Summary (for quick reference): A bland narrative, weak direction, and lack of creativity leave a frustratingly dull first outing for Supergirl, despite having some promising performances and a decent first 30 minutes.

reviews.title: Much Better Than the Early Reviews are Saying
reviews.review: This was a really fun superhero film, and I was hesitant going into it because of the early reviews. Also, I am a huge Snyderverse fan (MoS is still my favorite DC film I'm sorry) and so I've been very critical of Gunn's DCU, especially when Superman came out last year. But I have to say Craig Gillespie really did a good job with this film. The cinematography is incredible, the story is fast paced and flows really well, and the cosmic tone also really worked for me. The action sequences in this film are also absolutely incredible. Honestly, while Krypton's backstory in MoS is still my favorite, the way they handled it in this story was also really good. Also Milly Alcock's acting in this film is incredible especially during the story's climax, and I can't think of any parts where I really didn't like her. Jason Momoa and David Corenswet's scenes were also really good. Are there weak moments? Yes. Is the villain kinda lame as people are saying? Yes. But ultimately, this movie nails the character of Supergirl, and her story and the feelings that drive her actions are what makes this character shine. It's a fun superhero film and a good installment for a new era of DC, despite the fact that I still have many criticisms of the direction Gunn might take this universe into.

There are plenty of forced comedic moments, but personally, I didn't find them funny at all. On top of that, the dialogue is long-winded and tedious. reviews.title: Squanders a lot of potential with the character by offering us an inconsistent origin story with occasional flashes of greatness
reviews.review:
"Supergirl" is the second superhero film in the DC Universe (DCU) and the second solo live-action cinematic adaptation of the title character. Directed by Craig Gillespie ("I, Tonya", "Cruella") and starring Milly Alcock in the lead role, it squanders a lot of potential with the character by offering us an inconsistent origin story with occasional flashes of greatness.

To celebrate her 23rd birthday, Kara Zor-El / Supergirl (Milly Alcock), the younger cousin of Kal-El / Clark Kent / Superman (David Corenswet), decides to party across numerous solar systems with her dog companion Krypto by her side. Due to her inability to get drunk on planets with a yellow sun like Earth, Kara travels to worlds orbiting a red star where her Kryptonian biology acts almost identically to that of a human and allows her to properly feel the long-lasting effects of alcohol. One day, Kara meets Ruthye (Eve Ridley), a young girl seeking vengeance against Krem (Matthias Schoenaerts), a notorious space pirate who murdered her father. Just as the two are getting acquainted, Krem suddenly arrives to poison Krypto and steals Kara's spaceship, prompting the inexperienced hero to team up with Ruthye and bring this dangerous man to justice for all he has done.

First appearing back in 1959, Supergirl, otherwise known by her birth name of Kara Zor-El, has since gone on to become one of the most recognisable female superheroes in all of fiction. Though her big screen debut in 1984 was a major critical and commercial disappointment, the character nonetheless remained popular in the comics, as well as in her live-action and animated appearances in selected DC TV series. Due to the failure of the 1984 movie, there has been little attempt to bring the character back for a modern audience, aside from a supporting role in the DCEU's "The Flash", which also proved to be unsuccessful. Now in 2026, we have a second feature film focusing solely on Superman's cousin in the simply titled "Supergirl", which marks an improvement over the 1980s movie but still manages to flounder in other creative ways.

Differing considerably from her older cousin, we see that Kara Zor-El did not grow up enjoying the homely comforts he had on Earth, instead being exposed to the aftermath of her destroyed home planet of Krypton at an early age. As a result, Kara has turned out depressed, pessimistic, and disinterested in most of the events happening around her, culminating in her drowning her sorrows away by frequently getting drunk and partying hard on planets far from Earth. Despite her jaded apathy in comparison to Superman's optimism, Kara insists she is simply a "realist" in a universe filled with misguided positivity, an excuse she often uses not to get her hands dirty in dire situations. Although I did like the way the film presented this stark difference between Supergirl and Superman, it never really runs with this concept in a manner that feels entertaining or engaging. Instead, for a large amount of the film's runtime, all we see Kara do is mope around feeling sorry for herself, never caring to get her life together except when the plot eventually demands it.

That's not to say that Kara is entirely unsympathetic, as there are some parts in the story to remind us that she is a heroic figure at heart (even if that heart is at risk of alcohol poisoning). Most notably, we learn how Kara came into possession of her dog Krypto, having adopted him as a stray puppy when the two of them still lived on an isolated chunk of Krypton that was saved from destruction. Near the beginning of the film, we watch some nice moments of Kara bonding with the adorable superpowered canine, playing fetch with him in outer space and toilet training him inside her ship. In fact, the key reason for the film's plot moving forward is when Krypto is poisoned and at risk of dying without Kara finding an antidote within three days time. This endearing side to Kara amidst her other glaring insecurities is a welcome addition to her characterisation, but again the film doesn't utilise this aspect enough for it to sustain the entire story.

The biggest issue I have with this movie is the bizarre creative choices made during its first and second acts, where it is filled with scenes that can't decide whether it wants to be a standard origin story or a commentary on high-functioning depression. Moments where we would normally enjoy watching Kara overcoming her insecurity to single-handedly take out a group of villains become an exercise in patience when we see how absolutely blackout drunk she is. This robs us of any grounded realism in her emotional state, reducing Kara to nothing more than what can only be described as a female version of the eponymous character from 2008's "Hancock". In other words, it's hard to tell what kind of tone the film is taking during these parts, meaning I'm not sure if I'm supposed to be laughing or feeling sorry for Kara. Either way, the film should have picked one or the other, or better yet, found a way to properly combine the two together.

However, what almost makes up for these issues is the film's climax, which actually does contain some genuine emotional weight behind what is happening to most of the main characters. Without revealing any major spoilers, I was pleased with this one particular moment near the end that made me feel bad for Kara, even if it came far too late in the story at this point. Thanks to the way these scenes played out, I finally felt like I could see Kara as a realistically flawed person rather than some caricature of a drunken mess. Had the film found a way to balance this out from the very beginning, I would be inclined to rank it among the most interesting character studies of an anti-hero in recent memory, but instead it all felt pretty tacked on at the last minute.

Another important saving grace is Milly Alcock as the title character, who brings as much relatability to Kara as she can with the mostly weak material she is working with. Since Kara's upbringing was far less wholesome than her cousin's on Earth, Kara finds very few reasons to live happily without the desire to descend into alcoholism. With that in mind, Alcock portrays Kara more as a dejected young woman with little direction in life as opposed to an eager hero willing to save others from strife. Whether or not you see that as a good thing is entirely based on your own worldview, but I personally think the film went a bit overboard with her depressive state. Regardless, I do hope that there will be more of Alcock's Supergirl in future DCU movies, as I can definitely see the potential in her teaming up with her cousin Superman and/or other DC superheroes.

The supporting cast was decent, but the real highlight for me was Eve Ridley as Ruthye, who becomes Kara's travelling companion. I liked watching these two characters interact, with Ruthye constantly reminding Kara that there are some things worth fighting for in this universe. As well as this, Matthias Schoenaerts has a couple of memorable moments as the villain Krem, mainly because he actually feels like a real threat throughout the story. It's just a shame that many of Krem's best scenes were near the end and were handled in a rather anti-climactic fashion. However, I was disappointed by how underused Jason Momoa was as Lobo, a tough bounty hunter who reluctantly decides to work alongside both Kara and Ruthye. I would have liked to have seen more of Lobo throughout the story, but he only really shows up whenever the plot conveniently demands it. While Momoa is clearly having fun with the role, nothing particularly notable happens with Lobo's character until the final act, which I cannot discuss without revealing spoilers.

While it is a far better movie that its 1984 counterpart, "Supergirl" still leaves a lot to be desired in many crucial places, primarily in its screenplay. It almost seems as though the filmmakers read the first or second draft of the script and decided to rush the whole thing out instead of making the necessary final adjustments. This is frustrating as I can see a lot of missed opportunities going to waste with Kara's character and the ways in which she fits into the DCU. With all of that said, the only thing I can do right now is hope that Kara Zor-El / Supergirl is treated better as a supporting hero in future DCU movies, because her first film as a leading one just doesn't quite cut it.

I rate it 6/10.

DC vs Marvel has become an annoying war of "who sells better", which ultimately shouldn't matter for the audience, and get's in the way of more films being done for the enjoyment of general public.

I find the hate against James Gunn quite unjustified, even for Marvel fans, since he's responsable for really good stuff in that universe before jumping to do DC stuff.

He's clearly trying to give a lighter, more colourful tone than the previous take on DC characters, and I feel it's a very valid thing to do.

Supergirl is actually a bit darker than I expected, in some ways, a mix of superheroes, Star Wars, Mad Max, and Guardians of The Galaxy.. add Lobo to the mix (not much, but enough to please the huge masses that have been asking for the character to be played by Momoa) and you got a film that's not extraordinary or mind-blowing, but entertaining and well done.

I didn't feel at any point the pace was bad or any of the performances was on the way of having a good time.

I've read some comments on the CGI being bad, honestly, that comment is getting really random lately, I don't know what people consider bad CGI these days, but I didn't see a single frame that looked bad. If anything, the dog, Crypto is clearly CGI and not a real dog, but it makes sense in a practical point of view.

I wasn't sure about the main role casting, but I was actually pleasingly surprised, I thought she's done a good job and gives an interesting, fun personality to the character.

I enjoyed the film a lot and I'm looking forward to see Supergirl again, side by side with Sups.

I didn't mind the "dark tone" of the ending, like some criticised.

I think fans (and haters) need to chill out a bit and start enjoying more what is given instead of instantly (and constantly) trashing everything trying to "make their team win".. Definitely recommend to watch for some good, non-pretentious fun.

reviews.title: What Walt's Watching
reviews.review:
In a nutshell Kara Zor-El, aka "Supergirl" (Aussie Milly Alcock from "House of Dragons"), joins forces with an unlikely companion, Eve Ridley as "Ruthye", on an interstellar journey of vengeance and justice when an unexpected adversary "Krem" (Mattias Shoenaerts) strikes too close to home.

"Krem" the crim and his gang of people smugglers are a throwback to George Millers' "Mad Max".

The villains are not at risk teens, they are cold blooded misogynistic killers.

"Supergirl" is based on "The Woman of Tomorrow" comic.

She's on a bender pub crawl to celebrate her 23rd birthday showing her darker side, which is explained by some cool backstory on her home planet, Krypton.

The set designs are so good and would slip easily into the DM's of "Guardians of the Galaxy".

"Krypto", the Superdog, literally does a needle drop in the opening of the movie, then urinates on a Superman newspaper headline, before waking up the hot mess "Kara Zor-El".

Fans of the new Superman, David Corenswet, makes a few drop in moments.

Watch out for: Seth Rogan voicing an alien character.

The battle scenes are epic!

One of the highlights for this 90's comic fanboy was the appearance of "The Main Man" on his motorbike...the immortal with a god complex, "Lobo" (Jason Momoa from "Aquaman").

What a great addition and perfect casting for the DC Universe.

The intergalactic, cigar smoking bounty hunter bastich got even better when "The Eagles of Death Metal" joined the party in a soundtrack James Gunn would be proud of.

I can't wait for "Lobo's" own stand alone DC flick.

By the way Supergirl only dons her costume in the third act as if she felt she didn't deserve to wear the badge of honour that comes with the uniform, unlike her nerdy cousin Clark Kent who loves to frock up in the cape and tights with undies on the outside.

Director Craig Gillespie's moving journey for "Supergirl" lets Milly's light shine down for nearly 2 hours with a solid script. Yeah!

reviews.title: Supergirl's return to the big screen is sadly underwhelming
reviews.review:
I enjoyed Superman (2025), even though there were some definite flaws with the film. Still, I thought it was good start to the new soft-rebooted DC cinematic universe. Now, we have the next entry with Supergirl which was based on the phenomenal comic 'Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow" by Tom King which I adore. Is this another step forward for the DCU or a sad step back?

Let's talk about the new actress to play Supergirl, Milly Alcock. I think she does a great job as she is incredibly fun and charismatic as Supergirl. She also really delivers on the more jaded, pained and the slightly quirky nature to the character. There are some emotional moments concerning her past and Milly gives a strong performance that really sells it. The surprise stand-out though is Jason Momoa as Lobo. People have been fan casting Momoa as Lobo for years, including the actor himself. I can safely say that he is absolutely terrific! He is perfect casting and steals every scene he is in by embodying the absolutely chaotic energy that is Lobo!

In terms of action scenes, they are all mostly pretty enjoyable. There is a fun fight scene with space pirates, an entertaining team up with Lobo to fight Brigands and a cool full-powered Supergirl fight. There are also some excellent flashback sequences to Krypton that do a great job in separating what makes Supergirl different from Superman while also delivering some of the more emotional core of the film. The costume design are also magnificent, especially the alien designs which do a great job in showing the varied cosmic side the DC universe. Visually there are some good-looking shots when Supergirl is in space and the flashback sequence on Krypton look wonderful.

Unfortunately, the rest of the film looks dull and ugly. It baffles me that despite the film having Supergirl go to multiple different planets, a lot of them look similar and bland. They all either look brown or grey or look like any place on Earth. Where are the colours!? The writing is also what brings this movie down a lot! Supergirl is weirdly written to be quite unlikeable. She is mostly this party-type drunk and self-pitying character who is cold and distant to everyone. This is understandable due to her past and to make it so she develops a character arc by the end of the film. However, she remains like this for a majority of the film and her coldness to Ruthye (her young companion in the film) is kind of mean at times. It doesn't help that her character arc feels random and undeserved with no proper build-up of it. Supergirl also makes a mind-boggling stupid decision midway that makes it hard to take any lecture of her past this point seriously. She is also comedically always written to be under-powered in a lot of her fights which is so jarring.

The film is just a terrible adaptation of the comic book it is based on. Ruthye is just an annoying escort character in this film who doesn't do anything meaningful. This is in contrast to her comic counterpart who has genuine heroic moments and a wonderful character development that affects Supergirl. You actually buy that Supergirl and Ruth are friends while in this film, it doesn't make any sense for them to be friends.

Likewise, the villain Krem is just incredibly awful. He has no depth, no cool abilities or does anything remotely interesting. They changed his design to be more "menacing" looking and the actor gives him a more eccentric personality but it just makes him look silly and goofy. He is just a generic forgettable goon in the comics to be fair but that was kind of the point. He was the embodiment of pettiness and thoughtless evil. He rarely appeared in the comics and was more of macguffin. In the film, he appears a fair amount but just doesn't do anything that makes you interested in the villain. There are also some weird changes made in the story, including the ending, which are all for the worst. I don't get why they didn't keep the story beats from the comic it was based on?

It is sad to say but Supergirl is a big step back for the DCU. The film feels like it was made by a guy who wants to be like James Gunn and a writer who doesn't understand the character or the comic it is inspired by. This resulted in a film that lacks its own identity and instead feels like another generic superhero slop. Milly Alcock and Jason Momoa do a great job but they can't elevate this mediocrity. It is a shame to see Supergirl's return to the big screen to be so underwhelming. I want to believe in James Gunns DCU but this make me ironically lose a bit of hope.

reviews.title: Human trafficking? Seriously this is the plot.
reviews.review:
Supergirl was an absolute disappointment for me and easily one of the weakest DC films I have seen. From the beginning, it felt less like a Supergirl story and more like an attempt by James Gunn to recreate the style of Guardians of the Galaxy without capturing what made those movies work. The film spends most of its time in outer space surrounded by strange creatures, but very little of it felt connected to the core of the Supergirl character.

The visual effects were also inconsistent. Characters like Rocket and Groot worked because they felt expressive and believable, but I found several of the creatures here, including Cosmo and the two-headed rat, far less convincing. They distracted me instead of adding to the world.

I also struggled with several creative choices involving the main character. Supergirl spends much of the opening acting intoxicated, and scenes involving bathroom humor, including both her and another character, felt unnecessary and pulled me out of the story instead of adding comedy.

The central plot involving revenge and rescuing girls from trafficking also felt like an odd fit for a superhero adventure. While those are serious themes that can be explored in film, I did not think they blended naturally with the tone this movie was aiming for.

Overall, the movie never came together for me. I found the story unfocused, the humor ineffective, and the emotional moments underdeveloped. Personally, I would not recommend it, and I consider it one of the weaker recent entries in the DC franchise.

reviews.title: Beautiful movie in IMAX
reviews.review:
This was my very first time watching a movie in the IMAX format, and it did not disappoint. The visuals were absolutely stunning, and the sound design was fantastic. If you have the chance to see it on a premium screen, it is definitely worth it. I really liked Milly Alcock in the lead role; I hadn't ever seen her in anything before this, but she did a great job carrying the movie. I also really enjoyed Jason Momoa's performance as Lobo, and the girl who played Ruthye was excellent as well. The cast altogether made the film a lot of fun. I wish they expand more on Krypton and Argo City. They were dying but not dead.

As a big fan of the superhero genre-both DC and Marvel-I like to go into these movies without any outside bias. I didn't read any reviews or look at any ratings beforehand. Aside from watching a single teaser trailer, I went in completely blind, and I'm glad I did because it allowed me to just enjoy the movie for what it is. Overall, it's a really good movie. I already own most of the DC collection, so I will definitely be picking this up on 4K Blu-ray as soon as it releases. I can't wait to watch it again!

reviews.title: Not Enough for the DCU
reviews.review:
I went to the cinema earlier with the intention of booking my ticket since, being opening days, I was expecting a large audience, but upon seeing that the theater was half empty, I feared the worst.

The movie does not stand out for its direction and script, much less for the story, which is, to say the least, quite simplistic.

The film stands out for the female lead, the character of Lobo, and the performance of both actors. The settings, especially Krypton, are quite good, but it doesn't measure up to a new universe, especially having had a better movie before this one.

reviews.title: It's entertaining, but feels quite generic..
reviews.review:
The film is entertaining at the level of a typical superhero movie, but it still feels rather ordinary for today's standards. That's understandable, since this genre has been produced so frequently that it's become increasingly difficult to present something truly fresh or innovative.

I liked the first part of Supergirl the most. The dramatic buildup is well handled, and the main cast delivers strong performances. The production design is also visually impressive, making good use of practical effects. The lighting, color palette, and environments give the film a solid dystopian atmosphere.

It's a movie filled with action sequences throughout, which keeps it engaging, though it never quite reaches a truly outstanding level.

For me, the final act is the weakest part. It feels like it should have been the emotional and narrative peak, but instead it comes across as somewhat flat and underwhelming. It also lacks sharpness, and what bothered me most is that the villain is not memorable at all.

Overall, it's a decent film, but it feels like it could have been much better. I actually think it might have worked better as a six-episode miniseries, which would have allowed for a more balanced and satisfying story. A theatrical release also carries more risk, especially since superhero films with female leads often face heavy review bombing in recent years.

Still, for me, it's a 7/10, which feels like a fair rating.

reviews.title: How to turn an icon into a forgettable party girl
reviews.review:
The biggest crime Supergirl (2026) commits isn't that it's a bad superhero movie-it's that it completely misunderstands who Supergirl is supposed to be.

Instead of giving us a strong, compassionate, determined Kara Zor-El, we're handed a bizarre "party girl" interpretation that feels less like Supergirl and more like someone trying way too hard to be quirky and rebellious. The whole personality comes across like it wandered out of Ke$ha's Tik Tok music video and somehow ended up wearing the House of El crest. It's not edgy. It's not refreshing. It's just... weird.

The problem isn't that superheroes can't have flaws. They absolutely should. The problem is that this version feels completely disconnected from everything that has made Supergirl an enduring character for decades. Rather than confidence and quiet strength, we're given forced attitude and juvenile antics that never really land.

Then there's the casting.

After seeing Sasha Calle in The Flash, it's impossible not to wonder what could have been. Even with limited screen time, Sasha carried herself like Supergirl. She had the physicality, the presence, the intensity, and the emotional weight that made people immediately want to see more of her. She wanted to continue playing the character, and countless fans wanted exactly that.

Instead, Hollywood once again demonstrated its incredible talent for fixing something that wasn't broken.

Rather than building on a version audiences had already embraced, studio bureaucracy, executive reshuffling, and yet another franchise reboot hit the reset button for no compelling reason. It's the cinematic equivalent of trading in a brand-new Lamborghini for a rusty Trabant and then expecting everyone to applaud the downgrade.

It's a baffling decision.

The new interpretation simply lacks the gravitas that Sasha Calle brought to the role almost effortlessly. Whether it's the writing, the direction, the characterization, or the casting itself, the end result never convinces you that you're watching one of DC's most iconic heroes.

The film also suffers from a broader identity crisis. It desperately wants to be quirky, irreverent, emotional, funny, and cosmic all at once, but never commits to any of those ideas strongly enough. Every potentially emotional moment is undercut by awkward humor, while every attempt at humor feels like it's trying far too hard to be meme-worthy.

Instead of creating a memorable Supergirl, the movie creates a collection of random personality traits stitched together without any understanding of why Kara has resonated with readers for generations.

The tragedy is that the ingredients for a great Supergirl movie were already sitting right there. Sasha Calle had already proven she could embody the character despite appearing in a film that was itself surrounded by production turmoil. Many fans hoped she'd get a proper standalone opportunity.

Instead, the studio threw everything away and started over-again.

You can reboot a universe all you want, but if you lose the heart of the character in the process, you've already failed.

Supergirl (2026) doesn't just miss the mark. It feels like it was aiming at an entirely different target.

reviews.title: DC just dropped a banger
reviews.review:
Went into 'Supergirl' with pretty much zero expectations and walked out wondering why I ever doubted it. It was so much darker than I imagined, but underneath all of that was so much heart. The soundtrack absolutely slapped and the whole film had this weirdly addictive energy that I just completely vibed with.

It almost felt like if 'Guardians of the Galaxy' and 'Mad Max' had a baby, but with a story that hit on a much more personal level. I loved that it wasn't just about saving the day - it was about finding the place you belong and realising sometimes that place has to come from within.

Definitely one of my favourite recent DC films and one I wasn't expecting to connect with this much. Such a pleasant surprise.

reviews.title: Fury Road meets DC = Supergirl!
reviews.review:
I enjoyed it. A fun romp. Unique spin on the idea of what a supergirl or superman(franchise) film can be. Some scenes that straight up remind you of other films, in a good way. It doesn't pull any punches. It's fairly mature and has a strong, good or rather interesting message about revenge. Wasn't expecting to like the lead as much as I did, but she pulled it off. I enjoyed it far more than some previous superman films (including a few with henry cavil). I went into the theatres not expecting much, watched the trailer just before going in. Trailer had me a little hyped, I went in and it exceeded my expectations for a moviegoing experience. Sure there were some cons, the CGI dog, no matter how good it was (and the target audience probably couldn't tell since the CGI dog is animated very realistically), was still annoyingly CGI.

The blue-orange graphics and tone was very much Mad max. I loved it. I would like to see more movies take heavy inspiration from Fury Road, as this one did, so I thoroughly enjoyed it. Strong female lead, just like charlize theron was! I can't complain, I was entertained and the diagloue was a touch more thoughtful and nuanced than I honestly anticipated. Is it fun in theatres as a casual action flick ? Yes. Are there drawbacks? Yes. I just wished the budget was a bit more so that the camerawork and cgi scence could be even better, but it's certainly no slouch of a film. Good pacing, well directed but not perfect. I'd give it an 8 but for now it's a 7/10. You could tell they really tried with this film in quite a few areas, it has heart and is an honest film, capable of standing on it's own. That's what critics are missing when they hate on it. The costume designs for some of the characters are insane. Give it a watch.

reviews.title: Good, Not Great-but Still Worth Watching
reviews.review:
I watched Supergirl in IMAX, and overall, I thought it was a good movie not a great one, but definitely an enjoyable watch.

Milly Alcock delivers a fantastic performance as Supergirl. She brings both strength and vulnerability to the character, making her easy to root for. Milly Alcock is the heart of the film. Jason Momoa absolutely steals every scene he's in as Lobo. He was born to play this role, and his charisma and screen presence are outstanding. Eve Ridley also does a solid job as Ruthye and fits the character well.

Visually, the movie looks great. The VFX are impressive, especially on the IMAX screen, making the action sequences and cosmic settings feel immersive.

My biggest issue with the film is the villain. The antagonist isn't particularly memorable, and the character writing feels underdeveloped, which lowers the emotional stakes of the story.

Overall despite its flaws, Supergirl is an entertaining ride with standout performances, gorgeous visuals, exciting action, and plenty of fun moments.
