reviews.title: The movie is definitely above average!
reviews.review:
The movie is above average and definitely worth seeing in theaters. The acting is good, but I would have made Lobo much crazier, closer to the Joker than to Deadpool. The villain isn't very memorable and feels pretty bland. The story isn't anything special-it's a typical superhero movie. The atmosphere is great, and the soundtrack is excellent. Thanks, and I'm looking forward to more.

I honestly don't understand why so many bitter people are giving it a 1/10. What does a 10/10 movie look like to you? Or even a 7/10? Are you just Snyder fans who think he'll come back? He won't. Instead, this kind of review bombing could simply lead to DC reducing or even shutting down its film projects. Who benefits from that?

Judge the movie based on what you actually watched: the story, the acting, the atmosphere, the visual effects, the motivations of the hero and the villain, and everything else that makes a film. Henry Cavill's Superman will always have a place in our hearts, but this new DC Universe deserves to be judged fairly too.
reviews.author: ISinCaraI

reviews.title: Supergirl Review!
reviews.review:
🏆78%

I have a lot to say about this film. I have many issues with it, but for the most part, I did really enjoy it. First off, the thing most will probably be talking about is how different the end of the film is. In the comics, Kara spares Krem in the end. But in this, Kara actually kills him. Now obviously, Krem did deserve to die, but this change also does kind of ruin the message of the comics. Kara does say to Ruthie that revenge will just take you on a darker path, but her saying that just feels less impactful since she just kills him right after. I think the death could've worked pretty well if they made the scene a little darker, and they could've had it be some moment where Kara finally decides to never kill someone again, but the movie doesn't even go in that direction. I guess you could say that the main reason for these changes is because they want to keep Kara a little more different from Superman by having her be more open to killing someone, but all of this just makes the movie's message about revenge fall flat. That is easily the biggest issue with the film, so I totally understand why some might come out of this a little disappointed. But even with those issues I mentioned, there's a decent amount of things that this film does right. I really liked Kara's backstory, and it's arguably the strongest part of the film. Also, Lobo's character was cool and all, but it felt like his only purpose within the movie was just to get comic book fans excited. He does a couple of cool things, and has a couple of decent action sequences, but he does nothing in terms of moving the story forward. He's kinda just along for the ride. Also, Krem was honestly quite a lame antagonist in this. There's not much I can say about his character besides the fact that he likes killing people. His character has practically zero depth. Obviously, the best character of the movie is Kara. As I said, her backstory was pretty good, and there was a lot to like about her. Sure, she doesn't have as great of an arc as she did in the comics, but she was still mostly pretty good here, and I think Milly Alcock was perfect for the role. The film seriously could've been so much better, but I still can't get myself to hate this. If you hate the film for how much different it is from the comics, then I can't really blame you. Though, even with its flaws, I found it to be quite an enjoyable watch. I never really got bored while watching it. Definitely not the best comic book movie out there, and it's definitely not as good as Superman 2025, but I can't help but at least give it a decent rating.

THE GOOD

* I love the intro.

* I mostly like the way Krem is introduced.

* I love the Superman scenes.

* The soundtrack is fantastic!

* The score is good.

* The Argo flashbacks are perfect.

* Milly Alcock is perfect as Supergirl.

* Ruthye's actor is great for the role.

* I like the little alien on the bus.

* I like the idea of Krem being a sex trafficker, as it darkens the plot.

* The introduction of Lobo and his theme is awesome.

* I love when Kara acts like a white girl to Lobo. It is so funny.

* Space and the planets are beautiful.

* I really like that they actually speak Kryptonian on Argo.

* Kara's parents are great in this.

* "We are with you." - Zor-El * I love how much darker Kara's backstory is compared to Kal's.

* Jason Momoa is perfect as Lobo.

* Supergirl's theme is spectacular.

* This has the best character shots of any DCU movie to date.

* Every scene Superman is in is fantastic.

* I want more of Kara growing up on Earth!

* I like how the movie makes Kara weak.

* Ruthye telling Kara that she is exactly what her parents told her to be is good.

* "You're not always nice, but you're kind. And you're not perfect, but you're good." - Ruthye * This movie would benefit from 15 additional minutes to flesh out Krem, Ruthye, and Kara.

* The flight out of the water is so good.

* I do not hate the needle drop. It serves Ruthye's story well because the song is essentially what Supergirl has been telling her. I think it provides a good conclusion to Ruthye's story in this movie. Do I think there is a better song? Yes. Am I mad that this is the song? No.

* The final battle looks so good.

* I like that Supergirl kills Krem with Ruthye's sword.

* The cinematography is so good.

* The ending is phenomenal.

THE BAD

* I do not like how generic Krem looks.

* I do not like how early Krypto is taken out, considering he is Kara's dog but has more screen time with Clark.

* I do not like where the Argo flashbacks are placed.

* I do not understand why Kara did not simply put the helmet on instead of talking while they were on the bus.

* The story is thin and is essentially John Wick Lite.

* Krem is not fleshed out enough.

* The silent-scream scene is unintentionally funny.

* I do not like how Kara is constantly being saved, whether it is by Lobo or Ruthye.

* I really do not like how the entire sex-trafficking plot is never fleshed out.

* I do not like that Ruthye simply goes to stay with her aunt.

I can't wait for Man of Tomorrow.

reviews.title: Supergirl (2026) is a messy but spirited cosmic adventure whose uneven storytelling can't fully dim the excitement it sparks for the future of the DCU.
reviews.review: Supergirl (2026) delivers a chaotic but entertaining cosmic ride. The story feels fragmented, with abrupt transitions and a noticeably uneven flow, yet the film's energy keeps it engaging. Milly Alcock shines throughout her mix of toughness and charm grounds the narrative and gives the movie a beating heart. The rest of the cast help smooth over the rough structure. Strong world building and imaginative alien settings expand the DCU in exciting ways, making the film feel bigger than its flaws. Supergirl feels structurally uneven, but also fun, charming, and bursting with creative ideas. Thanks to Milly Alcock's standout performance and a likable ensemble, the film leaves you energized and genuinely excited for what the DCU might explore next.

reviews.title: Being 'good' doesn't mean that you can't be tough; it doesn't mean that you need to always be nice...
reviews.review:
Ever since first being introduced to the character of Supergirl when I watched the much-maligned 1984 Helen Slater movie, I've anxiously awaited another big-screen version. Each live-action portrayal of the character has been quite a different interpretation, from sweet/naïve (Slater) to seemingly-angry-most-of-the-time (Laura Vandervoort in TV's Smallville) to 'adorkable' (Melissa Benoist in the 'Arrowverse') to glum/morose (Sasha Calle in 2023's The Flash). Now Aussie actress Milly Alcock (who was a stand-out in the first season of GoT spin-off House of the Dragon...which is where most probably know her from, though I'd personally recommend checking out the two seasons of an Aussie show she did before that called Upright, as that was the first indicator she had 'star quality/potential') gives us a version of the character we haven't had before...one who's 'messy' (ie. Can be violent, cusses, doesn't succeed in saving every person, but is at least able to give freedom to those who need it and protect a young girl from the burden of dealing out justice). This is a more complex take on the character than we've had previously, and Milly proves why James Gunn regards her as one of his best casting decisions ever.

Nothing's much changed for Kara Zor-El since our brief introduction to her inebriated self at the end of 2025's Superman. 'This Summer' by Sleigh Bells (the first song in the film's killer soundtrack) awesomely kicks off the movie, as Kara's beloved super-pooch Krypto (yes, he's HERS. Get over it) continues to be one of the most brilliant CGI creations in recent times, behaving like a typical dog...except he can play fetch in space. For dog lovers (or just animal people in general), Kara's mission to save one of the only remaining pieces of her home (which we get brief flashbacks to, showing how these two best buds came together in a time when they needed each other most) will resonate deeply, as the bestest boy ever is put in jeopardy after a studded-faced brigand called Krem of the Yellow Hills shoots Krypto with a poisoned arrow/dart and there's only three days to get the antidote. As if poisoning a dog wasn't enough evidence Krem is the lowest of the low, he also slaughtered the family of young Ruthye, whose thirst for vengeance leads to her crossing paths with Kara during her pub crawl from one planet to the next.

The big sister/little sister-like dynamic between Kara and Ruthye is at the heart of the film and the latter shows that while she may be young, she can hold her own as the former starts off reluctantly allowing her to tag along but is always looking out for her/protecting her (considering what those aliens were going to do with Ruthye if they'd won the arm-wrestling bet with Kara, receiving a broken arm/getting their butts handed to them was the LEAST they deserved). In her first big-screen role, Eve Ridley does an admirable job keeping up with Milly, as her character eventually gets a wakeup call that Kara isn't the typical 'hero' she first believed her to be and even lashes out at her protector in a moment of anger, but nevertheless has her back, as they save each other on more than one occasion. Also along for the ride, popping in and out at various times, is the character of Lobo...a role Jason Momoa was born to play. While the character isn't a huge stretch for him acting-wise, he fits it well and despite his 'anti-hero' personality, he does have those rare moments of being impressed by both Ruthye (getting herself out of trouble) and Kara (showing her ruthless side).

Coming as little surprise, it's the film's main villain of Krem that falls somewhat short. Matthias Schoenaerts certainly *looks* nasty enough and he commits several heinous acts...but there's not much more to him than serving the purpose of providing a common goal for Kara and Ruthye to team-up. David Krumholtz and Emily Beecham do a better job making the most of their limited screentime as Kara's parents, Zor-El (brother of Jor-El) and Alura, who we see via flashbacks to Krypton. Apparently not ALL Kryptonians are jerks, as these two loving parents have no intention of their daughter ruling over Earth like Kal'El's did, but are eventually forced to send her there when they're slowly dying of Kryptonite poisoning (having lived for longer than the majority of Kryptonians thanks to a shield over Argo City provided by Zor-El which separated them from the rest of the planet when it exploded). These actors, plus Milly, do a LOT with the little they're given, conveying what a devastating situation this is for the young Kara.

Helping her adjust to being on a new planet which she can't even speak the language of when she arrives is her cousin who's now older than her. Although David Corenswet's appearances are only sprinkled throughout the film, he continues to show why he's the best Superman we've had in ages, displaying that light/friendly/welcoming/likeable side the character's *supposed* to have (and as he explains to Kara regarding their costumes, the bright colours are to let people know they're 'good'...which is something other interpretations have sadly missed the point of). While they only share a few scenes together in the film, both actors have given us more of the El cousin dynamic than any other big-screen versions have. Part of why this iteration of Kara/Supergirl is so different to those that've come before is obviously to illustrate the differences between her and Clark/Superman. They clearly have different moral codes and I look forward to further exploring more of their dynamic.

As for the film itself, it might come as a surprise that it's a more 'simplistic' story than what a lot are probably used to in superhero movies. While there are indeed action scenes (though personally I would've liked to see Supergirl at full power a bit more, as she's depowered on certain planets/weakened due to poisoning and the like at times and rarely gets to completely cut loose with her super-abilities). There's no world-ending/universe-destroying event here, instead it's a much more 'intimate' story and the 'spectacle' takes a backseat to the raw emotions of the main characters. Milly Alcock's praises can't be sung enough, as when those deeply emotional scenes come (whether it's her reacting to her furry best friend on death's door, tearfully saying goodbye to her father as she loses the only home she's ever known or finally getting through to Ruthye that the revenge she's been seeking won't make up for her loss), she's more than up to the task of making every one of them feel heart-breakingly *real*.

Female-led superhero movies have always had an uphill battle, having to fight twice as hard as their male counterparts to earn any semblance of respect. From the moment this film was first announced, there have been those determined to tear it down, spreading false information and even launching smear campaigns against the lead actress. Sadly, it's unlikely this sort of behaviour will ever change. However, for those who are actually willing to give the movie a chance and not let others dictate how they should feel about it, there's a really decent story here which delivers an important message that more people should take heed of: that female superheroes don't always necessarily have to be 'prim/proper', and they're allowed to be just as much of a 'mess' as certain male superheroes get to be. They shouldn't be judged differently, with one held to a higher standard than the other. As someone who's waited for a new Supergirl movie for SO LONG, I felt satisfied with the result. Sometimes a movie doesn't have to be great; it's enough to just be good.

reviews.title: Entertaining, but Generic
reviews.review:
With last year's SUPERMAN, James Gunn broke the mold of the dour, downbeat, "punchy, punchy" types of movies the the DCEU was known for (most notably with the Batman and Superman entries). And...at the end of that David Corenswet starring vehicle we were treated to a scene toward the end that delightfully introduces Clark Kent/ Kal El's cousin, Kara Zor El (a wonderfully disheveled Milly Alcock).

The question was as we entered the Cineplex to watch SUPERGIRL (this NOT directed by Gunn, but rather Craig Gillespie) would this film be able to keep the lighter tone of Superman.

And the answer is...it does...but it does so at the cost of depth of characters and really meaningful dialogue that this film would have benefited from.

Alcock, of course, stars as the titular SUPERGIRL and she is quite good (but not great) in the role. Her Kara Zor El is more interested in partying (at least in the beginning) than saving those in need. Alcock excels in this early part of the film, giving us an anti-hero that should be noticed but something was missing in her performance.

What was missing became obvious when she shared scenes with Corenswet's Superman - what Alcock was missing was charisma. That spark that makes her character jump off the screen and demand to be noticed and rooted for. Her character just doesn't have it.

A large reason for that is the script by Ana Nogueira that is light on character moments and heavy on wisecracks and action. The writing and the quick-cut, "keep the action moving" direction of Gillespie didn't do Alcock any favors.

Jason Momoa is along for the ride as LOBO, who is the Han Solo of this piece. His character would have been much much more interesting had we not have seen Momoa play these types of characters many, many times before (including in the DCEU as Aquaman).

The rest of the cast are "fine", Eve Ridley (the Netflix series 3 BODY PROBLEM) is the standout as the determined youth that enlists Supergirl's begrudging aide while Matthias Shoenaerts (AMSTERDAM) is about as generic as can be as the villain of the piece.

And that can be said for the CGI aliens, the CGI landscape and the myriad of fight scenes. They all are professionally completed and rendered but they are all very generic. You could take ANY of the fight scenes, or the CGI Aliens or the CGI backdrops in this film and drop it into any other SuperHero film and one would not be able to tell the difference.

The BankofMarquis was entertained by the proceedings of SuperGirl but, unfortunately, this film is destined to fade away like sand being washed away by the tide.

reviews.title: A Refreshing Cosmic Adventure, Overlooked and Underrated
reviews.review:
I walked into *Supergirl* with pretty much zero expectations, especially seeing the mediocre online ratings, but I was pleasantly surprised. Honestly, this felt like a genuine relief after years of predictable superhero movies.

What makes this film work so well is that it refuses to play it safe. We aren't stuck on Earth watching yet another hero save New York or fight the same old, tired villain tropes. Instead, the movie takes us off-world and dives headfirst into the galaxy. The world-building is expansive, taking Kara across new terrain, vibrant alien worlds, and unfamiliar cosmic cultures that actually make the universe feel vast and dangerous.

Milly Alcock delivers a fantastic performance as Kara Zor-El. She brings a raw, slightly jaded edge to the character that sets her completely apart from the typical polished Boy Scout routine we usually get in Kryptonian stories. The dynamic as she travels across the stars gives the film a gritty, sci-fi western energy rather than a standard formulaic comic-book plot.

It's definitely not perfect, but the low 5.9 rating feels harsh. If you're tired of the usual Earth-bound superhero formula and want a solid space-faring adventure with strong performances and a fresh setting, give it a shot. It deserves way more credit than it's getting.

The look of the film makes it worse, because it's shot so dark you can barely see anything, which is a bizarre choice for a hero defined by sunlight. The villains bring nothing too, with no real backstory or menace to make them feel like a threat. Worst of all is the writing, which is flat and lifeless, full of dialogue that clunks and a story that never builds to anything. I expect the critics to be generous, but I'd be amazed if regular audiences feel the same once they've paid for a ticket. A real letdown that I can't recommend.

Easter eggs abound for sharp-eyed (and sharp-eared) fans, including some deep cut references that are sure to make DC readers happy.

All in all, Supergirl is a emotional, slightly angsty, coming of age movie that works as a voyage of self-discovery; a solid if not pitch perfect flick.

reviews.author: marv_el

reviews.title: Supergirl Movie Review (Woman of Tomorrow)
reviews.review:
So I just saw Supergirl, and the film felt very interesting to me, like it had deep moments that could resonate with fans of meaningful storytelling, but at the same time it felt very weird in the way it was directed. The movie for me felt like a combination of two worlds; it has the deep and mature themes of the comic book it's based on, "Woman of Tomorrow", but then the film had moments where it felt like a James Gunn film, which isn't a bad thing. Still, it at times takes away from its emotional core, that being the life of Kara-Zor El, and having read the comic book as well, knowing her backstory from the Injustice 2 game and W. O. T. Comic.

The visuals in the movie are fun. Is the movie colorful? Yes and no. It is colorful in certain sections of the film, those being either Flashbacks or Calm moments. Still, I feel like they could've done so much more in the film to make it even more colorful than its comic book counterpart, which is a visual masterpiece, with its artwork moving and flowing even into the story's themes. This is highly noticeable since, for most of the film, we are in dark rooms and/or pubs with flashes of sunlight, which made me feel like I was watching a western rather than a Space Opera.

It also doesn't help that certain scenes feel like a direct homage and/or 1-to-1 copy of James Gunn's films, and I'm like, Craig Gillespie, you aren't James Gunn; you are a Visual director who made " I, Tonya" & "Cruella." Where did your visual flair go in those scenes? However, that being the case, the action scenes in the film I really enjoyed; most of them, weirdly, had Lobo (Jason Momoa), who brought the action scenes that flavor of chaos, and the action scene with Kara and Krem (Matthias Schoenaerts) was thrilling, seeing how she was decimating everything in her path. However, the film felt a little predictable around the 2nd half, and I wanted to see even more elaboration on Krem the Villain. This mix of strengths and weaknesses might influence how the audience perceives the film, but it also leaves room for future growth and improvement in future DCU Films.

I did enjoy the creature work and designs, some heavily inspired by the comic book and others created specifically for this film. I can tell this is where the majority of the budget went, which makes sense. The set designs of the locations feel very western, cowboy-aesthetic, which I think is what the film visuals were going for. And though the film did a fantastic job of matching those aesthetics, I also enjoyed how they represented the city of Argos, which I originally thought was going to be the city of Kandor due to its bubble shield, and seeing more of the Kryptonian architecture was a good addition.

The acting in the film is really good. Milly Alcock as Supergirl, or Kara Zor El, is fantastic, and having her slowly realize that the person she needs to be is someone who protects the innocent is another great addition that is fundamental to the Super Family. And I cannot wait to see how her character expands in the later film universe. I enjoyed seeing her backstory in her life of Argos and seeing how everyone she loved died by Kryptonite poisoning; to me, that felt very and I do mean very emotionally investing, only for her to arrive on Earth and still feel like it's not for her. For me, that's the hook this movie does beautifully, and having her do her action scenes and save people is great because that is what the family of EL does.

Eve Ridley as Ruythe is a likable character, but I felt she had the potential to do more, especially since, for the majority of this film, she is seeking revenge for the death of her family. Especially when in the film she states she knows how to fight with swords as well in the comic, but in the film I don't think she ever got the opportunity to show those skills in the film with the swordplay, but I did enjoy how resourceful her character was and how she was quick on changing her strategies in the situations that occurred. I also understand her motivations for wanting to kill Krem, but the film barely shows her family before their demise, so it felt like I was missing a good 5-10-minute scene before the villain appears.

Matthias Schoenaerts as Krem is an interesting villain in the comic because he has layers to his Evil. In the film, I was hoping they would show more of his personality. Still, he felt like a 2 note villian, my meaning with this is that he enjoys the kill, sometimes for no reason at all, and other times, he's creepy for the point of being creepy, and Idk if they wanted to lean into him being more of a psychopath than a sociopath, which is what I understood from reading the comic. Another factor from the comic and the film is that he has super strength, while in the comic he's a normal human without abilities, and I feel like that would've paralleled Superman 2025 in how the villain was portrayed, but that is a minor nitpick on my part. What I do think is probably going to affect this movie is how the character of Krem is shown physically, where I like the suit but the amount of Piercings on his face kinda gets a bit distracting and overdesigned in my opinion; nonetheless, I liked his acting; it's an interesting mixture of seriousness and crazy psychopath. I think in the film, that works by bringing the tension higher. The last factor was that the Brigands, well, they kidnap children, specifically female children, and force them into being brides for their Male race, and that, in itself, is a sensitive matter, but a matter that I like that DC comics has the balls and motivation to talk about that issue.

Jason Momoa as Lobo is great, and I thought he added a fun balance to the film's serious tone while creating Chaos along the way. It also helps that the makeup department did a fantastic job of conveying his personality and stature compared to how he looks in the comics; also, his having the bike and cigar is a welcome addition. Still, I also feel like the film introduces him and makes you excited to see him maybe be part of the crew, only to disappear and maybe head toward his own adventure, possibly in the bounty-hunting aspect.

The music in the film is enjoyable; it has a ton of emotional beats and serious action beats. And that adds to the complexity of the story they wanted to go into.

I can also understand why this film is having such a mixed reception with both Audiences and Critics (I am both a fan of DC and a critic). The story is complex. Still, I feel that because the film is 1 hour and 50 minutes, it feels short, and I believe if it was just a little bit longer, its theme of grief and loss might've hit me more. Another factor I would say is how the film ends; it felt like a good ending, but the comic, on the other hand, ends in a bittersweet way and, as I said, adds layers to an emotional story. I still enjoyed the movie, especially the way it addressed the sensitive subject of Sex Trafficking, which needs to be discussed more in films, especially superhero films. In which I think the film did a great job of showing us the hundreds of people who were imprisoned, and how that affects the journey toward the final choice Kara is faced with in the film.

Overall, this movie was good; it had a couple of issues that, for me, did not work. Still, I don't think it's a bad film; it has issues with the villain. However, I do think it's one of those films that may age well over time, especially because of its subject matter that needs to be spoken about more. This is just my opinion; however, when I was in the theater, some people did feel emotionally invested, and I did as well. Still, the film didn't hook me all the way and that's unfortunate because I really wanted to be and that may be due in part of reading the Woman of Tomorrow and seeing that Telenovela story be told, that when I saw the film it felt like we were so close to hitting that moment.

After heavy deliberation and writing this review, I give Supergirl a 7.5/10. I'm still excited to see what happens next, but I need DC to pull their A-game on the next project.

reviews.title: Dated, Clunky But Watchable
reviews.review:
Ignoring all the internet commentary and noise surrounding this superhero flick, Supergirl is just a dated and very average film. Had this come out in 2014, it may have been a hit when superheroes were really taking off in the world of cinema, but coming out in 2026, it feels horribly old, with every cliche in the book onscreen in almost every scene.

With MCU style quippy humour that never lets up, it's irritating that human moments are far and few between, with the lame jokes and tough guy lines taking precedent.

Visuals are a mixed bag of poor green screen, but then suddenly impressive landscapes filled with vivid colour. Good visuals and scenery are then overshadowed by some terrible music choices that add nothing to the film other than audible noise with ill-timed rock and pop tunes.

The villain is rubbish and very forgettable, at least Milly Alcock stays consistent in the role with rogue-ish charm, but she rarely gets the chance to truly shine in the role thanks to weak writing that has her trading one-liners and squaring off with henchmen.

Her co-star Eve Ridley needs to never act again, her wooden lifeless performance was genuinely a drain onscreen, she was irritating and tries to act tough but has the expression of a rock and the very little range, what a waste of time her character is too.

Action sequences are quite generous but lack impact despite some cool camerawork that seems to flow naturally with little cutting, but it's stuff we've seen before and done better.

Skip this one unless it's the only thing available to you.

reviews.title: Supergirl is a Fun But flawed step forward for the DCU
reviews.review:
After accidentally seeing the early reactions to Supergirl, I was worried. Fortunately, the movie turned out to be a really fun watch, though unfortunately also a bit of a mess.

The casting for the main characters is a real highlight. Milly Alcock as Supergirl and Jason Momoa as Lobo are genuinely great choices, and both characters are so compelling that they carry the movie even when it stumbles. I wish I could say the script was on that same level, but it is not.

Director Craig Gillespie clearly wanted this to feel like a James Gunn movie. You can see it especially in some of the action sequences, but it does not land as well as intended. The story is sometimes really great and sometimes feels rushed and all over the place. The movie can also be a bit predictable, which takes away some of the excitement. Visually, there are some truly spectacular shots, but ironically, some of the CGI in Superman is actually better. And where Superman gave me a genuine emotional connection, Supergirl never quite got there.

That said, the movie has plenty of great and funny moments, and despite its flaws it is still a really enjoyable watch.

I have seen polls on YouTube ranking Supergirl among the worst superhero movies of the last ten years. If you share that opinion, let me be clear: that is ridiculous. Supergirl is significantly more fun than last year's Fantastic Four, and more importantly, I actually cared about the characters. Something that has been missing from most superhero movies in recent years, with the exception of Superman.

I would definitely recommend seeing it in theaters. Just do not go in expecting it to match Superman. And as a step forward for the DCU and the characters they have introduced? This is genuinely exciting. After Supergirl, I cannot wait to see what comes next.

reviews.title: Far From Super But A Good Bit Better Than I'd Assumed
reviews.review:
It might have been to do with having low expectations but I rather enjoyed Supergirl. I didn't find it half as dour as some and appreciated the Mad Max-esque aesthetic and world that really hadn't worked for me in the trailers.

Milly Allcock is a likeable and charismatic lead; the plot is a somewhat over-simplistic but efficient revenge story/space adventure and the themes of imperfect heroism, revenge vs justice and survivors guilt are hardly groundbreaking but are done well enough. The run-time is sensible too.

It's pretty far from perfect with a thoroughly forgettable villain, decent looking but somewhat samey fight scenes, a few pacing issues, a fairly superfluous and tacked on feeling Lobo appearance as well as a bit of a stagey, occasionally wooden sounding performance from the young actress who plays Ruthye. I think the latter issue might be to do with accent struggles as the actress is from North East England and was playing the character with an RP accent that I occasionally caught her slipping out of.

Many seem to have a (largely inexplicable) bee in their bonnet about the rebooted DC films and in particular Superman, so this will no doubt get torn to shreds by shrieking man-children everywhere. Indeed, many seem to have gone all puritanical about a flawed main character drowning her sorrows while also engaging in the usual mental gymnastics to see Men being undermined at every turn. It is actually a pretty benign story about dealing with grief, trauma and survivors guilt while emphasizing heroism not needing perfection. It only handles those themes moderately well so doesn't really have the bandwidth or sophistication of writing for subtle anti-male subtexts too.

All in all, I thought it was a fine albeit pretty unremarkable film with one or two performances that deserved stronger material.

My 9 year old enjoyed the film a lot more than he did Superman, which was probably the biggest surprise for me given the less colourful palette and slightly more mature themes of this.

reviews.author: simonwalmsley

reviews.title: Thank God that I didn't read the comic
reviews.review:
I'm pretty glad that I did not read the comic, because most of the reviews I've heard is that its not as good, in fact in some areas a disappointment to the comic, but since I didn't read it, It don't matter. I do talk about Superman (2025) spoilers by the way, I mean duh:

I think my review will definitely be a near copy paste of more though because its simple Milly Alcock as Supergirl is great, I definitely liked her acting and I suppose yes, I liked her portrayal.

From the trailers and from the movie mainly she was shown as the Supergirl who's this Messy and Avoidant party girl using these parties, and constantly getting drunk as a coping mechanism from losing her planet and everyone she knew on Krypton.

Lobo might be the MVP, because Jason Momoa does have that sauce with this character and definitely should (and probably will) show up constantly throughout the DCU. I mean he just nailed Lobo.

Ruthye was not too bad of a side character. I think she was being hated on a bit too much from what I've heard. But again nothing special. There really is no comedy in this film also, I think.

Krem as the villain was definitely forgettable, nearly as forgettable as Dar-Benn (The Marvels Villain). I mean he didn't even feel like a main villain, felt like a side henchmen who gets screen time.

This definitely very much feels like a Phase 1 MCU movie, its solid, decent, nothing crazy, and maybe a bit forgettable.

In like the first 6th of the movie I definitely felt guardians of the galaxy vibes, and a bit of Suicide Squad (2021), the aliens, space adventure, Savage group (ravagers type) as an opposing force. Main character is messed up on the inside a lot (that part is specifically from Suicide Squad 21, and a bit from Guardians of the Galaxy 3).

I really liked all the flashbacks for Kara (not a spoiler, its in the trailer), How Krypton fell, her first interaction with her cousin. All that was very engaging even though how Krypton fell, and how Kara went to Earth there are some points I disagree on that's just my inner nerd, otherwise if I push that aside, it was still really engaging.

Since this is the 2nd movie in the DCU, also happens to be another member of the super-family. I have to compare it to Superman (2025), and I have to say this movie is obviously not as good. But I won't talk about everything Superman does better (which is a lot of things), but I am going to talk about mainly the 1 thing I thought it did better.

The Action: I thought the action in this movie had some really good action, only problem was Kara never faced a true opponent, if she fought someone like Zod, or Ultraman here, they could have cooked with the action. This movie definitely held itself back a bit by being a bit too generic, like Blue Beetle or Shazam Fury of the Gods, (also 2 DC movie).

The CGI people have mentioned saying its something like hit or miss. I personally thought the CGI overall was great, there were some pretty good cinematography moments, and since I did not read the comic, I'm not mad that its not nearly as good as the comic. I thought all the aliens looked great. The like flying moments, and the lasers they all mostly looked great. There might have been 1 or 2 moments with Kara flying that might be similar to the Flash CGI.

I loved having David Corenswet's Superman in this movie, the scenes he were in was actually longer than I thought. He just might be the greatest superhero/comic book casting of all time, he really does give that perfect Superman vibe.

It really is a shame that this is based off of the comic, because I'm sure the review would have been higher if it was not, and just its own thing. Which makes it even less likely people will see this movie in theatres. The studios behind the movie will consider anything above $300 Million as a win. That is less than half of what Superman made in total.

Which means its simple DC get that Batman movie script ready, we should have our Batman actor cast by the end of the year, green lit that Wonder Woman movie, a Flash movie, get it rolling folks. It really is simple I've heard it already, but use your heavy hitters, If there is a Batman movie, or a Superman movie, or a Wonder Woman movie, or a Flash movie, or any big heavy hitter like that, then people will show up.

Do it just like the MCU did. Iron Man, Hulk, Iron Man Sequel, Thor, Captain America, Avengers team with all previous hero movies' heroes. reviews.title: Milly Alcock: Woman of Tomorrow
reviews.review:
The movie delivers mostly on casting and technical execution. Milly Alcock is simply perfect as Kara and you can feel Jason Momoa waited a long time to transform into Lobo. The darker, space-western tone is a genuine breath of fresh air for the genre, and most individual scenes are well-crafted and confidently paced.

The film's central weakness, however, is inherited directly from the comic source material: motivation. Ruthye's revenge arc stays frustratingly surface-level, and Krem remains an almost complete cipher as his actions don't seem to be grounded in any motivation. To me this is the comic's and movie's weak spot, and no adaptation could fully paper over it.

Ultimately, I'm not sure the comic could have been adapted more faithfully for good or worse.
reviews.author: martin-otten

reviews.title: Superflop.
reviews.review:
Kara Zor-El spends her time partying and drowning her sorrows, attempting to forget her past. When the villainous Krem injures her dog, Kara teams up with an unlikely companion to take him on and help her beloved Krypto. A desperate effort to track down an antidote begins.

This is a remarkably slow-burning affair to start with, and it undeniably goes on way too long for what is ultimately a fairly thin premise. Reading the early reviews had me genuinely scratching my head; who on earth suggested all of those Mad Max comparisons, I certainly didn't see a similarity. The screenwriting is profoundly weak, and the narrative pacing moves at a glacial pace, it is a flat, uninspired atmosphere that even a massive Hollywood budget cannot mask. If the intention was to explore whether the audience is truly done with superhero movies-or if the genre is simply done with us-then this offering heavily tips the scales toward the latter.

Visually, the film flat-out fails to look good or capture the epic scale one should reasonably expect from a blockbuster of this magnitude. The cinematic colours are incredibly flat and often look inexplicably out of focus, proving once again that expensive digital effects absolutely cannot hide the glaring deficiencies of a poor script.

The film is mildly salvaged by its brief glimpses into the wider universe, and I genuinely enjoyed the early Superman and Krypton segments. However, the core character dynamics simply miss the mark; making Kara a bit of a slob was a definite choice, her transformation into the actual mantle of Supergirl completely failed to work for me. The fact it's proven to be a flop comes as no surprise.

Milly Alcock is a competent actress, but she is severely let down by how poorly developed the material is around her. The central villain is a total afterthought who barely feels like a threat, leaving you wondering why the creative team couldn't have put a little more effort into writing an engaging antagonist. Jason Momoa pops up as Lobo, but it is entirely the wrong tune for the character; he bizarrely looks less like an intergalactic bounty hunter and more like a bloke about to host a daytime television show about fixing up old cars. It is a thoroughly uneven, uninspiring cosmic misfire that struggles to justify its own existence.

3/10.

reviews.title: Honestly, not as bad as people made it out to be
reviews.review: While it's not the exact comic-book adaptation I'd been dreaming about for years, Supergirl is also nowhere near the disaster some online voices are calling it. I walked out feeling solidly entertained.. good enough for a 7/10. Milly Alcock delivers a committed, fiery performance as Kara Zor-El that gives the character real presence and edge. The visuals are often impressive too, with strong cosmic scope and some standout action sequences that actually have weight and creativity. Yes, it deviates from the source material in ways that will disappoint hardcore fans. Certain story choices, character beats, and structural shifts keep it from being the faithful adaptation some were hoping for. It's not reinventing the genre, and it doesn't fully satisfy the purist comic adaptation some wanted. But I genuinely don't see how people are calling this a terrible movie. It's a fun, well-acted superhero flick that respects the spirit of Supergirl while carving out its own lane. On a crowded summer slate full of loud blockbusters, this one actually has some entertaining value. It may not be perfect, but it's a worthwhile watch that entertains without insulting your intelligence. Solid debut for this version of Supergirl.

reviews.author: larsona_5

reviews.title: Horrendous
reviews.review:
I really wanted to love Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow. With Craig Gillespie from i Tonya directing and a premise about Kara Zor-El traveling through space alongside a young girl on a mission to save her poisoned dog, Krypto, it had all the ingredients for something fresh. Instead, it plays things frustratingly safe.

The biggest problem is the screenplay. It hints at interesting ideas but never commits to exploring them. Kara should be a fascinating character-a survivor carrying the trauma of losing an entire world-but the film mostly reduces her to a familiar "cool" heroine who drinks, cracks jokes, and fights. Those traits don't add much depth on their own, and the emotional complexity the story needs never really arrives.

The pacing doesn't help either. The film wanders through one generic space setting after another, filled with forgettable pirates and familiar sci-fi locations. Its central message that revenge can't erase pain is hardly groundbreaking, and the emotional climax feels more obligatory than earned.

The performances deserved better. Milly Alcock is charismatic and fully committed, while Eve Ridley brings genuine sincerity to her role. Both manage to rise above the material, even when the script gives them very little to work with.

Technically, the movie is competent but rarely impressive. The action is serviceable, and the visual effects are inconsistent. Krypto, despite being based on real canine movement, often looks distractingly artificial, making scenes built around his danger less effective than they should be.

Verdict: Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow is easy to follow, but not because it's layered or thoughtful. It's a polished yet formulaic superhero movie that never reaches the emotional or creative heights its premise promises, leaving two strong performances stranded in an otherwise unforgettable horrendous film.

reviews.title: Woman of Tomorrow

I've really been slacking when it comes to superhero-related comics as of late (with the exception of Absolute Batman, and I do plan on reading the other series from the Absolute universe).

It's a relief that we finally got a good adaptation for Supergirl. I swear, Kara has been some of the misused superheroes when it comes to majority of her comic book adaptations where she's typically dumbed down to the woman counterpart of Superman. Kara has always been much more complex and independent from Clark to outright make herself her own character able to be interesting on her own terms.

Only thing I didn't really care for was how the main antagonist was depicted, I feel like he could have been better. I'm not all too familiar with Krem in the comics so I can't really say he's a character I like to begin with, but for the sake of the movie on its own standards he felt like one of those throwaway villains we've been seeing in a lot of superhero adaptations. Jason Momoa was actually perfect for Lobo and it sucks that he was barely given enough screen time.

Kara's development was decent enough to be interesting. Ruth could have been better, and to be fair she did work for giving Kara the right push to actually be developed. However, outside of that she doesn't really do much to be that compelling. The revenge motive is all too familiar and we do not get enough to truly connect with Ruth or her family to even care about her journey.

I will be picking up a copy of Woman of Tomorrow soon.
reviews.author: CutlasSaber

reviews.title: "Woman of Tomorrow" With Yesterday's Problems
reviews.review:
"Supergirl" never quite rises above being just one of the many movies this year. It's certainly not one of those productions that will redefine the genre.

Technically speaking, "Supergirl" falls into that category of films where, a few months later, you struggle to remember more than two or three moments. It's definitely not the movie that will convince anyone that DC has finally found the magic formula.

Milly Alcock is fine as Kara Zor-El, but for now, I just don't feel much when watching her character.

The only small highlight is Jason Momoa as Lobo. Every time he appears on screen, the film gains a bit of energy...but only for about five minutes. Even then, I was expecting more from him. Momoa turns Lobo into one of the movie's most memorable elements. In many ways, he is the reason "Supergirl" rises above mediocrity and gains the spark it desperately needs...for a while.

The problem is that beyond that, the film doesn't offer much that truly stands out. The story serves its purpose but rarely manages to surprise, and the script is bland. The pacing is uneven, and the villain is one of the weakest aspects of the film, never becoming a particularly convincing or intimidating threat. There simply isn't enough here to make the overall experience feel special.

In the end, "Supergirl" is a forgettable movie. It offers a few strong performances and several enjoyable moments. However, it rarely reaches the level it is clearly aiming for. Milly Alcock does a good job as Kara, while Jason Momoa outright steals every scene he appears in as Lobo.

Beyond that, though, the film feels more like another attempt by DC to prove that this time they really do have a plan. Maybe they do - "Supergirl" just isn't the proof of it.

It's watchable, but not particularly rewatchable, and it's unlikely to be among the superhero movies that people will still be thinking about by the end of the year.
reviews.author: MiroslavKyuranov

reviews.title: I love it!! I can really feel Cara's charisma
reviews.review:
I went into "Supergirl" with low expectations after reading some mixed reviews, but I ended up completely invested in it. I actually love it!

What really resonated with me is the confusion and raw pain of its coming-of-age theme. Kara is just celebrating her 23rd birthday. The movie does a fantastic job of showing that no matter how powerful you are-even if you can fly or possess immense strength-you still have every right to feel exhausted, vulnerable, and to cry.

It beautifully captures the different paths of pain that everyone walks, and the limits of our own abilities. It reminds us that we all have moments of strength and weakness, which ultimately lead to understanding, trust, and relying on one another. It made me realize that even if a problem seems small to others, we aren't always strong enough to handle it alone.

Ever since "Superman," I've loved how these movies show that even a god-like hero can get totally wrecked and still display the same core humanity as the rest of us. Supergirl carries that exact same vibe.

On top of the emotional depth, I loved how the movie expands the lore into a true universal scale-complete with diverse alien lifeforms, fun cosmic humor, space travel, and the tragic downfall of planets. It didn't bother me at all that the villains felt a bit "underwhelming" or secondary, because honestly, our problems always seem small once we manage to move past them.

I just love the perspective this movie gives us... that at the end of the day, we are all just walking wounds-or perhaps, flying ones.

reviews.title: A sincere apology to Milly Alcock and the producers!
reviews.review:
I finally went to see this movie because my 14 year old daughter insisted that we should go see it.

I must admit that I had sort of jumped on the hate bandwagon for all the wrong reasons. I grew up with Helen Slater's version, then fully embraced Melissa Benoist's. When the trailer for the 2026 movie came out, I immediately disliked it. "Nothing majestic about it, which is sad" were my usual comments on the posts regarding this movie.

I was wrong and I apologize.

It's not the idealistic, beauty magazine cover version of the character, but it has heart and she actually becomes more and more beautiful and likeable as character development and story move forward.

Milly's performance was spot on and she carried the entire movie, which brings me to the unfortunate faults it definitely has.

The biggest one is that it's too dark. Almost every scene is dark and grim, which sort of fits the inner turmoil of the character, but many parts of the plot could have featured much more appealing surroundings.

Second, the main antagonist is totally uninteresting and therefore forgettable. The actor is not to blame, he tries hard, but the character is just poorly written.

Lobo was ok but I sincerely expected better.

Also, there are too many weird side characters that populate this movie that fall flat and look like Star Wars rip-offs.

But overall, a decent movie. And no, it didn't rely on the dog, as many would thing. It actually appears for about 5 minutes at best.

I'm actually looking forward for a sequel now. This Supergirl is ready to shine now that she's found herself!

reviews.title: Supergirl - A Darker Take on Kara
reviews.review:
I went into Supergirl a little nervous because of the mixed reactions after seeing early previews and because I grew up with the CW series. I also really enjoyed Superman, and really loved seeing all my childhood favorite characters in Superman. I went to an early preview because I was hoping to have similar feelings, and I left the theater surprised in a good way.

It's not that kind of movie, and I think that's the point. It's much darker, and it focuses more on Kara dealing with the loss of Krypton. One thing I always wondered, even watching the CW show, is how she could be so upbeat all the time. This version doesn't ignore what she went through. She remembers Krypton, her family, and her life there, and the grief actually feels like part of her character.

I liked that. It made her feel more real and grounded.

I also liked the dynamic with Ruthye. It gave Kara a chance to reflect on her own experience and offer someone else guidance in a way that felt meaningful.

If you go in expecting Superman, it's going to feel very different. But if you're open to a darker take on Kara and her story, there's a lot here that works.

reviews.title: Try & Kara More
reviews.review:
Okay, the original 1984 Supergirl spinoff set the bar SO INCREDIBLY LOW, all these people had to do was...make a movie to surpass it. They more than exceeded their goal.

Once again, I'm like in the 10% of the world/critic's corner/audience reaction and I unapologetically say: I really, REALLY liked this movie. That said, it absolutely wasn't perfect. In fact...

It wasn't anywhere near as good as 2025's Superman. Like lightyears away from that DCU intro film. It wasn't anywhere near as good as the Guardians of the Galaxy they were mimicking. And it was the same ole story of both revenge and redemption. And yet, I had a blast.

Full disclosure: while I grant this 4/5 stars, it's at the vey lowest point at 4/5 stars. Truthfully, this may range at 3½/5, but I never had a bad time here, WHATSOEVER, so 4/5 it is.

Survivor's Guilt Supergirl is drinking herself to oblivion after she survives the remaining Kryptonian extraterrestrial humanoid species when a young, fellow-grief-stricken gal enters her life. When our title character shares a common enemy with this gal, they have a deadline to evolve both storylines.

Reversing a bit, when I saw Superman 5x in theatres last summer - yeah, mock me, I actually didn't like either Krypto the Dog or his "master," Kara who made her post-credit debut. I knew the next DCU movie would be hers and frankly, I wasn't stoked about it. I was wrong.

She 100% grew on me, almost instantly. The House of the Dragon star had the right amount of charisma to win us over even though she was the opposite end of Kal-El, aka Clark aka Superman. I even liked how they swapped Kal-El's origin with hers and they both ended up at opposite ends. Trust me, it won't make sense until you see both movies.

This was definitely weird and there was SO MUCH World(s) Building here that didn't really matter. Since the story/journey is so familiar and done 100,000 times before, it's easy to just get on board.

This wouldn't be a major repeat-viewing for me. I will probably watch again on Streaming or if I buy this on Blu. And I am happy we're past this space race, learning Supergirl.

Just freaking train that dog. The schtick has gotten old fast. Yeah, he's rambunctious on purpose, but it's been done to death now in two movies. It's long past cute. While I love his introduction last movie and that they had the unneutered balls to have Krypto the Dog in a Live-Action, Official Superman movie, this dog NEEDS DISCIPLINE!

***

Final Thoughts: Funny, when I left the theatre, I heard a group rate this movie. One half gave it 8/10 and the other half, 5/10 and that lowered rating was specifically because this had Jason Momoa in it. I had to laugh to myself. I simply cannot blame them. The overuse of Jason Momoa is irritating. Much like the overuse of Zendaya, The Rock and...MOST DEFINITELY, Pedro Pascal. Hollywood...there are soooo many up'n'coming stars. Stop trying to be safe.

reviews.title: I'm afraid I didn't enjoy it, at all
reviews.review:
Oh Dear!

I didn't hate on 2025's 'Superman' as bad as some did. It was messy, with too many characters for a new start to the DC Universe, but I really like David Corenswet in the role, even if he was beaten up constantly for the entire film. It was okay, not a patch on the first two Christopher Reeve films but okay.

On the other hand, in my opinion, 'Supergirl' is awful. The script is painfully thin, everything looked horrid colour and aesthetic wise, the CGI and green screen made everything look unreal and plastic, I didn't like Milly Alcock in the role and I found the character insufferable and unlikeable, I liked Krypto in 'Superman' but my love for CGI doggy has already worn thin, Jason Mamoa was okay as Lobo and should have been in the film more but he's just playing Jason Mamoa and Krem was just dull and generic for a villain. It's not much of a review but I never connected with or felt anything whilst watching it.

Craig Gillespie has directed some okay films, this isn't one of them, there is no way writer Ana Nogueira should have been put in charge of writing this with such a limited résumé (that's if she did write it an wasn't just hired as a scapegoat) and I think James Gunn & Peter Safran will be gone sooner rather than later. They were never the right people to be studio heads and I thought that as soon as they were hired.

I'm not review bombing and I'm not swayed by political opinion or in a particular 'group' of people. I love films, genuinely want to enjoy them and my reaction afterwards is a true opinion of how I feel after watching something, not what I'm forced into saying or frightened to say because of backlash. Having said that I am very tired of the Hollywood machine turning out dud after dud, especially when they cost so much money and it's why I'm so pleased that indie filmmakers have broken through and been successful this year.

People will scream & shout, they'll blame 'superhero fatigue', The World Cup and 'toxic fandom' but I can guarantee you that 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' will be huge next month, regardless of the script quality.

I was never a huge fan of comics when I was younger but I did buy my fair share and when the films started to finally come out with decent effects I was over the moon and have embraced them ever since, even if the quality of writing has dropped off in recent years.

I found 'Supergirl' to be an insipid, boring mess and I was sitting in a virtually empty cinema, which isn't good for the first Friday. The only positive I got out of it was that, for someone with a disintegrating spine, the seats in these places are much more comfortable than they used to be!

reviews.title: Supertrash
reviews.review:
Supergirl is the kind of blockbuster that mistakes noise for excitement and spectacle for storytelling. The plot lurches from one set piece to another with little sense of momentum, while the characters feel underdeveloped and emotionally hollow. Despite a capable cast, the script gives them very little to work with beyond generic dialogue and predictable conflicts.

The humor rarely lands, the villain lacks any real presence, and the visual effects fluctuate between impressive and surprisingly unfinished. Most disappointingly, the film never establishes why this version of Supergirl should be compelling. Instead of delivering a fresh perspective, it leans heavily on familiar superhero clichés without adding anything memorable.

By the time the credits rolled, it felt less like watching the beginning of an exciting new chapter and more like sitting through a two-hour trailer for future projects. A forgettable, formulaic superhero film that never finds its own identity.

I was very impressed by how well they handled the complex story line, focusing on things like grief and feelings of not belonging, and they didn't shy away from some very real feeling darker themes with the villains.

reviews.title: What a shame.
reviews.review:
I was really looking forward to Supergirl, but I honestly thought it was a very bad movie. Milly Alcock is good as Kara and I have no complaints about her portrayal of the character. Some of the spaceship and alien designs are also excellent, and Kara and Lobo look very close to their comic counterparts. Unfortunately, almost everything else falls apart.

The biggest problem is the screenplay. It constantly establishes rules and motivations only to ignore them a few scenes later.

The movie opens by establishing that Kara celebrates her birthday on a red sun planet because it suppresses Kryptonian powers, allowing her to get drunk, feel pain, and generally experience life like a normal person. When Krypto is poisoned there, we're told he'll die unless he receives an antidote. The obvious solution is to fly him to a yellow sun, since the movie itself has already established that Kryptonians regain their powers almost instantly under yellow sunlight. Instead, the film claims moving him would spread the poison faster, which makes little sense. Later, Kara is poisoned with the same substance while powered and simply drinks milk to throw it up. Even later, she's injected with crystal kryptonite that supposedly attacks her on a cellular level, yet yellow sunlight immediately cures it. The film ends up implying that ordinary poison is a greater threat to Kryptonians than kryptonite, effectively reducing Superman's most iconic weakness to a minor inconvenience.

The flashback to Krypton's destruction is equally inconsistent. Kara tells Ruthye that "Krypton didn't die in a single day; the gods weren't so merciful," only for the next scene to show the planet going from perfectly normal to exploding within about an hour. We're told Kara's father and Superman's father warned Krypton's government that the core was unstable, but an incredibly advanced civilization somehow couldn't verify the claim independently. Kara's father also builds a bubble containing part of the city that survives in space for roughly twenty years, where Kara grows up normally until kryptonite from the ground begins poisoning everyone. The movie has already established that Kryptonians can survive in space and regain their powers under yellow suns, so why doesn't anyone simply leave the bubble or relocate to a yellow sun system?

Lobo is another major disappointment. Kara introduces him as an immortal, terrifying bounty hunter with a god complex, yet he ends up contributing almost nothing to the story. He's shown effortlessly killing enemies before somehow ending up imprisoned by those same enemies after they've already teleported away from him. He later claims he intentionally allowed himself to be captured, but the film explicitly shows that he couldn't escape without Ruthye rescuing him. If you removed Lobo from the script entirely, almost nothing about the plot, themes, or ending would change. His only objective in the film is hunting down one of Krem's goons, he's not interested in the leader of the group.

The opening scene with Ruthye's family is equally confusing. The family has supposedly known for years that raiders would come for the family sword. When Krem arrives, they immediately offer him exactly what he wants. After Ruthye's brother startles him, Krem kills the boy. The parents attack him and are killed in return. Then Krem leaves without taking the sword or killing Ruthye, despite later being described as someone who murdered the family "for sport." The movie never clearly establishes what his actual objective was. If he wanted the sword, he abandoned it. If he wanted to massacre the family, he inexplicably spared Ruthye. Later revelations about his gang only make his behavior even less coherent. Ruthye's father's last action wasn't to save her or kill the villains, instead he just destroys their ship for no logical reason, leaving them stranded in the planet for one day until they steal Kara's effortlessly.

The sword itself ends up being almost irrelevant despite how important the opening makes it seem. It appears to be the object everyone is willing to kill for, yet afterward almost nobody cares about it. Krem barely pursues it, Kara doesn't care about it, Lobo doesn't care about it, and Ruthye is willing to give it away as payment to anyone who helps her kill Krem. It ends up functioning as little more than the weapon she happens to carry.

The movie's themes are also contradictory. Ruthye's story revolves around vengeance, and Kara repeatedly insists that killing Krem would change Ruthye forever. Yet Kara herself kills numerous people throughout the film without hesitation and ultimately kills Krem with Ruthye's own sword after convincing Ruthye not to do it herself. The movie never explores any consequences for Kara or suggests she regrets killing. Superman behaves similarly in this cinematic universe, so killing clearly isn't presented as morally unacceptable. As a result, the central message about revenge and violence feels completely undermined by the story's own events.

The supporting cast also struggles. Milly Alcock carries the film well, but Lobo, Krem, and Ruthye all gave performances that felt flat and unconvincing to me.

Even the art direction is inconsistent. The spaceships and alien species are imaginative, but Ruthye and most of the villains are visually anonymous. Ruthye looks like she could disappear into a crowd of background characters, while the villains all blend together as generic Mad Max-style raiders. Characters who should stand out, like Krem himself or the man Lobo is hunting, are visually indistinguishable from random extras.

In the end, I don't think the movie fails because of comic book accuracy or because it takes creative liberties. It fails because it repeatedly introduces ideas, rules, objects, and themes without following through on them. Characters stop pursuing their stated goals, the world stops obeying its own logic, and the moral message changes depending on what the next scene requires. Milly Alcock deserved a much stronger script.

* Jason Mamoa was there for some reason?

reviews.title: A classically fun James Gunn superhero film, just with a convoluted ending.
reviews.review:
This movie is a great choice for summer entertainment, especially if you go in with low expectations.

The film has all the classic James Gunn fingerprints all over it. With the classic James-Gunn-Superhero-Hits:

An impressive world-building with a variety of creatures and species from different planets.

A subplot involving someone's pet that will resonate with animal lovers and likely encourage them to rewatch "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3."

And, most of all, not just one, but four (yes, four) classic James Gunn fight scenes. You know, some fast-paced, slow-motion, in-and-out bangers, each accompanied by a catchy song from the past. I loved these from James Gunn, but four is excessive. I'm starting to wonder if he's a one-hit wonder.

Supergirl's origin story offers a touching and somewhat dramatic scene amid all the action, which was, for me, the crown jewel of the film. The scene not only showcases Miley Alcock and the actors who play her parents in their acting roles, but it also brought a bit of a tear to my eye.

However, my two nitpicks were the film's convoluted ending. There's so much happening in the final battle. It feels messy.

Perhaps the biggest surprise (for me) was Supergirl trying to convince her friend of the classic lesson that "revenge isn't the answer," only to turn around and take the villain's life herself. This perplexed me to say the least-practice what you preach, Supergirl.

Overall, it was a good film. It looked great, and each actor performed their role well. However, I believe the plot could have been tightened up a bit.

reviews.title: Super Brawler

Milly Alcock does a great job conveying sadness and inner turmoil from losing loved ones and fighting for the one you love. However the punch-drunk character loses it appeal pretty quickly and it kind of doesn't make sense given how initially distressed she was about finding the cure for Krypto. The pacing was way better than the Superman movie; it felt much less choppy and the scenes more connected. The trailers also did a much better job of not showing the entire story this time. As for Lobo, great to see the character but there were times were his delivery felt a little campy -- kind of like seeing Channing Tatum as Gambit: Great for fan-service, but something felt off. The writing didn't lean too heavily on crass jokes or sexist remarks like the Superman movie, it was refreshing to see open criticism for the name "Supergirl" vs "Superman" and similar comments throughout the movie, although at times was stifled or the main gist left unspoken. Personally, it feels like a better movie than Superman, but for the DC Film series, it felt like a one-shot graphic novel.

reviews.author: SelinaT-39

reviews.title: A disastrous script harms plenty of things that actually work.
reviews.review:
It was thankfully something I didn't find as bad as others have... but Supergirl is flawed. I really think it all comes down to the writing. Visually, it's not ghastly like an Ant-Man 3 or anything, and I think it's sometimes striking. A level of visual consistency with last year's Superman without it feeling and looking exactly like last year's Superman was nice. Speaking of that film, I liked the few scenes David Corenswet had here. I liked most of the cast, honestly. It was fun to see Jason Momoa having fun and Milly Alcock is great, considering what she has to work with. She's right for this role, so I'd definitely want to push back against some of the naysayers as far as the casting and acting goes, but this script wasn't right for her, or anyone, really.

This is badly written. It just is. Or if it was well-written, an editor could potentially have mishandled all the material they had to work with and fudged it up that way. Even then, there are some clunky edits and scenes starting a little too abruptly early on, but I stopped thinking about editing problems, at a point. It just feels like more of a screenplay thing. The arc the titular character goes through makes sense on paper, but you don't really feel it during the film itself, even if the actors come close to selling it.

I'm not sure any jokes here I actually found funny. Maybe a couple of Corenswet's lines. But it tries to be funny a lot in the first half and nothing is well-timed or properly funny. And the humor stands out against an unusually grim tone whenever the villains are focused on. I think they're needlessly nasty for this kind of movie, and they're not even nasty in a good way. They're just underdeveloped and forgettable, even if, in the moment, they're jarringly brutal. It's the worst of both worlds, in that they don't make an impression and yet somehow, paradoxically, they also overwhelm the parts of the film that occasionally work.

Food analogy time! We've got good ingredients here, for the most part. If we're making a cake, everything but the flour is high-quality or promising. But the flour is off. Flour being this off is rare, but it happens. And it ruins the cake, at its foundation. The icing is good. The icing is almost everything except the flour. The writing is the flour. The flour expired years ago. They should not have cooked with it.

This does not tank the new DC universe, but it's a pretty big pothole the whole thing has driven into. I would imagine they rushed the writing of this, wanting to keep the momentum going just a year on from Superman. The other parts of this movie weren't so much rushed, or mishandled, but they were let down by the writing. You can't okay a script like this and not think it needs some serious revision. It's quite surprising, and honestly really frustrating, since so many other people involved in this felt like they were giving it their all (most of the actors, the effects artists, the prop/set people and so on). The people at the top, and the writers, have to do quite a bit more than this going forward, if they want to keep it all working into the future.

reviews.author: Gip35

reviews.title: Super Disappointing Screenplay
reviews.review:
Supergirl (2026) was one of the most disappointing superhero movies I've seen in a while, because it wastes a great lead actress inside a script that never finds its identity. Milly Alcock brings attitude, emotion, and presence to Kara, but the writing around her feels thin and unfocused.

The biggest issue is the villain. Krem never feels like a main antagonist more like a side character who accidentally wandered into the climax. There's no weight, no tension, and no real connection to Kara's journey. When your villain feels forgettable, the entire story loses impact.

And then there's Lobo. He steals every scene he's in, has more personality than the actual villain, and honestly should've been the main antagonist. Instead, he's treated like a chaotic side character with no real purpose. The movie had a chance to give Kara a villain who matched her energy, but it didn't take it.

The colored suns gimmick doesn't help either. Instead of adding depth or meaning, it feels like random cosmic decoration that changes the vibe without adding anything to the story.

Overall, Supergirl (2026) is a 4 out of 10 for me not the worst movie ever, but definitely a huge missed opportunity.

reviews.title: Disappointing slog

reviews.title: Another superhero misfire
reviews.review:
I love superhero movies, probably because real-life, quite frankly, sucks. Escapism - both the fun, silly kind, or the more serious, tragic kind (I'm thinking something like "Watchmen") - in this day and age, is important, and no matter if a superhero film is dealing with true-to-life topics or simply having fun with its subject matter, I enjoy spacing out for two hours while watching super-powered people punch things. With that said, "Supergirl" has a fun climax where super-powered people punch things.

That's about all "Supergirl" has going for it, which pains me to say. After the unabashedly hopeful, colorful, cartoony, and comedic take on "Superman" in James Gunn's new DC Universe, "Supergirl" tries and fails to emulate Gunn's signature style while retaining next to none of it. Sure, there are needle-drops aplenty - maybe one or two of them worked for me, but most of them felt distracting, unnecessary, and ill-placed. There are slick and stylish action sequences, too - the conclusion was a stand out, and especially in 3D looked quite stunning. Unfortunately, unlike James Gunn-directed films, all the other action sequences in "Supergirl" are incomprehensible; for some reason, the action always occurs in the background while the camera focuses on someone in the foreground, ensuring that you will never get a clear look at what's happening, and who it is happening to. And compared to "Superman's" color overload, "Supergirl" feels weirdly drab, muted, and generic.

What really makes "Supergirl" feel so bizarre as the second entry in this newly revamped DCU is for how small-stakes and depressing of a story it is. I don't need superhero movies to have earth-shattering stakes every time (in fact, I'd prefer they didn't), and I don't need superhero movies to always be happy-go-lucky, but for the second entry in a brand new universe that's purpose is to introduce an important new hero, the whole thing feels sort of "eh" and unlikable. For one, the story of Supergirl trying to rescue her dog fails to make an emotional connection with the viewer, because said dog, Krpyto, isn't really in the film a whole ton, and there are no real sequences of Supergirl and Krypto bonding or interacting in a meaningful way. Secondly, besides the movie already dealing with a tough to swallow subject - a dying dog - the film also has its villain act maybe just a tad bit too ruthlessly for a PG-13 summer blockbuster, shockingly killing parents in front of their children, and vice versa. Sitting in a theatre with at least one very young little girl, I felt kind of uncomfortable and even a bit disturbed at what I was seeing on screen.

Milly Alcock makes a fine Supergirl, but our introduction to her as a rude alcoholic didn't endear me to her as much as the movie probably wanted to. I'm a fan of Milly the actress, but her version of Supergirl didn't feel like a hero that people can necessarily look up to at this point in time. I know the purpose of this film is to show evolution and build up to Supergirl's heroism, but I couldn't shake the feeling of how odd it was as an intro to Supergirl. Having this character drink and party might appeal to some, but certainly not all, and for whatever reason, it did nothing for me. The film does attempt to explain what turned Supergirl into the cynical drunk she is, but this explanation occurs oddly placed in the middle of the film, taking away the emotional resonance; I think this movie would've been more dramatically impactful if it took place in chronological order instead of having flashbacks peppered throughout.

Overall, I thought that "Supergirl" was "mid," as the kids say. I mean, I just really feel kind of indifferent toward this. I didn't hate it, but I didn't really like it. I saw a teaser for this movie, quoting things such as "the most fun movie of the summer" and "an entertaining thrill ride." I wish that was the case, but for that to be true, "Supergirl" would have first had to be both thrilling and entertaining; it is too often neither. Tonally confused, visually dull, and needlessly dark, "Supergirl" is yet another superhero misfire.
