reviews.title: A Disappointing Step Back for the New DCU
reviews.review:
After really enjoying Superman, I had high hopes for Supergirl. Unfortunately it's nowhere near one of DC's worst movies, but it's also far from being a great start for the next chapter of the new DCU.

The biggest weakness is easily Krem. He never feels threatening or charismatic, and he barely has any dialogue. Most of the time, he is just walking around or eating. For the main antagonist of a Supergirl movie, that is just not enough. I never felt like Supergirl was facing a truly dangerous opponent.

What I did like was the basic idea behind Supergirl herself. She is clearly different from Superman. She is bitter, damaged, and has basically given up on being the kind of hero people expect her to be. That could have made for a really interesting character study. Sadly, the script does not explore it nearly well enough. I still think Milly Alcock has the potential to be a great Supergirl, but she is held back here by weak writing.

Another thing that really bothered me was how badly the movie seems to want to be Guardians of the Galaxy. Songs are thrown into scenes to make them feel fun or stylish, but most of the time they just feel completely out of place. Since Supergirl does not really see Earth as her home, the constant use of Earth music feels especially forced. It comes across like the movie is desperately trying to copy James Gunn's style without understanding why it worked in the first place.

The action is actually decent. There is a lot happening on screen, so the movie is not boring visually. The CGI is uneven in a few places, but overall it is fine. The issue is that some of the action scenes are weakened by awkward music choices or strange direction that undercuts the moment instead of elevating it.

One thing I genuinely enjoyed was Lobo. Jason Momoa brings exactly the kind of energy I would want from that character. He does not have a huge role, but every time he shows up, the movie becomes more entertaining. His scenes are easily among the highlights.

What really frustrated me, though, was the way the movie handles Supergirl's powers. The script constantly looks for excuses to weaken her. She gets poisoned, loses her strength, ends up under different suns, or just forgets abilities that could solve problems instantly. Because of that, Crim never feels powerful. It feels more like the movie has to constantly nerf Supergirl just so the plot can keep going.

The ending was especially disappointing. After spending most of the film as a cynical, broken character who does not really want to be a hero, Supergirl suddenly gives a moral speech about revenge being wrong. The problem is that this decision immediately leads to more innocent people dying. That makes the message feel not only unearned, but almost ridiculous. Her sudden moral high ground does not feel like real character growth. It feels like the script forced it in because the movie needed a lesson.

The movie is not a complete disaster. It has solid action, a lead actress with real potential, and a fun version of Lobo. But it is dragged down by weak writing, a forgettable villain, predictable storytelling, and a strange need to copy better movies. After the promising start with Superman, this feels like a clear step backward.

reviews.title: The real villain was the script
reviews.review:
For context, I don't care about the drama surrounding the actress. I went in knowing barely anything about the plot of the movie and having seen only one trailer and a TV clip, but nothing more. Going in, I had decent expectations. I was hearing mixed things; some were saying the script was pretty bland, others that the movie itself was bland, and many said it wasn't good at all. After gathering my thoughts, I'd like to give my honest, unbiased review, and give a small comparison to the 2025 Superman movie.

I'll start with the good, since there isn't that much of it: The visuals are stunning. The space travel, the planetary shots, and the scenery really hit.

Some of the humor actually lands. If you're someone who's bored of the cliché humor most superhero movies try to force on you, this movie has some genuinely funny moments and characters.

Superman really carried this movie; his scenes were really good. (And that's not a good thing at all in my opinion, more on that later.)

Lobo is a pretty good character, and his intro is pretty good.

The Krypton flashback is OK; I think that's the most emotionally tied to the characters you'll feel.

When Kara is first exposed to the yellow sun at the start of the movie and she gets her powers, that scene is really good and honestly pushed my expectations higher for the rest of the movie.

Now for the bad: The plot and the premise of this movie are ridiculously bad. You feel almost nothing. There is no mystery, no twists, no tension, and you will feel almost no emotional tie to the characters.

Ruthye was given more screen time than the main protagonist herself. Why? And throughout the whole movie, I just couldn't bring myself to care about this character one bit. Actually, anytime she had a scene, I wanted to punch myself in the gut. Her character is ridiculously generic. And just because the movie jokes about how boring and dull her mission is doesn't make her character any less boring. She was so dull. I don't get the heavy emphasis on her. I doubt she'll even be back in future movies. And how on earth was she able to overpower one of Krem's goons? Looking back, why was she even in the movie? She didn't add anything to Kara's arc, her story was redundant, and it was mostly Superman flashbacks that advanced her journey to self discovery.

Why are they doubling down on the Superman conqueror nonsense? Was this all just to make Kara look better? To show that her parents aren't as evil? It seems like a poor attempt to give her character more moral superiority over Superman.

Where is the score? Was there even a score? I can't remember. There is nothing memorable about it. The 2025 Superman movie had a really good soundtrack, Man of Steel had Hans Zimmer, and even Superman Returns with all its issues had a beautiful score. This literally had nothing memorable. Midway through the movie, I realized it.

Lobo was a generic, nonchalant tough guy and funny guy. He had a good intro but was very useless throughout the movie. His scenes were OK.

Repetitive plot. Aside from being bland, it's just so repetitive. Fight scene, jokes, long boring conversations with Ruthye, save Ruthye, repeat.

So many scenes in this movie keep dragging out. There is so much talk that literally doesn't add anything to the plot of the movie, and it made me want to punch myself, especially the scenes with Ruthye. In Superman 2025, the only part that kind of dragged out was the interview scene, but even that wasn't all that bad. With this one, it's like 80 percent of the movie is just meaningless dialogue.

The villain is disgustingly weak. He poses no threat at all, everything he does is comedic, he's not very strong, not very smart, and just goofy overall. I honestly thought he was just a side character at the start of the movie and was kind of disappointed when I found out he's the main antagonist.

What's the deal with sound in space? Did the writers not take basic physics at school? One scene we get sound in full force, and the other complete silence and I'm not entirely sure if it's for dramatic effects or what but it's goofy.

Does Kryptonite just grow on trees in this universe? Why would this generic villain have access to one of the rarest rocks in the universe? Krypton is literally dust. And how would he even know Kryptonite is deadly to Kryptonians? Krem doesn't come off as all that bright, and yet he has access to Kryptonite AND made a fully functional weapon out of it? Sure, buddy. Kryptonite should be the final trump card against a Kryptonian, but it feels like in this movie, anyone can have it if they want it badly enough.

Superman carried this movie, and that's not a good thing. This is a Supergirl movie. There shouldn't even be a Superman, or maybe just a little, but they gave him like 10 minutes of screen time because I'm guessing they knew the script was incredibly weak. His scenes were really good though, and they had me wishing I was actually watching a Superman sequel instead of this snoozefest.

One of the biggest issues with the movie is the actress herself. She's just not charismatic at all. Superman 2025 was significantly more charismatic, both in his own movie and this one. I don't know if it was the actress or the script she was given, but it felt lacking. For example, in the flashback to Krypton, her crying scene ALMOST hit, but not quite. I just couldn't feel the depth of "hey, my whole reality is coming to an end, my people and parents are dying, this isn't good." It just didn't hit at all. And when her father puts her in the pod to send her to Earth? Man. I expected screaming, yelling, trying not to get in, her father forcing her in, an actually heartbreaking moment. But no, she seems empty being in there. You can call it shock, but I'd rather call it lazy acting or a lazy script. It was just so bad. For comparison, when the Viltrumites in Invincible were getting eradicated, you could feel the depth of destruction and death significantly more.

So much action slop. Explosion here, building destruction there, gunshots, loud noises. And don't get me started on Supergirl's action scenes.

Supergirl's action scenes: Damn. All she does is kick, punch, throw, and laser. Repeat. Kick, punch, throw, laser, repeat. Where are the martial arts? Why can't we see more detailed fighting? And the amount of times they switch frames when there's a fight... It's really not captivating at all. Punch, switch, laser, switch... I would just find myself checking my phone throughout. The action scenes are super loud, there is so much meaningless slop going on in the background, and when she actually fights, it's super mediocre; she has no fighting skill at all. Take away her powers, and it's like a drunk trying to compete in an MMA fight.

The best way I can describe this movie is that going in, you expect to eat good food at a 5 star restaurant. They serve you really fine bread and butter, and you just can't wait to dine on their main dishes. But you keep waiting, and the server comes back with some more bread and butter. OK fine, it's cool. Then more bread and butter. Then more bread and butter, till you wanna slam your head on the table and go eat out of a Wendy's dumpster.

Even Superman couldn't save this movie. I wish we got a Superman 2 movie instead of this. I actually saw that movie more than once and enjoyed it.

5.5/10.

Honestly, nothing about this film was awful. But other than Milly Alcock, none of it was particularly good either. The result is just a highly average and forgettable superhero flick.

reviews.title: Supergirl has personality to spare, but she still needs a more memorable journey.
reviews.review:
Supergirl is basically DC saying, "Okay, Superman was all about hope and hugs; now let's go for the dust, booze, vomit, bar fights, and Jason Momoa screaming like he was born to do it." And honestly? It works better than it should.

The movie has a distinct identity within this new DCU. It's part space road movie, part punk western, part Guardians of the Galaxy after spending a week lost in the Mad Max desert. Milly Alcock is the standout here: she portrays Kara as someone who's broken, impulsive, funny, and trying not to fall apart in the middle of the galaxy.

The problem is that the film doesn't always keep up with her energy. The villain is generic, some subplots fall flat, and the visual effects are hit-or-miss. Still, when Supergirl embraces the protagonist's chaos, grit, and rebelliousness, it delivers a fun adventure. It's not a perfect flight, but Kara has already arrived with a bang.

reviews.title: Borderline Unwatchable
reviews.review:
5/10, heavily considered giving it a 4/10. The main issue was that there was massive plot holes / inconsistencies in the story.

Firstly, and most importantly, if she really really cared about her dog, then Supergirl would have 1. Not taken the young girl with her. It is not only obviously extremely dangerous for the young human girl, but also quite clearly something that would slow her down as she could not travel and survive things that Supergirl could. Given the tight deadline to get the antidote to her dog, this was extremely unwise and highly unrealistic.

2. At least try to enlist the help of someone powerful like Superman even if they would say they are busy.

There were many other flaws I noticed throughout the movie, not all of which I can remember. I will provide some of the ones I can remember. Towards the end, after being shot with darts that inject kryptonite into her, mere seconds after being (predictably) saved by the motorcycle guy, she regained some of her powers that allowed her to shoot the lazerbeams. During this period of time, she also burned a massive whole with her beams to free the wives that were being held captive. These women instantly ran across the hole that she created which, unless her beams possess the unique quality of instantly cooling down whatever they touch after they stop incinerating it, would be far too hot for humans to simply run across.

There were many more, but this was a common theme where the decision and actions of characters would make little sense. Lots of these issues did have potential answers that I thought of, however they were never even attempted to be explained away. There is only so many times I can happily accept a highly unlikely potential solution, like her beams possessing the quality of instant cooling, as fact when its not even stated in the first place. Another example of this is opponents deciding to not give finishing, or at least incapacitating blows, to one another and then turning their back on them and being surprised when they get attacked again. This could be because they didnt want to kill, but that does not explain not at least incapacitating them. That could be because they think they have aura doing so, or they want to assert dominance, and while these reasons would still irk me as I do not think they are particularly good, they would still satisfy me if they were at least given as explanations.

Despite this, some fighting scenes, particularly during the final fight, were rather enjoyable. Furthermore, Supergirl deciding to kill the main antagonist at the end was a redeeming quality for me as I expected a far more wholesome decision.

The main reason for the low rating, and why I heavily considered <5 stars, was that I was nodding off in the cinema at times. I never actually fell asleep properly, but I would fall asleep and have spasms such as kicks that wake me up instantly.

reviews.title: A Kryptonian Crash Landing That Even Superman Couldn't Save
reviews.review:
In the ever-expanding dumpster fire that is modern superhero cinema, Supergirl arrives like an uninvited cousin at the family reunion-loud, messy, and desperately trying to prove she belongs. Directed by Craig Gillespie with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer to the face, this 108-minute exercise in corporate brand management squanders a game lead performance and leaves you wondering why anyone thought adapting Woman of Tomorrow into this needed to happen. Milly Alcock, bless her, throws herself into the role of Kara Zor-El with scrappy charisma and sardonic edge. She's the one bright spark in a film that otherwise feels assembled from leftover pieces of better movies: a dash of Guardians of the Galaxy's ragtag vibe, some Mad Max dust, and a whole lot of nothing original. Alcock's Kara is a traumatized, vengeance-driven Kryptonian who reluctantly teams up with an "unlikely companion" (Jason Momoa as Lobo, naturally) for an interstellar fetch quest involving her dog Krypto. It's cute on paper. On screen, it's a grimy, small-scale adventure that never quite takes flight.

The plot? Oh, where to begin. When a ruthless adversary strikes too close to home (vague enough for you?), Kara embarks on a journey of justice and revenge. Motivations boil down to "Kill the bad guy! Save the dog!"-profound stuff. The villains are forgettable cardboard cutouts, the action sequences are underwhelming and poorly lit, and the emotional beats land with the grace of a meteorite made of wet tissue paper. For a movie ostensibly about a powerful young woman finding her place, it feels oddly hollow, like it's afraid to commit to anything too bold or interesting.

Momoa as Lobo is... fine, I guess? He chews scenery like the lovable brute he's paid to be, but the film doesn't seem to fully grasp what makes the character fun. David Corenswet pops up as Superman in what critics call "peak casting," yet even that cameo can't inject life into this thing. The whole enterprise screams "James Gunn DCU house style": quirky on the surface, but cynical and underdeveloped underneath. Technically, it's competent enough for a $170 million production, but the visuals are drab, the pacing lurches between faux-profound character moments and generic CGI brawls, and the script (by Ana Nogueira) feels like it was rewritten by committee until all personality was sanded off. This is the kind of movie that thinks naming the dog Krypto is enough to earn goodwill. It isn't. In a summer full of capes, this one feels like it was made by people who've seen too many focus groups and not enough actual human stories. Skip it in theaters. Wait for streaming, or better yet, go reread the comics. At least those had soul.

1 out of 5 stars. A hero for the algorithm age: flashy, forgettable, and fundamentally unnecessary.

reviews.title: Neither Good nor Bad, Just Mediocre
reviews.review:
I wanted to like this movie more than I did, but it ended up being just okay. The visuals are good, the action is entertaining, and the humor lands often enough to keep things from feeling too serious. The acting is solid across the board, even if nobody gives a particularly standout performance.

My biggest issue is the pacing. The movie feels very uneven. One moment it's engaging with exciting action or interesting scenes, and the next it slows to a crawl with long stretches that completely lost my attention. It never really found a consistent rhythm, which made it difficult to stay invested.

Supergirl herself is a perfectly fine protagonist. She's a classic character, so it's hard to go completely wrong with her, but I also didn't feel like this movie added anything especially memorable to her. The villains are even less memorable and lacked the presence needed to leave a lasting impression.

I also watched the film in 4DX, and that was a disappointment. The effects felt surprisingly underused and didn't add much to the experience. For a superhero movie with plenty of action, I expected the format to be much more immersive.

Compared to Superman, I think this is a step down. I gave Superman around a 7.5/10 because I found it more consistently entertaining, whereas Supergirl never quite reached that level.

Overall, it's not a bad movie, but it's also not particularly memorable. I'd recommend it to superhero fans looking for a decent time at the cinema, but I wouldn't go in expecting anything special.

Rating: 6/10.

reviews.title: You Won't Believe a Girl Can Fly
reviews.review:
The good news is that the movie is not a total failure. The bad news is that neither is it a triumph. The second film in James Gunn's DC Universe falls as flat as last year's Superman soared. The movie always faced an uphill battle. She may be loved by comic fans but to mainstream audiences she was the star of a mostly forgotten 1984 film and a sidekick to the far more recognizable Superman. While there is potential in any character, focusing a new universe's first two movies on two very similar characters seems a poor choice. It would be like if Marvel's second film was about War Machine. Not necessarily a bad choice, but another character from a different corner before doing someone so similar.

The movie is based on the critically acclaimed 2021 story Woman of Tomorrow, which itself is based on the novel/movies True Grit. The problem with so closely adapting a specific story is that it invites comparisons and as any book reader knows the movie is never as good. That's why other movies that are based on one story like Captain America: Civil War and Avengers: Infinity War reimagined their comic book stories. Even without knowing Woman of Tomorrow, it's hard not to see the seams of the source. The story too often is episodic as it adapts the individual comics rather than flowing together as one story. As such, there's too much that's underdeveloped. Too many ideas half-formed. It seems confused as to what kind of story it's trying to tell.

Similarly, the tone is all over the place. Too often it feels like it's trying to be Gunn's Guardians of the Galaxy but comes off as Taika Waititi's Thor. Too many jokes that don't land. Too much music that doesn't fit, the worst being "Cheek to Cheek" in the alien bar. The last DC movie universe got off to a bad start with everything trying to be Zack Snyder, so this feels the other side of the same coin.

Milly Alcock is the fifth live action Supergirl and also the weakest. She does a fine job as the drunk party girl, but hardly feels like this is a person who can bend steel with ease. Not helping is that the movie keeps nerfing her with red suns, Kryptonite, and poisons. While last year's Superman seemed to be holding back, this keeps knocking her down just as she gets going. There's not really that joyous moment when she gets to go all out. The character also follows a once-dead trend where she tries to spend the entire movie not being the hero only to reluctantly get pulled into it. It wasn't interesting then and isn't now.

The movie could have made up for that with a good supporting cast, but it doesn't. Eve Ridley as Ruthye is pretty dull. She tries but she's definitely no Kim Darby or Hailee Steinfeld. Worse is Matthias Schoenaerts as antagonist Krem. A superhero is only as good as their villain, and this one is as forgettable as the worst of the MCU. True Grit made a point of keeping the villain mysterious so when he's finally caught he's revealed to be a loser doing bad things. This movie does too much with him so it's hard to really be threatened by that. Plus, making him a child sex trafficker may have certain real world parallels to current events but feels needlessly shoehorned in.

The best parts of the movie are the ones it deals with least. Krypto once again steals all his scenes. The dog is proving to be the heart and soul of this universe. David Corenswet's few scenes as Superman provides a morality the movie is otherwise lacking. Of course, it's Jason Mamoa as Lobo who steals the movie. While fine as Aquaman, this was the role he was born to play. He captures the character perfectly. Too bad none of them are in the movie enough. A better adaptation would have had them go along playing the angel and devil on Kara's shoulders.

There is one major technical issue, the movie doesn't look very good. Gunn's Superman was bright and colorful, but this one is dominated by dull browns and grays. Comics in general pop with color, especially Woman of Tomorrow. Some simple color correction could have made the look more visually appealing.

It's not all bad. Kara plays well off both Ruthye and Lobo. The action scenes are fine, even if not reaching the highs of other better superhero movies. It does show some promise for future movies. Director Craig Gillespie has done plenty of good work before, from crowd pleasers like Fight Night and The Finest Hours to strong female-centric movies like I, Tonya and Cruella. So he knows how to do a good job with what he's got.

Too much of the movie screams that the movie was trying to do too much rather than just being a good story. Like too many MCU entries, it was trying too hard to continue the universe while setting up the future. It feels like the DCU needed something to strike while the iron was hot from Superman, more than just the upcoming Clayface. But with so much DC history and potential, there were plenty of better options. Subverting expectations works great, but not when this universe has very little expectations to subvert. The cross-movie universe has been difficult to do, with only Marvel nailing it and even then the MCU is doing pretty poorly right now. Gunn proved adept with Marvel, but DC can't handle another universe that repeatedly flip-flops between success and failure.

reviews.author: mitchband1960

reviews.title: A Super-Disappointment
reviews.review:
Kara Zor-El, the cousin of Superman is celebrating her 23rd birthday when her dog Krypto is poisoned by a warrior. Kara only has three days to find the cure to save her dog, but she will travel from planet to planet to find the cure. She is joined by Ruthye, a young girl whose family was slaughtered by the same guy who poisoned Krypto.

Let me start with the one major positive I have for this movie: Milly Alcock as Supergirl. Alcock is great here as she makes Kara into a cool but vulnerable hero who is a kind person beneath the snark. She is committed in every scene having solid comedic timing during the humorous moments, great line delivery during the emotional scenes and holding her own in the action scenes. I really like what Milly Alcock brought to the table as Supergirl making her a very flawed, but noble hero to show how even though you might be down on your luck, you never lose your sense of justice. I just wish the movie surrounding her was better.

Craig Gillespie's Supergirl might just be the most disappointing movie I have seen in the last few years. Unlike Superman, Supergirl is a space opera where Kara and Rutheye journey from planet to planet to take down the bad guy that took their worlds away. I like the idea of a space opera superhero movie which could be filled with epic chases, fun characters and some cool worldbuilding. Sadly, this movie's script is dull and static throughout. The pacing is choppy, the way the revenge theme is handled is sloppy and the movie lacks any originality. It is a story about a grumpy hero taking a child who is not as capable as she thinks she is on a dangerous journey to face an evil villain. There is no twist or play on the tropes dealt with here as Craig Gillespie takes the easiest ways to move the story forward making the movie feel really cliche.

The humor falls completely flat here. There are maybe two or three times that I chuckled and smiled here, but the humor has no timing or cleverness. It even has some grossout humor that falls flat. Even the people I was with in the auditorium were pretty dead silent aside from a few chuckles. Even the emotional scenes fall flat. The flashbacks to Kara's past never moved me at all despite the very horrific fate of her people because it feels out of place. This could have worked as the opening scene rather than a 10 minute scene that happens in the middle of the film that completely breaks the pace. The writing just did not do it for me at all.

While Milly Alcock brings everything she has to table here, the supporting cast is very average. Eve Ridley does a pretty good job as Rutheye, but she is stuck with a character who is unlikable, annoying and pretty useless. This girl made Supergirl's quest so much harder and even blames her at one point for some deaths in the movie. She has some sweet moments especially in the third act, but Rutheye is a pretty generic tagalong kid who only gets a little more likable towards the end.

Jason Mamoa as Lobo is pretty fun to watch, but he is not that prominent of a character. Mamoa is awesome in the action scenes and he undeniably looks cool here, but Lobo feels kind of wasted overall. David Corenswet is only in the movie for about five minutes and yet his scenes are my favorite parts of the film. Corenswet just has that charisma to make Superman such a lovable hero especially in this universe. Krypto is completely wasted here. I understand that the movie is about Kara saving him, but I wish we got a few more scenes with the dog because Krypto was one of my favorite parts of Superman.

The worst character in this movie is the villain played by Matthias Schoenaerts. Krem is such a bland and boring bad guy that he sucks the energy out of every scene he is in. I know this guy is supposed to be despicable and heinous as he is a human trafficker so this is someone the audience should root against. On paper, this should make for the perfect villain for this story. The problem is that he has no presence to make him scary and his character is bland so instead of wanting him to get the most painful punishment possible, I just wanted him to disappear and never come back. Milly Alcock carries this movie performance-wise and the supporting cast is okay, but the villain is incredibly lackluster.

Even the visuals are bad here. The cinematography by Rob Hardy has some decent shots here and there, but what makes this movie an eyesore is the color grading. All of the colors are monochromatic and the whole film looks brown and yellow which is already unappealing, but it is even worse when this is supposed to be a cool, lively comic book space opera. Even the scenes in Argo City look visually flat which is another reason why those scenes did not work for me. I hate to give the 1984 movie credit, but at least that movie had more color than this.

What sucks is that the terrible color grading gets in the way of some of the better aspects of the production. The sets, costumes and makeup all have some visual flair to them and give this movie a fun sci-fi fantasy vibe, but the colors just clash with all of it. The action scenes are admittedly enjoyable and decently shot, but there is one scene that once again is hampered by the horrible color grading when Supergirl and Lobo first team up. It honestly can make the action confusing to watch at times because everything blends in. To give the movie some credit though, the third act does have much better looking action.

The musical score by Claudia Sarne is decent, but it kind of pales in comparison to some of the other blockbusters I have watched recently. However, it is pleasant to listen to while watching the movie. That is more than I can say for some of the needle drops here. There is a needle drop towards the end of this movie that I heard was awful, but I was thinking people were overreacting and that it was probably a cool song used at a bad time. I was dead wrong. It is needle drop so crazy that it kind of shook me. Honestly though, it is a minor problem that I find somewhat amusing especially compared to some of the other major problems this movie has.

I hate to be so hard on this movie. I understand that this movie is getting a lot of unfair hatred before the movie comes out and I really wanted to be one of the defenders of this movie. Unfortunately, Supergirl is a super-disappointment. There is nothing in this movie that you cannot get from better comic book movies. I think the hardest part for me is that I walked out of Superman feeling energized and happy while I walked out of this movie feeling nothing but indifference which is not what I want to feel after watching a movie.

Last thing I will say here is that Milly Alcock deserved so much better than the insane amount of hate she got. The fact that there are grown men mocking her looks is disgusting. You can dislike a movie or even not care about an actress without being gross and childish about it. I hope she gets to continue being Supergirl or go on to do more movies after this.
reviews.author: jaredkjacoby

reviews.title: Supergirl offers great performances from Milly Alcock and Jason Momoa, but it's the theme of grief that kept me engaged throughout the film, great cinematography too
reviews.review:
Supergirl (2026) is the second installment of the DC Universe (DCU), and this is one of those times where the critics were dead wrong. This film is flawed in many places but it does so much and especially giving us a character and story that is easy to sympathize with. The theme is grief and vengeance, with the film focusing heavily on the former and its then the film is incredible. With every over the top and comic book performance like Jason Momoa's Lobo and Matthias Schoenaerts' Krem of the Yellow Hills (which is good by the way) comes stellar performances from Milly Alcock as Kara Zor-El / Supergirl and Eve Ridley as Ruthye Marye Knoll. When these characters share a scene, or Milly is on screen by herself, the emotional weight is there. This is also where Craig Gillespie's direction and Ana Nogueira's screenplay works the best. The planets and sets used are fine but doesn't stay true to the source material, neither does the style. This film feels more like Mad Max in space than a true adaptation of Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow. Although I really liked Jason Momoa as Lobo, it's his dream role after all, I couldn't help but think how he was an after thought to the script. Because, he isn't in Woman of Tomorrow. My understanding is that Ana Nogueira's screenplay remains faithful to the broad shape of Woman of Tomorrow. But Krem, the villain, could have been done better. I read how he was this memorable villain in the graphic novel, there was also stuff they cut out to make the story fit a film other than a mini series which wouldn't have worked in my opinion. What worked is the film's pacing, there was never a dull moment. It truly is as James Gunn described it, an action space epic. But it isn't epic in the grand scale, I would call it an epic because of a superhero film set in space, that keeps a human story.

The film's premise: Kara Zor-El, aka Supergirl, joins forces with an unlikely companion on an interstellar journey of vengeance and justice when an unexpected adversary strikes too close to home.

To the casting of Milly Alcock, an actress whom I really like. I have only seen her in House of the Dragon though but she was one of the best things of the first season. Before the film there were backlash to her casting and well I get why, when people think of Kara Zor-El they think of an actress like Melissa Benoist who starred as Kara Zor-El in six seasons of television, that version of the character was a naive and kind-hearted person who was the typical girl-next-door. That works and I liked her performance, but this is a different version and you'll have to understand the difference, Milly Alcock is playing a rougher, more damaged Supergirl because of the grief and trauma which shaped her which is the opposite of the optimism Clark Kent has and the kind of person he is. That is what makes it interesting in my opinion, how different they are. Kara Zor-El in this film is very flawed and extremely human. There's things you can criticize of the screenplay and direction but her characterization is spot on and brilliantly executed. Regarding Milly Alcock, Kate Erbland from the IndieWire wrote, "Alcock, tasked with playing a character that might strike some as "unlikable," instead finds both the very human dimension and the out-of-this-world charisma necessary to make Kara worth rooting for." That summarizes it perfectly. The cast also includes: David Krumholtz, Emily Beecham, and David Corenswet.

What surprised me was the action sequences, how grounded they felt, from the scenes with a normal Kara on a red sun planet and a powered Kara on a yellow sun planet. I loved the camera movement, camera placement and the choreography. With that said, I liked the action sequences better here than in Superman (2025) as those felt too CGI. The characters in this film felt more grounded, even Lobo the space bounty hunter, but especially the villain Krem who was powerful and used brute force on top of his cool gear, a good foe for Supergirl I would say which fits perfectly thematically with her as a character. I also buy the whole reason why Kara chooses to help Ruthye Marye Knoll, because of how Krem has the antidote for the poison which is slowly killing Krypto. Anyone who has had a dog or has one, would do whatever to save them, and Kara's bond with Krypto is shown closer in the flashbacks (which I loved by the way). Other things I liked, the musical score and Rob Hardy's cinematography, I really found the cinematography to be brilliant in this film, especially the composition. Like often with these superhero movies, critics normally get them wrong. By all means, this isn't a perfect superhero film and a long way from a perfect film. Yet, it offers you something, well thought out themes and a character that is unlikable at first but that's what makes her round and three dimensional. I really liked this version of Supergirl and I can't wait for what else DC has in store for the character and her cousin.

reviews.title: Entertaining movie...
reviews.review:
Of course I was familiar with this 2026 movie, and of course I had to watch it. Not that I was expecting a masterpiece or anything here, but the trailer looked interesting enough, and the fact that Lobo was in it was more than sufficient for me to check it out. In all honesty, then Lobo was the primary reason for why I opted to check out this 2026 "Supergirl" movie.

Writers Jerry Siegel, Joe Shuster and Ana Nogueira put together a fair enough script. It was enjoyable and entertaining for what it was, but at the same time it was also a pretty standard superhero script. But that is, of course, great news for diehard fans of the superhero genre.

As for the villain in the movie, well, uhm what? Talk about a one-dimensional villain character. I am sure that come tomorrow, then I will have entirely forgotten about that character.

Of the entire cast ensemble in the movie, I was only familiar with David Corenswet and Jason Momoa. The acting performances in the movie were good. And while I wasn't familiar with leading actress Milly Alcock, then I will say that she carried the movie nicely.

Visually, well, I didn't doubt that DC would skip out on the special effects. And true enough, the special effects and CGI in "Supergirl" are quite good, and do bring the story to life on the screen in a rather nice manner. They certainly have come a long way with the special effects in comparison to the good old days with Christopher Reeve as Superman.

If you enjoy superhero movies, then "Supergirl" is certainly a movie well-worth checking out. And I do sincerely hope that they opt to give Jason Momoa his own Lobo movie.

My rating of director Craig Gillespie's 2026 movie "Supergirl" lands on a six out of ten stars.

And the film does have its good moments, like the packed action sequences, wasteland space biomes, and, what is most pleasantly surprising, the recounting of Krypton and Argo's tragic ends through Kara's perspective. But my god does this story try so little to make itself creative: Ruthye is like all the "innocent and honorable" burden characters that get their growth, Krem is like any average villain except he can't even put up a final fight, the dog has been the driver of the plot for two out of the two DCU movies, and the brides on the ship are equivalent to the animals on the High Revolutionary's in GotG3 - speaking of which, wasn't Rocket also paralyzed and needed saving in that one? What's worse is when Supergirl, who's usually the most badass and straight-to-the-point, twice preaches the antique lesson that "revenge won't take your pain away," as if she was suddenly possessed by butterfly-seeking flute-playing screenwriters. In the words of Tony Stark: "I don't care, he killed my mom"; and in the words of Wade Wilson: (shoots Francis). It's truly, truly a shame how a 2026 superhero film could be so cliche at the core.

The images are larger than life but the only grey area is you can see the pixels even if you are in the middle row. The cinematography and visuals are mind-blowing. Everyone looks so cool with the colored lens landscapes that justifies the comic-books. The good part is I am not having an eye-strain!

Milly Alcock caught my attention when I saw her in the hit TV Series - House of the Dragon. Her presence grabbed my attention and I wished she could have continued with Season 2. In fact, she sometimes makes my heart flutter!

Also, check the average IMDb scores of TDWP-2 and M&M. Both of them have scores of 6.5. Most likely, M&M's score will definitely go down after a couple of months. reviews.author: hossler28

reviews.title: Brand Damage Continues.
reviews.review: As a fan of comics & someone who has spent most of my adult life in that industry it saddens me that we are now at a stage where nearly every superhero movie or TV show that is being churned out bears almost no resemblance to the characters I remember reading, admiring or even seeing on the big screen in the early days of the MCU. It clearly shows that modern writers fundamentally don't understand their subject matter, have no knowledge of the history & have no idea how to use these hero's to connect to an audience through the power of storytelling. You have been given the chance to stand on the shoulders of giants & tell a grand story that can get to the root of what makes a superhero & you choose to champion the opposite & write them as insufferable, trauma laden self inserts that might connect to a small minority who are that way inclined (look at Tik Tok or Reddit to see that side of things) but will ultimately push the majority away. Supergirl 2026 is probably one of the worst examples of this I have watched in recent times, since 'Infinity War' the genre seems to be reaching a level of no return as far as brand damage is concerned, trust me outside of Spider-Man & Batman, the big 2 comic companies are slowly dying & a large reason for this are films like Supergirl. A character who was bright & sunny in the comics for a long time, heroic & a nice counterpoint to her cousin Kal-El who in this movie is one of the worst written females I've ever had the misfortune to see, I don't blame the actress although she seems really miscast in this role but largely it's the direction (Muddy, Dark & horribly Edited) & the writing which is absolutely awful, it's a movie without a story or an arc, a movie with the most forgettable villain you will ever witness, you won't remember most of this movie a few minutes after leaving the cinema & if you've read the source material by Tom King, which I will add was a terrible choice to begin with when you had Otto Binder, Leo Dorfman, Cary Bates, Steve Englehart to pick from amongst others, you will not really see much of that King story in here as it's really loosely based but I thought I would never say this, it's worse than that comic book. I don't know who wrote this but the blame has to be laid at the feet of James Gunn who has said that films from DC would not go into production if the script wasn't locked in, it makes me wonder if this is his idea of a great script I doubt he will get many more chances to continue his vision for this universe, if you can even call it that at the moment as imo I don't think he has done anything actually good yet, Superman was a decidedly Meh movie that spent too much time with the supporting characters rather than concentrating on your main hero, it's a bold choice for sure that really didn't set the world on fire & if this is the best he has for a 2nd movie i think it's pretty much dead, sorry I love DC but it's the same with Marvel, outside of Spider-Man the brand damage caused by really awful movies & TV shows is really real, the first phases of the MCU understood their characters, they hired writers & directors who had close connections or love for the source material & it showed, but since Endgame (a very flawed movie but very popular) what MCU project has actually mattered? Or has caught the publics imagination? Ironheart? Echo? The Marvels? It's the same with DC, from the moment they started trying an interconnected universe they have been trying to run before they can walk, instead of building up their characters they rushed to the JLA & crashed & burned, Gunn is doing the same but with characters most people have not heard of outside of the comic world, who really knows the history of Supergirl or Clayface, he's even jumping years of Green Lantern law to skip to John Stewart probably using the only GL that mattered Hal Jordan as a washed up subversive miserable old man passing on the mantle before going out in a blaze of toxic masculinity to use the modern audience vernacular. Anyway back to Supergirl, outside of a small cameo from Jason Mamoa as Lobo which injects a little life into the otherwise miserable proceedings there isn't much here I can say is worth watching, the lighting & filters are awful, the CGI is in the same place it was 10 years ago, it's all the same sci-fi channel level visuals, Kara is not likeable or relatable in any way unless you are a drunk or a slob who spends your days contemplating how grim the world has been to you, this is not what cinematic heroes should be, where are the role models? Is this what modern Hollywood thinks a superhero should be? If it is I have some advice to anyone looking for good heroic stories, go back to the source material, start at the beginning & stop around 2013 this is when the writing started to decline to a point now where no one is buying most of the modern comics produced outside of Batman or Spider-Man. Such a shame, there was a point around 2010 when there was such an excitement in my industry & now we have Supergirl 2026 a movie that perfectly sums up an industry in decline. Can it be saved? Only if you start to choose writers or creators that understand the core values that made these characters so iconic in the first place, we are years past the subversion era, it's not connecting with anyone!

reviews.title: Supergirl - A Story of Perseverance
reviews.review:
I actually enjoyed the expierience that Supergirl was, however I had some criticism towards some aspects of the film. That goes without saying that this film delivered some really good aspects that surpassed my expectations

To start, I enjoyed the emotional depth and overall seriousness of this film. Comparing it to its predecessor, Superman, this movie felt more dark and had larger stakes than Superman. The overall tone felt more serious, and thats what I like to see in a Supergirl movie. The scene showcasing Kara's backstory was tragic and it was executed really well. I wish more of her origin could've been shown in this movie. Another aspect that I enjoyed a lot about the movie is how easy it was to digest. The movie does a great job at telling its audience about the differences between Supergirl and Superman, as well as their motivations and reasoning behind there actions.

Now time for the criticism. My biggest issue personally is the forcefeeding of our side characther. By the end, it felt like she was the main characther and it wasn't even about Supergirl anymore. The final action sequence featured her at the forefront and not Kara. I feel like the movie could've been better if either her story/arc would've resolved faster, or if she wasn't as significant of a characther as the movie made her out to be. Secondly, there should've been either more Lobo or no Lobo. Instead, we got this mushy middle where he was there, but didnt contribute much to the story except for Supergirls Plot Armor.

My other issue is the dialogue at times. There are times where Rutheye is just constantly saying gibberish, to the point where the villain even made a joke about it. There were many instances where it felt like her characther was out of place, or just simply said/did too much. Another thing too that I didnt really get was why Krem was kidnapping young girls to be brides. I feel that was simply a plot device to drive the movie forward, even though it didnt have any significant meaning to the overall story.

Overall, I enjoyed watching the film, and I feel it had a relatively decent, but enjoyable story to it. I just know this movie couldve been significantly better and more enjoyable as long as they fixed many things involving Rutheye's characther along with other criticism.

reviews.title: Supergirl Crashes: Hollywood's Latest DEI Disaster Desecrates the Heroin
reviews.review:
One staggers out of James Gunn's Supergirl-or rather, Craig Gillespie's dutifully Gunn-adjacent exercise in corporate brand extension-with the weary conviction that the superhero genre has finally reached its decadent phase: loud, murky, and desperate to signal every approved virtue while forgetting why anyone ever cared about the archetype in the first place. Milly Alcock, to her credit, throws herself into the role of a hard-drinking, traumatized Kara Zor-El with a feral energy that briefly convinces you the film might have a pulse. The rest is cinematic sludge: muddy visuals, incoherent action, and a script so flaccid it makes one long for the relative coherence of a Saturday-morning cartoon.

The casting, of course, provides the first and most reliable source of unintended mirth. Alcock's Supergirl is presented as a messy, party-girl anti-heroine who apparently "goes both ways" and isn't terribly interested in men-an edict delivered with the subtlety of a press release. One does not object to an actress playing the part; one objects to the part being rewritten into a vessel for contemporary pieties about empowerment, fluidity, and the irrelevance of heroic masculinity. The character who should embody Kryptonian might and moral clarity is instead a walking DEI checklist: traumatized enough to be "relatable," rebellious enough to thumb her nose at tradition, and just ambiguous enough to court every niche audience while alienating the core one. The result is not empowerment but parody-a superheroine less concerned with truth, justice, or the American way than with proving she doesn't need any of it.

The liberties taken with the source material (Tom King's Woman of Tomorrow) are not bold adaptations but acts of vandalism in service of the quota. What was a stark, elegiac comic becomes a muddled road-trip buddy picture laced with needle-drops, weak villainy, and girl-power sermonizing that lands like a lead balloon. Jason Momoa's Lobo cameo offers fleeting relief, but even he cannot salvage a film that treats its own mythology as an afterthought. The direction fails across the board: action sequences lost in murky CGI murk, emotional beats that ring hollow, and a tone that veers wildly between grimdark posturing and quippy irreverence without committing to either. It is filmmaking by algorithm-safe enough for the boardroom, insulting enough for anyone who remembers when these stories meant something.

This is not cinema in service of wonder or heroism; it is product engineered to flatter the age while emptying the archetype of its power. Alcock deserved better material. Audiences deserve better than to watch a once-mighty franchise reduced to lectures dressed in a cape. The wine-dark cosmos of Krypton has never looked so gray, nor so pointless. Avoid at all costs; the Man of Steel's cousin has been press-ganged into the culture wars, and the ship sinks before it ever clears the launchpad.

reviews.title: people do not know how to write compelling female characters
reviews.review:
I went into this with already low expectations, came out shocked by how much they surpassed it.

This could have been a wonderfully executed movie if it weren't for the fact it was too centred around a random little girl looking for revenge, and quirky one liners from lobo. It was as if they sidelined supergirl in her own movie.

also, and this is not a dig against lobo, but why was he really in this film? Did i enjoy his funny one-liners? Absolutely, without question this movie would've been a 3 at best without him. But why couldn't they have made more fun dialogue and scenes without him between supergirl and this little girl? Not to mention him being in the end fight scene and saving kara. In the end, i was left hoping and praying a different director would pick up supergirl and take her somewhere far away from this boring ass movie. She of all characters deserves better dialogue, better cinematography of her fights, and a better chemistry with her side characters.

reviews.title: A Super Mess: The D Stands for Dog 🐶 in the DCU
reviews.review:
James Gunn once said he wouldn't move forward with a DC film unless the script was rock solid because weak writing was the biggest problem facing superhero movies. Ironically, Supergirl ends up proving exactly why he made that statement.

The script is a complete mess. Instead of giving Kara Zor-El a focused emotional journey, the film piles on one random side quest after another space pirates, revenge missions, kidnapped brides, bounty hunters, Krypto's antidote, random planets, green suns, yellow suns, and Lobo. It feels less like a movie and more like a collection of unrelated comic issues awkwardly stitched together.

The biggest casualty is Kara herself. One of DC's most emotionally complex heroes defined by surviving Krypton's destruction and carrying memories Superman never had is reduced to an alcoholic party girl whose emotional depth is buried beneath jokes, drinking, and endless spectacle. The film never earns the emotional payoff it keeps chasing.

Then there's Krypto. I love Krypto, but the emotional core revolves around saving the dog more than understanding Supergirl. At times, it genuinely feels like a movie about a dog featuring Supergirl. The "D" in DCU might as well stand for Dog "Dog Cinematic Universe"

Jason Momoa is another disappointment. He was fantastic as Aquaman because Zack Snyder knew how to present characters with presence and mythic weight. As Lobo, he never disappears into the role it's just Jason Momoa in makeup acting like Jason Momoa. For all the marketing, he feels more like a glorified NPC.

The technical side doesn't help either. The CGI is inconsistent, the green-screen work is distracting, the editing never lets emotional scenes breathe, and the action often feels weightless. Instead of building momentum, the film rushes from one joke, fight, and location to the next.

The biggest failure is the tone. This doesn't feel like Supergirl it feels like Guardians of the Galaxy wearing a Supergirl skin. James Gunn keeps recycling the same quirky, joke-heavy formula until every character starts feeling interchangeable. Rather than embracing what makes Kara unique, the film turns her into another generic space adventurer.

Supergirl deserved a story about grief, survivor's guilt, identity, and hope. Instead, she got buried beneath Marvel-lite humor, endless side quests, and spectacle.

A joyless, directionless, and deeply disappointing adaptation.

reviews.author: romanosdaniel

reviews.title: A Mediocre Romp that I like 👍🏼
reviews.review:
You can feel the mediocrity of this project at every corner. But in a weird, meta-contextual way that isn't for everybody, it kind of adds to the message of the film.

Kara is grieving the loss of her loved ones, and the only reminder she has left of her upbringing is her rowdy, rambunctious dog, Krypto, whose life is in jeopardy. Yes, this movie is definitely generic and, in every sense of the word, predictable. But despite its flaws (in a lot of areas), it's a decent movie about grief and how hard it is to overcome while still choosing to fight for what we have left.

Kara flying into space and screaming into the void was a very powerful depiction of what grief feels like. I'm sure most of us wish we could do that as well. The flashback sequences on Krypton were effective at evoking that feeling of connection and showing what she would inevitably lose.

**Some more of the good:**

The creature and alien designs were pretty awesome in this movie-I can't deny that. I really loved the designs of all the aliens on the space bus the space pirates invaded. The costuming was also very sleek, and I loved looking at the details of the various characters' outfits.

Which brings us to Lobo. Jason Momoa wasn't born to play this role. Lobo was born to be played by Momoa. Every time he's on screen, I'm giggling with joy. Jason is **CLEARLY** having the time of his life in this movie, and his design is *chef's kiss*.

Some of the visuals in this movie are decent as well...which leads us to the bad.

**The Bad:**

Yeah, some of the visuals are okay, but most of them are bad. I don't need to say much-it speaks for itself.

The main issue with this movie is that the dialogue is garbage: formulaic and predictable. I can think of a few places where it's good, but they're very few and far between.

The humor is also bad. Just predictable. I think I laughed at one thing Lobo said. Otherwise, my theater was silent. No one laughed at this movie, which is...sad.

The story itself is simple, but it's serviceable.

This next part has me very torn. Initially, I was kind of excited that we weren't getting another predictable revenge story. I thought, *"Wow. She actually convinced Ruthye not to compromise her soul by killing generic villain boy for murdering her parents."* ...but then **she** killed him and, in no way, practiced what she preached.

Which, in a weird way...I sort of like...but also hate...I don't know.

It's a semi-decent way to differentiate her from Superman in that she's not the straight arrow he is. So she's inconsistent and a hypocrite in some ways...a lot like most of us. It made her feel very human.

So yeah...I don't know. It's kind of cool. 🤷‍♂️

reviews.title: Supergirl (2026) - A $170 Million Screensaver Packed with Nostalgia and Nonsense
reviews.review:
If you loved James Gunn's Superman earlier this year and thought, "Wow, I really want to see that exact same movie again, but with a drastically mismatched tone, an hour of aggressive boredom, and a complete lack of originality," then boy, does DC have the summer blockbuster for you.

Supergirl is finally here, and it manages to achieve the impossible: making a 1-hour and 50-minute space epic feel like a 4-hour lecture on the limitations of green screen technology.

The film takes off with a first act that is aggressively "just okay," before settling comfortably into a deeply boring midsection, and then frantically throwing action scenes at the wall to see what sticks. But the real peak cinema comes from the writing.

Take Kara's super-hearing, for instance. Much like her cousin Clark, she struggles with overwhelming acoustic overload. The film's brilliant, groundbreaking solution to this crippling sensory trauma? She puts on retro headphones and turns the volume up. Yes, you read that right. To fight a deafening sensory overload of noise, our hero blasts music directly into her eardrums. It makes absolutely zero sense, but hey-the retro headphones looked so cool in the trailer, right? The movie is absolutely packed with these "please think we're edgy" moments that crumble the second you apply a single brain cell.

The atmosphere tries to distance itself from Superman, but instead of finding its own identity, it just desperately cosplays as Guardians of the Galaxy-if Guardians was stripped of its charm and injected with DC's classic lack of originality. By the time the final scene rolls around, the movie isn't even hiding it anymore; it is sweating, panting, and aggressively trying to catch up to an Avengers-level ensemble climax without doing any of the actual legwork.

Speaking of things that didn't work:

The Costume: Why does Superman's suit look completely deformed here? Did the costume department shrink it in the wash between movies?

The Plot: Kara's character arc is so inconsistent it'll give you whiplash.

Lobo: We finally get Jason Momoa as Lobo, and the movie gives him so little to do that I actively lost interest in the casting altogether. He's just... there.

The Dialogue: Truly pathetic. Half the time, Kara sounds like a AI-generated script trying to speak "disaffected youth."

The Green Screen Epidemic Remember when the internet spent an entire decade crying about Zack Snyder using too much CGI? I can't wait to see those same critics defend this movie, because Supergirl looks like it was filmed entirely inside a giant lime-green void. The backgrounds are so painfully artificial that you'll spend half the movie wondering if the actors were even in the same room, let alone on an alien planet.

And finally, we have our big villain, Krem. For an interstellar threat, he looks shockingly... human. He doesn't look strong, he doesn't look imposing, and he has all the presence of an angry landlord demanding rent rather than a universe-threatening menace.

The Verdict: an hour and twenty minutes into the film, I wasn't watching Kara try to save the day-I was staring at my watch, wondering why a movie this short was taking so long to install itself into my memory. Skip this one, or just mute it and play a Guardians soundtrack in the background. It'll make just as much sense.

reviews.title: For surviving the bait and switch
reviews.review:
If you want to experience true, spine chilling horror, don't bother buying tickets for the new Evil Dead. Just do what I did, accidentally book those tickets at a theater a 40 minute drive away, show up at your local cinema looking like a fool, and panic swap them for Supergirl. Talk about a terrifying premise.

I walked into that auditorium fully prepared to endure two hours of cinematic waterboarding. I braced myself for the absolute worst, clunky dialogue, a plot held together by hope and hairspray, and the kind of secondhand embarrassment that makes you want to slide out of your seat and vanish into the sticky floor.

But a funny thing happened on the way to the disaster, it actually wasn't that bad.

Don't get me wrong, it's no masterpiece, but as far as accidental consolation prizes go, it holds its own. The action scenes are surprisingly decent and kept me awake far better than the crushing realization of my own booking incompetence ever could.

Is it the gory, chainsaw revving bloodbath I wanted? No. But if you lower your expectations all the way to the Earth's core, Supergirl manages to soar just high enough to be thoroughly entertaining.

Pro tip: Always double check the theater location on your confirmation email. Or don't, if you're in the mood for a surprisingly okay superhero movie.

reviews.title: Disappointing
reviews.review:
Supergirl is a perfectly watchable superhero movie, but it's one that ultimately settles for being merely fine when it could have been so much more. The film is coherent, competently made, and never completely loses its footing, yet it struggles to give viewers much reason to become emotionally invested in what unfolds on screen.

The biggest issue is the story itself. At its core, the narrative is incredibly basic and lacks any real depth. It follows familiar beats without adding meaningful layers to its narrative or characters, leaving the entire experience feeling predictable and somewhat hollow.

The supporting cast doesn't help matters. The side characters range from underwhelming to underutilized, underdeveloped, and one-dimensional-sometimes all at once. Few of them leave a lasting impression, and several feel as though they exist solely to move the plot from one set piece to the next. The villain, in particular, is a major disappointment. Despite occupying a central role in the story, the antagonist lacks complexity, compelling motivations, or any presence, resulting in one of the film's weakest elements.

While the lead performance is solid, it isn't enough to compensate for the lack of engaging personalities surrounding her. A superhero film thrives on memorable relationships and dynamic conflicts, and Supergirl never quite delivers either.

In the end, Supergirl is neither a disaster nor a triumph. It's a functional, coherent blockbuster that accomplishes the basics but never really reaches beyond them. Unfortunately, its uninspired story and a cast of boring, underwritten characters drag the experience down, leaving behind a film that is easy to watch but equally easy to forget.

reviews.title: SUPERGIRL: WOMAN OF TOMORROW (2026) if not entangled in executive cold feet and studio trimming.
reviews.review:
Where James Gunn's Superman soared on earnest Midwestern optimism, Craig Gillespie's Supergirl attempts a serrated, dirt-and-blood cosmic western about grief, trauma, and vengeance-only to wind up entangled in executive cold feet and studio trimming. It is a jagged, wildly uneven fragment of a movie, kept afloat almost entirely by Milly Alcock's spit-and-fury lead performance.

Milly Alcock is magnetic. She refuses to play Kara Zor-El as a sun-drenched, polished hero; instead, her Kara is a hangover-nursing, deeply scarred survivor who watched her planet slowly rot from Kryptonite radiation before landing on Earth. Her dynamic with Eve Ridley's stoic, revenge-obsessed Ruthye gives the story its genuine emotional core. When the film embraces its space-western roots-sunless bar brawls on alien outposts and desolate red-sun showdowns-it crackles with genuine edge. Jason Momoa also brings a jolt of kinetic, unrefined comic-book energy in his brief appearance as Lobo.

Studio panic is written all over the runtime. Reports of a heavily edited 108-minute cut down from a longer, slower burn show in the narrative seams. Pacing feels frantically rushed through key character transitions, reducing Matthias Schoenaerts' Krem from the terrifyingly insidious villain of Tom King's source comic into a generic fantasy target. Furthermore, shoehorned check-ins from David Corenswet's Clark Kent undercut the desolate isolation that ought to define Kara's journey.

Cinematographer Rob Hardy attempts to capture the painterly, cosmic grandeur of Bilquis Evely's graphic novel artwork, but his visuals frequently collide with director Craig Gillespie's signature kinetic, needle-drop-heavy style. Instead of letting vast interstellar landscapes breathe with wide, silent wonder, the camera often grows restless, retreating into handheld franticness during key action sequences. Claudia Sarne's score fares much better, delivering an eerie mix of distorted industrial synth and weeping string motifs that evoke isolation whenever the editing allows a moment to land.

Adapted from Tom King and Bilquis Evely's landmark comic Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow, this film was designed as the tonal counter-weight in the DC Universe's Chapter One lineup. Where Gillespie's previous character studies (I, Tonya, Cruella) succeeded by fully diving into tragicomic anti-heroes, Supergirl wavers awkwardly between an indie-minded road movie in space and a compromised corporate summer tentpole.

Aside from potential long-shot nominations for Best Costume Design or Best Visual Effects for its dirt-stained space-punk aesthetic, the film lacks the narrative cohesion to make waves in major guild or Academy races.

Struggling against budget bloat ($175M+) and lukewarm box-office numbers, Supergirl stands as a cautionary tale for franchise building. It proves that adapting dark, subversive source material requires total directorial commitment, rather than trimming runtime to placate casual audiences.

Milly Alcock demonstrates the fierce, iron backbone needed to anchor a blockbuster, but Supergirl feels like a bold 130-minute sci-fi tragedy forcibly streamlined into a 108-minute compromise.

Overallover.

Supergirl is my favorite super so I really wanted this to be great. But it made the critical mistake of basing it on the Woman of Tomorrow comic.

Woman of Tomorrow ruins the chances of hitting those emotional highs and lows by going for an unsympathetic, melancholic half-nihilistic version of Kara. They are trying to combine a spaghetti western or revenge movie with trauma telling and it just doesn't work.

I'm a big cryer, ugly cryer... and nowhere do I care enough to get even half emotionally invested in the tragedy that bubbles in her background. And that's with this being my favorite character.

It's not a terrible movie. It's an ok movie. But it's a forgettable popcorn flick. The action scenes saves the movie from being a pale copy of a movie you've seen before.

It should have gone for broke on something. It could have been an endorphin kick of hope, it could have been a tear jerker tragedy... It could even have done a Masters of the Universe and just had fun with the zanyness of her comic lore trove.

This never takes off from emotional sepia and will be forgotten next week.

I loved seeing Jason Mamoa play up this crazy heavy metal mercenary, and Supergirl's offhand comment on his backstory leaves me intrigued to hear more about him. But I'm not sure if just vibes and aura would be able to hold up a full lobo movie, but I'd be perfectly happy if he stays a long term side character.

I didnt like how elements of this movie tried to copy James Gunn's style instead of creating it's own style, as there's already are so many movies that have tried and failed to imitate guardians of the galaxy and this is no exception. The needle drop scenes specifically fall flat with poor music choices and bad sync with the action beats. Speaking of the action, you can tell that this was the director's first time directing action as there's no keneticism, the wrong techniques are used at the wrong times or are obscured by clouds of dust or cut away to other scenes.

The movie also doesnt know what to do with supergirl's raw power and tries to write in everything possible to nerf her, from red suns, drunkenness, mysterious poisons, kryptonite bullets, you name it. And at a point, it stops becoming clever and turns contrived and lazy.

Overall, a mid second addition to James Gunn's new DCU. I hope clayface or man of tommorow are the movies I'm looking for.

reviews.title: Failure? No. Disappointment? Sure thing.
reviews.review:
What's everybody's problem with this movie anyway? I mean, sure, it's no art. It's a heavily recycled commercial product that relies on ancient tropes and simple jokes. But so what? It's a comic book movie. We all knew what we came for. We came for Milly Alcock's Supergirl that was teased at the end of the Superman movie and, surprise-surprise, she's still that.

And again, it's yet another one of those ancient tropes. I mean, a heavily traumatized, yet extremely adorable character. People love that. But honestly, Milly's, like, a perfect fit for the role. She's totally on par with Melissa Benoist to me now, and coming from a HUGE Arrowverse fan, that means a lot. No, seriously, she's awesome and is EXACTLY what DC needed. Comes with one heck of a suit too.

What really sucks about this movie is that there isn't anything fresh in it-nothing, like, NEW. Nothing we didn't see before. I mean, let's just admit it, it's hard to impress people with superhero movies and CGI nowadays. It's not like it's Richard Donner's Superman or Tim Burton's Batman. It's not a milestone movie. OK? Still, it's hard not to expect at least something. Something to make the experience stand out. And Eve Ridley's Ruthye? She just isn't enough.

Don't get me wrong, though. Ridley herself did great. She's a good fit for the character and comes with lots and lots of "Aw-w-w!" moments. That cute little character that constantly tries to show some attitude? Again, it's a trope everybody loves. But come on. Serving us The Golden Child formula as the main dish, where Milly Alcock constantly tries to pull an Eddie Murphy? Again, it's not bad, it's just... not enough. While watching the movie, I kept waiting for big things to start happening, but somehow they never did.

Let's forget 'bout DC and talk MARVEL for a sec. Remember Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings? Solid cast, good fit for the characters, solid production, yet... Can you even remember what it was all about? Personally, I can't. Same exact thing happened to Supergirl. The villains are just a bunch of nobodies, the plot is painfully straightforward, and there isn't a single part of the story to make you, you know, feel the feelings. There are a couple of solid laughs, but that's pretty much it. Some generic things keep happening on screen while you keep stuffing your face with popcorn. That's how this movie works.

But again, it's not terrible. Despite the fact there's nothing to love here, there's also nothing to hate. Comparing this movie to, say, Andy Muschietti's The Flash, which was all about cringey scenes and ruined characters (it was hard to ruin Michael Keaton's Batman but somehow that movie managed), Craig Gillespie's Supergirl actually feels good. I call that the "bubblegum effect". It's quite "yummy" while it lasts, but after the taste disappears, you instantly start to feel hungry for more flavor. And when you get a new flavor? Like I said, you completely forget about previous one. Just because of them all being kinda the same.

So... Yeah. Failure? No. Disappointment? Sure thing. With such a good cast, it was hard not to expect more. Much, much more. Note that I didn't mention Jason Momoa's Lobo. You know why? Because he's, like, completely unimportant and exists only to provide some laughs. He doesn't play a proper role in the story. He just appears now and then and that's it. How do you feel about that? Yeah. That's exactly how I feel about the whole movie. I'd love to see all those faces again, I'd love to see all those characters again, but I'd also love 'em to have... You know. A good story to be a part of. Dixi.

reviews.title: Several questions need answered.

As another overpriced, modern audience, monstrosity lands in theaters, it begs several questions. First, do we really need another superhero movie in general? This genre feels overdone. From oversaturation on streaming to cinema, I feel we need a break from these "cartoons" with digitally added human faces. Second, why does Hollywood keep doubling down on criticism of traditional American values? Superman was always, "Truth, Justice, and the American Way." Hollywood's disdain for anything that acknowledges America for having any good qualities is also exhausting. We want to feel good about America. Make something positive for a change. Third, how can a person as young as Supergirl in this movie be so tired, jaded, and world weary? She's barely had any adult life at all. If this was Super Woman or Super Grandma, the premise might make sense. But as it stands, the fundamental premise of the movie is anachronistic and unbelievable. Think about your script at the most basic level. It needs to be believable. Otherwise, you'll never set the hook for the audience.

Do better, Hollywood.

reviews.title: A Solid Supergirl Story That Deserved a Fair Chance
reviews.review:
I went into Supergirl expecting to enjoy it, and I came away thinking it was a solid film with more strengths than weaknesses.

The biggest win for me was that the storytelling stayed true to itself. It never felt like it was trying to be something it wasn't or constantly chasing bigger spectacle for the sake of it. The pacing was also one of the movie's strongest qualities. It kept me engaged from beginning to end without dragging scenes out or overexplaining story beats the audience had already picked up on.

Milly Alcock did a great job as Supergirl. I thought she fit the role really well, and her performance felt sincere. The writing was better than I expected too. The dialogue and delivery felt natural instead of overly dramatic or forced, which helped the characters feel believable.

Jason Momoa absolutely stole every scene he was in. His comedic timing was fantastic, and he brought a ton of personality without feeling like he was trying too hard. He was easily one of the highlights of the movie.

That said, it wasn't perfect. The musical score wasn't really my style, although that's completely subjective. There were also a few plot holes that stood out if you stopped to think about them, and while the visual effects were good enough, they never quite reached that "wow" level I'd expect from a major superhero film.

One thing I do want to mention has nothing to do with the movie itself. Before release, I saw a lot of negativity online directed at Milly Alcock. After watching the film, I genuinely don't think she deserved any of it. She's a talented actress who carried herself well, gave the role everything she had, and should be proud of being Supergirl.

Social media has become an exhausting place where outrage spreads faster than thoughtful discussion. Too many people get swept into echo chambers where hating something becomes more important than giving it a fair chance. It's disappointing to see, especially when it gets directed at real people simply doing their jobs.

Overall It's an enjoyable superhero movie with strong performances, good pacing, and plenty to like, even if it's held back by a few story issues and effects that don't always hit the mark.
