reviews.title: I wonder if the people who criticize this movie have even seen it.
reviews.review:
Yes, it's not an adaptation that sticks strictly to the source material, but name one superhero movie based on a comic book that adapts it 1:1. It's always a reinterpretation; the comic book is simply the inspiration. Also, remember that the film is part of a larger universe; certain changes had to be made to make people feel like it was a natural part of that universe, continuing existing storylines.

If you go in expecting this to be an adaptation of the comic book, I can guarantee you'll be disappointed. But if you treat it as a standalone work that merely draws inspiration from the comic book, you'll probably enjoy this movie.

The movie does a great job of highlighting the contrast between Superman and Supergirl; for the first time, I felt she was a fully-fledged character, not simply a female version of her cousin. To be honest, because Kara's character is so much more complex, I find her simply much more interesting. And by the way, Milly Alcock is absolutely brilliant in this role.

I also don't understand the criticism of Lobo's appearance, claiming he adds nothing to the plot. First of all, his presence is logically justified within the story; second, he's the one who reinforces Ruthye's belief that revenge is a good thing, which is a contrast to what Supergirl is trying to convey her.

I've also heard that, according to some, Krem comes across as a one-dimensional villain. In my opinion, that's actually a good thing in this movie. Krem has no motivation or justification for his actions; he's simply a ruthless monster. Not every villain has to be driven by something; some are just evil for no particular reason. My only problem with Krem's character is that his design was changed completely unnecessarily-not every monster needs to look like a monster.

I also noticed that a lot of people complained about the change to the ending. It couldn't be the same as in the comic book, because, first of all, we don't know if the Phantom Zone even exists in this universe. Yes, Supergirl decides to kill Krem in this movie. And it still makes sense. She herself told us earlier that Superman sees the good in people, while she sees the truth in them. Superman would have spared Krem, but Kara didn't, because she knew full well that Krem wouldn't change-showing him the moral superiority of the main characters wouldn't have made an impression on him-after all, he himself told her that mercy wouldn't save Ruthye's life. Supergirl didn't kill him out of revenge; she did it to serve justice and make sure he would never hurt anyone again.

reviews.title: Supergirl is Super Bad - And NOT The Good Kind.
reviews.review:
Supergirl, starring Milly Alcock as Kara Zor-EI AKA Supergirl and Jason Momoa as Lobo, delivers loads of humor, heart and girl-power. There are loads of other fine actors and actresses in the film, and they all deliver serviceable performances.

The problem does not lie with the actors, but the script and the story. The only time the film is on track and serious, giving the "Super" gravitas expected, is at the very beginning, and also when we learn the origin of Kara and her parents on Krypton. After and in between these scenes, what remains of the movie plays like a bad, adults-only charicature of a Saturday morning cartoon episode. There is drinking, there is swearing, there is punching, stabbing and fighting. There are also lots and lots of unfunny moments which nevertheless draw nervous laughter from the audience.

This movie spends so much time and so many scenes showing us that Kara Zor-El doesn't care about anything other than her dog. Half of the movie's run-time is wasted - literally wasted - on showing us almost nothing at all.

The movie forgets what it is supposed to be about: An alien orphaned from her home world, attempting to figure out her place in the present world. Instead, the movie focuses on the misdirection of a storyline no one paid to see about a character previously unknown.

This iteration of the D. C. icon prefers that we not take its heroine too seriously - she is portrayed as a drunken, slovenly, irresponsible lout who cares about little other than her own satisfaction. Towards the end of the movie, this trajectory is slightly bent and crudely fashioned into a semblence of a character arc by suddenly proclaiming that Supergirl does indeed care about others. Too little, too late.

Poor, poor form. Supergirl is only fun if you don't think women and girls can aspire to more. Do better. D. C.

6 out of 10 stars.


* Chipper F. Xavier, Esq.

reviews.title: A pretty generic superhero movie with a few notable things in it
reviews.review:
To be completely honest, I was expecting to like this way less than I did. This is definitely not a good movie, and the only reason I'm giving it a like is because I'm feeling generous. But there's a decent amount of decent stuff in here. It's just a shame that everything else is aggressively mediocre, generic, or outright bad.

I'll get the negatives out of the way first since this will be a largely negative review. This movie's biggest problem is the fact that it's the most bland, mediocre, stereotypical, cookie-cutter superhero film I think I've ever seen in my entire life. With the exception of a very select handful of plot points and scenes, there is essentially nothing in this movie that avid superhero fans haven't already seen dozens of times. The message is generic, the characters are generic, the villain is extremely unremarkable, the side characters are mid, there's a gazillion licensed songs, and the cinematography is the film equivalent of plain oatmeal. That's this movie's biggest issue. I don't really need to elaborate on it that much. If I call a superhero movie generic and bland, you can probably picture what this movie feels like with some decent accuracy.

Now for my other complaints. I was not impressed with the script. The dialogue is extremely clunky and unnatural all throughout the film. A lot of the lines just sound so stupid and poorly written. I kind of mentioned it above, but the incessant music got on my nerves as well. I swear to god, there's a needle-drop like every 15 minutes. I'm aware that James Gunn didn't direct this movie but it sure feels like he did. For me personally, that's not a compliment, I think James Gunn is an incredibly overrated director. Yes, the Guardians trilogy is outstanding, I loved Superman, and Peacemaker was pretty good. But a lot of his tendencies REALLLYYY get on my nerves. His needle-drops are cool sometimes, but other times it just feels like he's trying to farm 70s and 80s nostalgia because he thinks it's the tuffest thing ever. This movie is no different. Even though James Gunn wasn't behind the wheel, I recognized all of the unprotected left turns. So either the director was trying to poorly emulate the James Gunn style, or Gunn himself was spreading his influence a bit too well.

As I mentioned, the cinematography is also kinda poop. This movie is genuinely UGLY at times, it has no shortage of sequences that look so grimey, dim, and colorless, which is wild considering Superman was the complete opposite in every single way. I guess that's the point, but there's a way to convey that without throwing every actor in front of a greenscreen with poor backlighting. I got major Phase 4 MCU vibes at times which is obviously not good. Thankfully not EVERY scene is like this, but a depressing amount of them are.

Lastly, the plot did not impress me. I really did not care for the little girl whose name I already forgot. Idk why but I can't stand when movies have a perfectly fine plot and then have to shoehorn an obnoxious kid into it. The girl in this movie isn't annoying, but I still did not care for her. It was really hard to take her seriously sometimes and her arc about "revenge" is just so overused. I can name like 10 characters who encapsulate that theme 100x better. They don't even TRY to do anything interesting with it. The plot about Krypto is fine, but once again it's hardly nuanced. I will say I liked that the plot had the balls to make the villains s3x traffickers, that was dark.

As for the positives, the action is cool sometimes, and Supergirl herself is incredible, Millie Alcock is a fantastic Supergirl. I really liked her character overall. Her backstory was quite easily the best part of the film and pretty emotional. I thought her character arc was solid and I can't wait to see more of her. And as everyone else has been saying, Jason Momoa as Lobo was an absolute delight, he was truly born to play him. I don't know how to describe his character, but he's genuinely so sick and effortlessly hilarious. Dude was aura farming in every single one of his scenes and that comically large cigar just made it funnier and cooler. If we got an entire Lobo TV series I don't think I'd even complain.

To sum it up, this isn't a bad movie, but certainly not a great one. I understood what they were going for with this, I truly do, but unfortunately the execution was incredibly bland and generic. It was decently enjoyable however, and Supergirl herself was great. I just can't believe that this movie is getting some aggressively negative reviews, this is no where near some of the worst superhero movies we've gotten this decade, and no the DCU is not "dead." In fact, if this was a Marvel movie, I don't even think it'd be bottom 10. People forget that Phase 1 went 3/6. We have a long ways to go for the DCU, and I'm confident that it'll turn out great. Or at the very least, far, far better than the DCEU/Snyderverse. This unironically clears a concerning amount of those films. Whatever happens, I have faith.

reviews.title: Flawed but entertaining

It also felt like the creatives were trying to force a Guardians of the Galaxy aesthetic, with forgettable needle drops replacing a soundtrack. Even though the movie isn't directed by him, Supergirl feels like a James Gunn movie, and I was hoping for a little more variety in the franchise. If Clayface is rocking out to top 40 hits in his movie this fall, I think there's going to be a real problem. Also, the villain, Krem of the Yellow Hills is given a very disgusting, but unique motivation that sets him apart from most other villains, but he's not developed enough. That intriguing motivation just becomes a strange moment that doesn't really effect anything. The visuals are also so-so and reminiscent every other space movie that comes out nowadays. Overall, though IMDb doesn't give me the option to, I'd give Supergirl a 6.5/10. It's not The Dark Knight, but it isn't Madame Webb either.

Jason Momoa's Lobo is also incredibly charismatic, and fight scenes are badassery, carrying a raw, long suppressed rage in every move. What touched me the most was the character's inner world. Kara's pain has nowhere to go; she doesn't embrace her own power and is even ready to give it up at any moment. Her past has robbed her of the chance to ever be an innocent young girl again. That's where Ruthye comes in, she is the literal embodiment of the "good self" that Kara desperately wants to protect. She represents the innocence and kindness that Kara refuses to completely abandon. So when Kara helps Ruthye, I don't see it as being held back by her. It's a form of compromise. reviews.title: Milly Alcock's Supergirl is great in an okay movie
reviews.review:
I've loved Supergirl ever since I read Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow by Tom King, so of course I was looking forward to this as it was supposedly based on it, and despite all the stupid controversies around the movie, not to mention the box office failure (not that movies need to be a success to be good), it looked to at least be a very fun time.

And sure, it was, it just doesn't have much to do with the Woman of Tomorrow comic, it was definitely inspired by it but I would not say it is based on that comic, a comic which, by the way, has amazing visuals and colors which the movie clearly lacks, it's just so... brown and muted, makes every planet they go on look the same.

But hey at least, Milly Alcock as Supergirl is great and definitely the best thing in the movie, which you would hope so from a movie named after her. I just loved how messy and sloppy she was as that's something we haven't really seen in a female-lead superhero movie until now.

Really makes me understand why they chose Craig Gillapsie for this, since he's known for messy female protagonists, though i do think it should've been directed by a woman, especially a woman like Cathy Yan (who directed Birds of Prey), who could've given the movie some much needed visual flare.

Maybe then they would've used a Blondi song, like c'mon it was all over the marketing and wasn't even used once? Seems like a big missed opportunity, cuz they really should've used "call me" for the needle drop by the end and it baffles me that they didn't.

I know the writer is a woman, Ana Nogueira, (and i don't want to send any hate towards her since it seems to me she gets enough), who's script is just fine, i don't know what that one variety writer was smoking when he said it was the worst he's even seen, but it's perfectly serviceable, it's honestly the weird editing that's not helping it.

Also why was Lobo even there? I mean, don't get me wrong, I liked what we did see of him but still, why was he there? He wasn't even in the comic book, and yeah I know we established it isn't actually based on it but i'm still wondering why they decided to include him at all if he gets only a few scenes that doesn't change much.

Okay, it may seem like i don't like this movie at all, and i do admit i wished i liked it more but it's such a standard superhero movie that it makes it hard to have any strong opinion on it, but that doesn't mean i didn't enjoy my time, and you know what, that's fine, sometimes a movie can just be fine.

Do I think the DCU is dead? Um, no. I'll have you know the MCU's second ever movie was way worse than this, hell, a lot of recent MCU movies are actually way worse than Supergirl could ever be.

I'm just glad little girls can look up to a heroine who kicks the butts of human traffickers, oh yeah i should've mentioned this, but they made Kram a real piece of crap in this, i mean holy.

Anyways, i'm running out of things to say, but before i go, let me say this..watch the movie before forming your own opinion, don't just listen to some incel on youtube complaining about Milly not being hot enough, maybe try to think on your own, art is subjective after all.

reviews.title: Supergirl herself shines, but a poorly executed plot and choppy pacing make this film feel disjointed
reviews.review:
Cons: This movie had a couple of convenient moments that just felt like lazy writing. For example, towards the beginning of the movie, Krem of the Yellow Hills just randomly walks into Supergirl's ship out of nowhere and somehow neither Supergirl nor Ruthye even notice till he has taken over the ship. While the action scenes in this movie were stellar, there was just one needle drop in the final battle that was absolutely unnecessary and made me cringe. It reminded me of the 2 cringe needle drops in Superman (2025), the one that plays while Mister Terrific is fighting while Lois watches and that stupid Punk Rocker song at the end of Superman. Anyway, another issue I had with this film is how unserious it took the whole child trafficking thing. If you are going to have a heavy theme like child trafficking in your film, then it needs to be taken seriously and handled with care. Saving the victims of trafficking should not be treated like an afterthought. For example, after Krem killed a whole victim's family, instead of being mad at Krem, she is mad at Ruthye for wanting to do something about it which is ridiculous and it felt to me like Supergirl really needed to get her priorities straight. I get that she's worried about her dog and Ruthye's soul but after finding out that the guy you are hunting down is also involved in child trafficking, I would think that would take priority in your reasons to go after him and shut down his operations for good. Furthermore, the CGI looked cheap in a few scenes, especially the scene right before the final battle where Ruthye is running away from the broken debris of Krem's ship. However, I understand that cheap CGI is an issue for most films unfortunately in the modern day. It really sucks. Finally, I did not care for that scene where Supergirl gets blasted out of the space bus and then just happens to float right into the light of a yellow sun. First of all, the scene lasted longer than it needed to and felt awkward. It sort of reminded me of that scene in Star Wars: The Last Jedi where an elderly Princess Leia is using the force to float in space in a very cringe fashion. Second of all, the scene is just another example of a convenient moment in this film that felt like lazy writing. Yeah, of course she just happens to float right to a yellow sun and gets her powers back.

Pros: The casting for this movie is fantastic. Milly Alcock owns the Supergirl role. She is perfect as Kara, and she just looks so good in that Supergirl suit. Jason Momoa as Lobo is another perfect casting. He blends into the role so well that I almost forgot it was him. Loved Lobo's charisma and Supergirl's as well for that matter. Finally, I thought that Ruthye and Krem were also perfectly casted. Eve Ridley played the innocent and driven Ruthye so well. Most characters like Ruthye usually come off as annoying, but I found myself rooting for her which was delightful. Finally, Matthias Schoenaerts made Krem into a presence on screen, and I adored his accent. Furthermore, I gotta say that the action/fighting scenes were great. Supergirl in action is just so cool to watch. I just wish it wasn't ruined by that awful needle drop at the end. Also, I have to give a shout out to Krypto. He's just so adorable, and his emotional scenes in this film really pulled on my heartstrings. Some of the dialogue in this film was also fantastic. This movie has some of the best humor that I have seen in a superhero film in a while if I am being honest, especially that line by that alien bus driver where he says, "Yeah, sure, if I had a bigger engine or some balls, but I have neither. So, no." The dialogue wasn't just capable of being funny though, it was also capable of being pretty deep and meaningful. For example, the line said by Supergirl, "Your life will be your revenge" really stuck with me. The Superman cameos were another highlight of this movie for me. David Corenswet's Superman is just such a scene stealer and his presence is always welcome. I love his and Kara's dynamic.

reviews.title: A Boring, Cheap-Looking Narrative Mess That Undermines Its Own Message
reviews.review:
An absolute letdown, delivering a disjointed, uninspired narrative that feels entirely made-up on the fly. Dragged down by subpar visual effects that fail to meet modern blockbuster standards and pacing that results in a checklist of boring scenes, it ultimately feels like a complete waste of a premium ticket.

The story struggles significantly with emotional weight and character motivation, completely misplacing its stakes. While the film attempts to establish dramatic tension through a tragic family backstory early on, it quickly squanders that genuine emotional momentum. Instead, it relies on incredibly lazy, unimpeachable plot devices to drive the main characters into action. Major turning points that are supposed to feel urgent and heavy land with a complete thud, played out in flat, non-emotional sequences that fail to make the audience care.

Worse, the script completely collapses under its own thematic hypocrisy. The final act features baffling character decisions and a glaring double standard regarding revenge and morality that completely undermines any message the film tries to send. It insults the audience's intelligence by lecturing on one hand while immediately contradicting those actions with the other.

Ending on a jarring, unearned resolution that completely fails to match the tone of what came before, the movie is a hollow and frustrating experience. Between the cheap-looking visuals and the boring script, it is highly recommended to skip this one entirely.

I enjoyed watching this character-driven movie more than any of the recent Marvel entries. The CGI battles are short enough that they didn't induce sensory overload. The plot was straightforward and included enough back story to understood character motivations. The villain lacks the megalomania to take on the universe; he is a more plausible ruthless humanoid-trafficker. Perhaps use of alien languages was too frequent; the music score lacked a theme or even coherence. My own pet peeve was depicting night clubs on distant planets swinging to 1960's bossa nova and Irving Berlin. Disregarding these nitpicks, this is a pleasant diversion. More, please (with perhaps a lower price tag).

reviews.title: A really fun time
reviews.review:
Mild spoiler warning Yesterday evening I was in the Theater for Supergirl with two friends of mine (the 3D version even). One already read the comic, same as me, the other didn't. And we thoroughly enjoyed it.

First a little bit of backstory. I never was a big fan of DC. Of course I enjoyed the dark knight trilogy, or the batman of 1989, but the new stuff was just too dark and broody, and everything was grey etc. I want to have fun if I go see a superhero movie, not look at some guys in a bad mood just punching each other. I was more of a marvel guy. Well, up until endgame (to be honest, even just to infinity war). After that I felt like the air was just out (is that an English idiom, too? Eh...) i was in deadpool and wolverine and gotg was good, but the rest? Meh. Too many shows, too many movies, and the quality just went down. I guess it was just Bad guy, good guy, they punch each other, fin (greatly exaggerated, but at least in my personal perception true).

Then came the DC reboot. I actually didn't watch superman, but the reviews were promising, and the colours and tone of it all seemed fun. And then I heard about supergirl. I thought, a supergirl movie, from James Gunn (I know he's not the director, but anyways), with Milly Alcock, the trailers and the music seem fun, and it's based on a comic, and the comic is fire?! Sign me up.

So I grabbed my two friends and dragged them off to the theater. And all three of us? We thought it was really good! We didn't mind the changes from the comic, some things just wouldn't translate well to film, others could be very confusing (I'll just say Comet) and other changes were absolutely fine. reviews.title: I haven't read the original comic.
reviews.review:
For the past few weeks my feed has been flooded with negative reviews. It honestly feels like someone launched a targeted campaign simply because the adaptation isn't what people imagined while reading the comic, or listening to someone else read the comic)))

To me, a book, a comic, a manga, and a movie are completely different experiences. The Lord of the Rings is a great example of that.

Back to Supergirl. The movie isn't bad. It's obviously not a masterpiece, but it's nowhere near a disaster either. Based on the apperception of my subjective objectivity, I'd say it's leagues better than Fantastic Four, The Flash, Captain America, and it'll most likely end up being better than the upcoming Spider Man movie with Tom Holland.

The biggest highlight, and the movie's real decoration, is Milly Alcock's performance. She absolutely carries the film.

Other positives include the road trip vibe. I won't spoil anything. The soundtrack is solid, and there are plenty of genuinely cool action sequences.

As for the screenplay and the story, I'd say they're perfectly fine for the average moviegoer. It's a decent movie for an evening watch. Hardcore fans will probably disagree. Then again, hardcore fans are notoriously difficult to please.

As for YouTubers making frame by frame breakdowns of every Easter egg and reference, don't worry, they'll have plenty of material to milk.

Now for the weak, and honestly pretty dumb, parts.

First, Lobo.

Whether it's the comics or the animated stuff I've seen, Lobo has always been that one guy who simply doesn't fit in. The guy who ruins every party just by showing up.

Here's the paradox. Jason Momoa absolutely nails that "annoying dude nobody actually wants to be around." The problem is... that's exactly what makes him a downside of the movie. The character himself is the problem. Momoa plays him well, but Lobo is still a negative presence.

As for the main villain, there's a ridiculous amount of hate online about him too. Personally, I wouldn't say I liked him. What I actually liked was the concept. He's small, immature evil. Almost absurd. Evil played as comedy. At least that's how I understood what the character was supposed to be.

The antagonist's threat level is basically that of some neighborhood thug. He's that loser who picked fights with everyone in school and then never moved out of his parents' house afterward.

Don't get me wrong. The main villain spits poison at a dog. Morally speaking, that's practically Hitler level.

So if you look at the antagonist through the lens of an irrational bully who acts first and maybe thinks later, then the character actually does exactly what he's supposed to do.

Overall, I don't think the movie is bad. I'd give it a strong 7 out of 10.

Maybe even a 7.6...

reviews.title: Supergirl: an enjoyable, emotional and entertaining summer superhero movie...
reviews.review:
I honestly came away from Supergirl wondering if everyone else had watched a different film. I really don't understand the amount of hate it's been getting. Is it perfect? No. But is it an enjoyable, emotional and entertaining summer superhero movie? Absolutely.

Milly Alcock is excellent as Kara Zor El, balancing vulnerability and kindness throughout. She's also an absolute badass and completely won me over, feeling like the perfect choice to lead this new era of the character. Jason Momoa is equally pitch perfect as Lobo... chaotic, funny and impossible not to enjoy whenever he's on screen.

The flashbacks give Kara's story real emotional weight, helping us understand who she is and why she makes the choices she does. I also loved the third act, which delivers plenty of action set to a brilliant soundtrack.

One change I preferred over the graphic novel was the ending. In the comic, Ruthye confronts Krem and witnesses his suffering, but he ultimately survives. In the movie, Krem is killed, and Kara shields Ruthye from seeing it... a choice that preserves her emotional innocence and gives the story a more satisfying conclusion. And Lobo watching Krem of the Yellow Hill's fate unfold from a distance made me smile wide.

It was also great to see David Corenswet return as Superman, setting up Superman: The Man of Tomorrow perfectly.

No, this isn't a masterpiece, and it doesn't reinvent the superhero genre... but not every comic book movie has to. Sometimes it's enough to tell a heartfelt, entertaining story with characters you care about, and Supergirl does exactly that. I was invested from start to finish and left the cinema with a big smile on my face.

I'm also disappointed that it feels like Ruthie was more the main character than Supergirl in her own movie. Those complaints aside though, Milly Alcock shines like a yellow sun as Kara Zor El, her performance embodies the reckless and filthy party girl version of Supergirl perfectly, her facial expressions and mannerisms often being the only real human on screen that doesn't feel somewhat robotic, she really brings an energy and a finesse to the role that would have been very challenging for anyone to succeed with, but she does a good job being sassy and sarcastic even in the face of danger and she pulls it off. The villain Krem is very terrifying and intense, the actor does a great job, but I almost wonder if the fact that the villain is only terrifying and awful and doesn't have any redeemable or 'likeable' qualities could be seen as a negative trait of this film, even though the villain is absolutely terrifying, is he a little one note? Maybe, I still thought he was impressively intimidating either way. Ruthie Marie Knoll (hope that's how you spell it) was a decent performance, unfortunately though the trope of a child being protected by a comic book character is beyond beaten to death at this point, she was appropriately annoying and overbearing for an annoying child sidekick character (sorry, I thought she took up way too much screen time) the best part of this film is the absolute landmark performance of Jason Momoa as Lobo, he is absolutely perfect for the role and in one movie they proved all those fancasters right after all, he was born to play Lobo. I can definitely see Lobo returning later in this DC Universe. Overall, while Supergirl is far from being perfect and I would argue it's a slight step down in focused greatness compared to the Superman film, the great standout performances of Milly Alcock as Supergirl and Jason Momoa as Lobo along with some improved flight scenes and some edge of your seat action makes this a worthwhile summer blockbuster and a solid return to the James Gunn led DCU. 7/10.

reviews.title: Trash
reviews.review:
CW's Supergirl is a frustrating masterclass in squandered potential. What should have been an inspiring, high-flying exploration of one of DC's most iconic heroes instead devolves into a repetitive, heavy-handed soap opera that constantly gets in its own way.

From the outset, Melissa Benoist absolutely shines as Kara Danvers. She brings a genuine warmth, charm, and bright optimism to the role, doing the absolute best she can with the material she's given. Unfortunately, that material is the show's greatest villain. Instead of focusing on compelling superhero narratives or nuanced character development, the writers consistently prioritize clunky, on-the-nose social commentary. There is nothing inherently wrong with exploring real-world issues in a comic book adaptation-genre fiction has been doing it brilliantly for decades-but Supergirl handles its themes with the subtlety of a sledgehammer. The messaging is so aggressively force-fed to the audience that it frequently grinds the actual plot to a complete halt.

Visually, the series struggles to maintain a baseline standard. While network television budgets are notoriously tight, the CGI often dips into early-2000s video game territory, making the climactic action sequences feel floaty and weightless. The fight choreography rarely gives Kara a chance to showcase her Kryptonian might in a way that feels earned or impactful.

Furthermore, the supporting cast is constantly dragged down by endless CW melodrama. Artificial relationship drama is manufactured out of thin air simply to pad the runtime, turning capable sidekicks into bickering teenagers. The villains are frequently one-dimensional, introduced with grand, world-ending plans only to be defeated by a tearful monologue rather than a clever tactical victory.

Ultimately, Supergirl relies entirely on Benoist's star power to stay afloat. However, even her brilliant performance isn't enough to rescue a series bogged down by preachy writing, cheap effects, and exhausting tropes. It's a bird, it's a plane-no, it's just a massive disappointment.

At the center of this debris, Milly Alcock delivers a powerhouse performance, embodying the survivor's guilt of Kara Zor-El with a fierce, uncompromising vulnerability that completely commands the screen. However, this artistic ambition is severely undercut during the final act. The narrative abruptly surrenders to generic, overlong CGI spectacles, exposing a fatal pacing issue and structural editing flaws. It seems the commercial demands of a summer blockbuster have once again diluted a director's singular vision into predictable studio formula.

reviews.title: Lobo Is the Real Star of Supergirl
reviews.review:
I went into *Supergirl* (2026) expecting a fresh take on the character, but instead I got what felt like a *John Wick* clone dressed up as a DC superhero movie. The action, choreography, and overall style constantly reminded me of *John Wick*, except without the same level of creativity or charisma.

The biggest disappointment was Supergirl herself. I found her to be an unlikeable protagonist for most of the movie. Rather than rooting for her, I spent much of the runtime annoyed by her personality and the way she was written. She lacked the warmth, charm, and inspirational qualities that make great superhero leads memorable.

Ironically, Lobo completely stole the show. Every time he appeared, the movie became more entertaining. He was funny, charismatic, and effortlessly lovable. In fact, he deserves his own standalone movie. His larger-than-life personality, outrageous humor, and screen presence made him far more interesting than the main character. I'd gladly watch a Lobo solo film over another *Supergirl* movie.

What worries me even more is that the writer of this film is reportedly set to write *Wonder Woman*. Based on the quality of this screenplay, I'm not optimistic. If the same writing carries over, I wouldn't be surprised if that movie struggles with audiences as well.

Overall, *Supergirl* feels like an uninspired action film that borrows heavily from *John Wick* while failing to make its own lead character compelling. Lobo is the only reason I didn't regret watching it completely, and he deserves to headline his own movie.

reviews.title: It Didn't Need to Be Perfect
reviews.review:
I'm a huge DC fan, and I absolutely loved this movie.

Yes, it doesn't follow the comics 100%, but honestly, finally getting to see Supergirl on the big IMAX screen is such an honor for a DC fan like me. You have no idea how big of a fan I've been since I was a teenager, watching Smallville, Green Arrow, and all the other DC heroes. Seeing Superman on the big screen, and now Supergirl, made my inner teenager burst with joy.

And yes, I'm a guy. Some people might say, "Isn't this a movie for girls because the hero is a woman?" My answer is: so what? If it were Batman, Robin, Green Lantern, or even a DC villain like Joker, I'd still be first in line to watch it in the cinema. I'm a DC fan through and through.

As for the movie itself, I don't think the plot is incredibly strong. There were a few moments where I found myself thinking, "Why did they do that?" But overall, it was simply fun.

My philosophy is simple: when I sit in a cinema for two hours, I want to be entertained. Was I entertained watching Supergirl? Absolutely. 100%.

Some people say the script and screenplay are weak. Maybe they're right, maybe they're not. But I also think that for many true DC fans, finally seeing Supergirl on the big screen is something special in itself.

Don't expect a masterpiece like The Dark Knight trilogy or Joker. Those movies were made with a much darker, more mature tone, and I love them too. But Supergirl is trying to be its own kind of movie. It's not perfect, but it's definitely not boring.

Without spoiling anything:


* Is the plot excellent? No, but it's still good.



* Is the acting perfect? No, some scenes could have been better.



* Is it Oscar-worthy? Definitely not.



* Is it fun to watch? Absolutely. 100%.


So go watch it. Don't let all the negative comments stop you from enjoying it. Milly did a great job as Supergirl-I genuinely enjoyed her performance. In fact, I'm already planning to watch it again with my friends next week.

Overall, I'd give it a 7/10.

It's an entertaining movie. Not perfect, but a lot of fun. At the end of the day, I don't go to the cinema expecting every movie to have a flawless script, screenplay, or Oscar-worthy acting. I go to be entertained.

Did this movie entertain me for two hours?

Without a doubt. 100%.
reviews.author: assyo

reviews.title: Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow... Script with No Tomorrow!
reviews.review:
I really wanted to disagree with the critics, YouTubers, or pretty much anyone who had already seen Supergirl. Unfortunately, I can't. Everything they've been saying is true. James Gunn's latest DCU entry is nothing more than an hour and thirty-eight minutes of your life you'll never get back.

The one thing I do disagree with is the criticism aimed at Milly Alcock. She didn't bother me as Kara Zor-El. Honestly, she does the best anyone could with the weak script she was handed. I understand why some people take issue with her public image, especially after falling into the same Hollywood PR trap that convinced Rachel Zegler being outspoken in all the wrong ways was a great idea. But on screen, she's far from being the movie's biggest problem.

What's really hard to believe is that Warner handed one of Supergirl's most beloved and critically acclaimed stories to such an inexperienced screenwriter as her first major blockbuster adaptation. This isn't a personal attack on Ana Nogueira. Maybe she'll write great movies in the future. But adapting Woman of Tomorrow was never supposed to be a training exercise. When the final product turns out this weak, the blame belongs just as much to the executives who thought this was the right project for someone with so little experience.

The most frustrating part is that the blueprint already existed. The comic had already done the heavy lifting. Just follow it. You don't need to reinvent something fans already love. Instead, the movie changes key story beats, loses sight of its own narrative, and bends over backwards trying to justify plot conveniences that constantly break its internal logic.

Sure, asking for realism in a movie about aliens whose powers depend on the color of the sun sounds ridiculous. But somehow it's easier to believe that than all the narrative gymnastics this script pulls just to get from one scene to the next.

The problem isn't that the movie has a message. Every story has one. The problem is when the message starts taking priority over telling a compelling story. More than once, the narrative feels like it's serving its themes instead of the other way around. Character development, consistency, and emotional payoff all take a back seat. Hollywood still seems convinced this formula is worth protecting, even after audiences have spent years saying otherwise with their wallets.

Jason Momoa was born to play Lobo. That's not an opinion anymore, it's a fact. His roughly eight minutes on screen are the only real breath of fresh air in this entire mess.

Eve Ridley is another pleasant surprise. She brings confidence and sincerity to every scene, despite having to work with dialogue that feels like it was scribbled on a bar napkin somewhere on the planet where Kara goes to get wasted.

One technical aspect that really stood out to me is how visually confused this movie feels. It's stuck somewhere between James Gunn's colorful style and Zack Snyder's darker aesthetic. There are slow-motion shots everywhere, washed-out colors, and a soundtrack desperately trying to imitate Gunn's trademark needle drops, but without understanding why his musical choices usually work. Craig Gillespie's fingerprints are there, but James Gunn's are impossible to miss.

There's still time to course-correct the DCU. But right now, Hollywood seems far more committed to pushing its own creative agenda than to learning from the millions of dollars these movies keep losing.

It genuinely hurts to write this about a character who was part of my childhood and teenage years. There was a time when a DC movie meant excitement. Today, it mostly means lowered expectations.

I went in hoping to watch Supergirl.

I walked out after watching Super Garbage.

reviews.title: Unlikable characters with horrid dialog and cheesy aliens.
reviews.review:
It only takes a thin cloth hood to block Supergirl's X-Ray vision. Yep. They HAD Sasha Calle, and instead made this mess. The characters in this flic are some of the most persistently unlikeable people to occupy a shared screen.

Just as the action starts to become remotely interesting, they interrupt the movie for a dry, drab, heartless origin story no one was asking for. Remember Star Trek IV "The Voyage Home", the guy on the bus with the ghetto blaster playing too loud?

Well, photocopy him and you have your bad guys - and hey why not copy the bus scene too. If this is the new DC, then I'm done with their product. They aren't making entertainment, they are making visual and audio noise wrapped in a beloved IP.

In this universe, everything is rusted out, bland, and the people all in poverty and look like they stink of rotting fish.

The "nyet, this is alien speech, not bad Russian accent" acting, bad guys who crash through walls instead of a door, and you've got an Idea what the producers think a good story is.

The horrid music doesn't trust the audience to understand even the most obvious moment without assistance. It's a distraction at best, insulting at worst.

Jason Momoa's appearance only adds to the inconsistency, delivering what comes across as one of his weakest performances since Stargate Atlantis. The usual charisma is absent, replaced with a flat, disengaged presence that mirrors the show's broader issues.

In the end, Supergirl isn't just disappointing-it's exhausting. It insists on its own importance while delivering shallow characters, uninspired sci-fi, heavy-handed dialogue, and a soundtrack that refuses to let a single moment breathe. What should have been uplifting instead feels like a drawn-out exercise in missed potential.

reviews.title: Often hovers; rarely soars.
reviews.review: I quite enjoy 'Supergirl (2026)', but I'm not actually quite sure why. It has all the various elements it needs, but it never quite clicks. Much like its eponymous Kryptonian, who spends much of the movie depowered in one way or another, the flick often hovers but rarely soars. I can see why some people find it disapointing, especially since it doesn't really feel like a Supergirl movie - or, at least, like the Supergirl movie you may expect. Yet, the words of wisdom imparted to Kara by her mother also feel applicable to her debut solo feature: it doesn't have to be perfect, it just has to be good. And it is good, even if it can't quite shake the appropriate-yet-dampening messiness that serves as perhaps its defining feature. Its themes and morals are confused (the latter especially so), its action often vaguely underwhelming, its special effects sometimes a little ropey, its villain uninteresting, and its performances frankly hit-or-miss (the lead is great; some of the supporting cast not so much). At the same time, it's well-paced and fairly distinct (at least compared to what it could have been), includes a handful of entertaining set-pieces (even if the needle drop that accompanies one of them is undeniably distracting), makes a few relatively bold choices, and serves as a suitably compelling introduction to its eponymous hero, who I personally can't wait to see star in something more holistically fulfilling. Despite its relative roughness, the film is still a fair bit of fun. It doesn't quite get out of second gear, perhaps, but it's enjoyable enough to keep you amused for a couple of hours and that's all it really needs to be. Anything else would be a bonus. I can't quite shake the sense that it's only ever so entertaining, though. Something tells me that it isn't especially accomplished, even though it's perfectly enjoyable for what it is. Perhaps my final rating leans towards the harsher side, but I can't quite bring myself to totally embrace the picture and I'm not entirely sure why. Sometimes you have to go with your gut, I guess, and my gut tells me this is a 6/10 movie.

reviews.title: The best Supergirl to date.
reviews.review:
When I say that this is the best Supergirl to date, I don't mean it as it's a perfect movie. What I do mean is that this adaptation of Supergirl is undeniably excellent. Milly Alcock brings the character to life and makes it feel like she jumped off the comic pages. A thing the movie does really well is that it makes a clear distinction between Superman and Supergirl as characters as a common misconception being that Supergirl is just a the female version of Superman, which to fans of the character know, couldn't be further from the truth. The movie ultimately does an amazing job getting the audience familiar with who she is as a character.

As for the movie itself? It does have a very simple plot with a very simple and easy to understand villain. The villain of the movie is rather forgettable, but does manage to pose a threat Supergirl as the villain is very generically evil, yet still capable. The does do a good enough job to engage the audience in the story, but it also have a few moments there the pacing of the movie slows down a little too much (I'm looking at you, beginning of the third act.)

But despite a few pacing issues and a forgettable villain, the movie itself isn't forgettable. The movie has a lot of heart with a deeper message about being good above all. It has a lot of funny and heartwarming moments, and it does nail every single action sequence.

As for the performances? I can't really put a finger on any issues I have with it. Milly Alcock is an amazing Supergirl. Jason Mamoa is quite literally Lobo cosplaying as Jason Mamoa, and Eve Ridley is a brilliant co star to stand next to Milly Alcock.

All in all, Supergirl is a fun a entertaining movie with a heartwarming and important message about choosing to be good.

reviews.title: She Could Lift Mountains but Not Her Grief
reviews.review:
Supergirl is at its best when it stops trying to be another spectacle and allows Kara to remain painfully human. Beneath the cosmic battles is a woman shaped by loss, carrying memories too heavy for even extraordinary powers to erase. That emotional foundation gives the film its strongest moments.

Milly Alcock delivers a committed performance that makes Kara feel wounded, stubborn, and deeply alive. Unfortunately, the screenplay does not always trust its own emotional core. Several supporting characters feel underdeveloped, the pacing becomes uneven, and the central villain never reaches the complexity needed to match the heroine's inner conflict. The result is a film that often promises more than it ultimately delivers.

Still, I found myself caring because the story understands an important truth. Heroism is not measured by invincibility. It is measured by the quiet decision to keep moving while carrying a heart that never fully healed. Supergirl may not become one of DC's greatest films, but it gives Kara something more valuable than perfection. It gives her humanity, and that is the reason I will remember her long after the credits fade.

If you were excited when this film was first announced or thought the trailers looked fun, there's a good chance you'll enjoy this one too. It may not reinvent the superhero genre, but it's an entertaining ride with some memorable characters.

Certain scenes had great build up, but they lingered on a bit much or were paced a little slow that any built-up tension seemed to escape as fast as it arrived or not be present at all.

reviews.author: Rigovs

reviews.title: Fun, Fresh take on Supergirl
reviews.review:
Great movie. I honestly don't understand a lot of the online hate. It feels like much of it is coming from people who either haven't seen the film or already decided they were going to dislike it.

I really enjoyed this version of Kara. Giving her legitimate PTSD after witnessing her planet's destruction and losing everyone she ever knew makes her feel much more relatable and gives the character a compelling emotional foundation. Milly Alcock was a fantastic casting choice and did a great job portraying a traumatized, rough around the edges Supergirl without losing her heart.

There's what some people would consider "female empowerment" throughout the movie, but it never feels forced or like it's preaching to the audience. It fits the story and the characters naturally, which I appreciated.

Jason Momoa absolutely nailed Lobo. He was a lot of fun to watch, and I really hope this isn't the last we've seen of him. The Superman cameos were handled well and added to the story without stealing the spotlight.

The action was exciting, the CGI looked great, and the soundtrack fit the movie perfectly. It also has that fun, cosmic adventure vibe that reminded me of Guardians of the Galaxy: colorful worlds, memorable characters, humor that lands, and a sense of adventure, while still feeling like its own movie rather than a copy.

Overall, I had a great time and would definitely recommend seeing it for yourself instead of letting internet outrage decide for you.

reviews.author: Astrobruce

reviews.title: Snyderverse Died for This?
reviews.review:
Watching Supergirl only reminded me how much stronger the Snyderverse was, especially when it came to visual storytelling, atmosphere, and making heroes feel larger than life. Whatever criticisms people had of Zack Snyder's DC films, they at least had a distinct identity. Every frame felt carefully crafted, every action sequence had weight, and the world felt mythological and epic. In comparison, Supergirl feels surprisingly weak, generic, and forgettable.

The biggest issue is the screenplay. The story lacks focus, the pacing is inconsistent, and the emotional moments rarely land. Instead of allowing scenes to breathe, the movie rushes from one event to another while constantly undercutting itself with humor. Characters are given dramatic situations, yet the film seems afraid to take any of them seriously for more than a few minutes.

Visually, the difference between this and the Snyder era is night and day. Films like Man of Steel, Batman v Superman, and Zack Snyder's Justice League had iconic imagery that stayed with audiences long after the credits rolled. Whether you agreed with Snyder's approach or not, his movies looked cinematic. Supergirl, on the other hand, often feels like a streaming project with a blockbuster budget. Very little stands out, and many scenes blend together into the same CGI-heavy spectacle we've seen countless times before.

The action is technically competent, but competence isn't enough. Great superhero action should make you feel something. Here, the fights happen because the script requires them, not because the story earns them. There is little tension, little suspense, and almost no sense of consequence.

What disappoints me most is that the current DCU continues to feel directionless. The Snyderverse had a clear vision and ambition. You could see where the story was heading, even if you didn't agree with every creative choice. The new DCU seems more interested in chasing trends, appealing to everyone, and filling every serious moment with jokes. As a result, it ends up feeling like everything else rather than something unique.

I wanted this movie to prove that DC was moving in the right direction. Instead, it convinced me that the franchise is still struggling to find its identity. Supergirl isn't just a weak film-it is another example of how far DC has drifted from the cinematic scale, visual ambition, and memorable storytelling that once made the Snyderverse stand out.
reviews.author: moizansari-47307

reviews.title: Much Better Than You've Heard
reviews.review:
Strong central performances, a fun sci-fi aesthetic, and genuine heart turned this into a win for me.

Milly Alcock is fantastic in the title role, conveying Kara / Supergirl's conflicted place in a difficult and cruel world. Jason Momoa has the time of his life as Lobo, and David Corenswet continues to embody down-to-earth goodness in his appearances as Superman.

The creature design was fun, with what felt like nods to Star Wars in several tavern scenes. The costume and character design (particularly Supergirl's uniform and Lobo's entire vibe) were ripped right from some of my favorite comics. The flashbacks to Krypton were well-placed and added depth to the narrative and to Kara's journey. And, in a world full of superheroes who refuse to kill, I appreciated that Kara isn't afraid to permanently end evil people.

That said, there are definite weak points. The villain was not particularly engaging or memorable (hardly unique in the Superhero genre), despite being even more despicable than one usually finds in a PG-13 film. He is heavily implied to be a s*x trafficker (which is a major plot point that seems skirted around to keep the PG-13 rating), and murders two different families (including teen children) in different scenes. This definitely made him more vicious than expected, but somehow no less generic. (The scenes may also surprise families taking younger kids to the film.)

Also, the final big needled drop (a Jimmy Eat World cover) didn't quite hit, and was somewhat distracting, and the action scenes in the second half felt very generic.

My son found the character Ruthiye (or however it's spelled) "annoying," and was less impressed overall with the movie. My wife thought Krypto was annoying. I disagreed with them both.

So, this isn't a top tier superhero movie, but I'd say it's a good one. It's certainly far from mediocre or bottom-of-the-barrel, and doesn't deserve the critical and box office drubbing its taking. If you like superhero flicks, especially DC, I give this a solid 7.5/10 and recommend you check it out.

reviews.author: Exsosus2

reviews.title: James Gunn's Creative Vision for DC Isn't Working Anymore
reviews.review:
As someone who has supported James Gunn for years, I genuinely wanted Supergirl to succeed. I loved what he accomplished with Marvel, especially how he turned lesser-known characters into fan favorites while balancing humor, emotion, and action. When he took over DC Studios, I was optimistic. I believed his fresh approach could finally give DC the consistent universe it deserved. After enjoying Superman, I walked into Supergirl expecting another step forward for the new DCU.

Instead, I left the theater completely disappointed.

Almost everything about this movie felt like a misfire. The story was all over the place, constantly jumping from one event to another without giving the audience a reason to care. The pacing was uneven, with long stretches that dragged followed by rushed action scenes that lacked any real impact. Rather than building emotional stakes, the film relied on awkward dialogue and forced humor that rarely landed.

The characters were another major problem. Supergirl deserved a compelling journey, but she felt underdeveloped throughout the movie. Her motivations never felt fully explored, and the supporting cast existed mostly to move the plot forward instead of feeling like actual people. Even the villain lacked presence and came across as forgettable, making every confrontation feel hollow.

The action sequences looked surprisingly generic. For a superhero film with this budget, many of the visual effects felt unfinished or uninspired. Instead of delivering breathtaking moments, the movie often resembled a collection of CGI set pieces with very little excitement behind them. The soundtrack also failed to leave an impression, which is especially surprising considering James Gunn's reputation for using music effectively.

Perhaps the biggest disappointment was the tone. The movie seemed unsure whether it wanted to be emotional, comedic, or dark, resulting in something that never found its identity. Serious moments were interrupted by jokes, while emotional scenes failed to connect because the script never gave them enough weight.

I really wanted to love this movie because I believed in James Gunn's vision for the new DCU. I defended his appointment and was excited to see where he would take these iconic characters. But after watching Supergirl, my confidence has taken a huge hit.

For me, this wasn't just a weak superhero movie-it was a warning sign. James Gunn proved he could create something special in the MCU, but so far his work in the DCU hasn't reached that same level. At this point, it feels like his creative vision for DC is completely off the mark. He may have been the right filmmaker for Marvel, but based on this movie, his creative vision for the DCU feels like a complete mess, and I honestly think it's dragging these characters in the wrong direction.
reviews.author: jacksparrow-76755

reviews.title: Potential for the future
reviews.review:
This movie got a lot of unnecessary hate, I think. Here's my summary:


* I loved Kara, I loved Ruthye, I loved Lobo. They did a great adaptation of the characters from the comic book.



* The contrast with Superman and Supergirl was conveyed well.



* The movie encapsulated Kara like in the comic book fairly well. She's messy, imperfect, indecisive, and struggling. She doesn't have her life together but she wants it to be.



* Ruthye was portrayed well just like her character in the book. She had the naive, tenacious and stubborn down.



* Krem was a whole different villain in the movie compared to the comic book with both design and personality. I probably disliked that the most. Only thing that stayed the same is he had little value for human life but I wish it did have more of an emphasis on this due to adding to the moral struggle supergirl was facing throughout her journey (since Krem was an absolute monster in the book and in the movie, he was horrible but not horrible enough). The villain style they chose to take in the movie was too cut and dry. Not every villian is so simple and adding more complex traits to horrible people would make it more interesting, imo. And who thought of Krem's design? Worst decision ever....
* It makes sense why they chose the ending that they did. The book was too ambiguous and was left up to reader interpretation. I understand if they chose that ending for their target audience due to not everyone being a comic book fan.



* The timeline was scrunched down quite a bit since they're making a movie and not a TV series. I do wish they added a few of my favorite scenes but I understand the direction they took it.


Overall, it was a good movie. I think a large part of public opinion was either biased due to political commentary or social media. It can also be because the book was absolutely excellent and some expected more of the book adapted into the film.

There are some let downs, ngl but I would watch it again.

And tbf, a good comparison is I love the animated HTTYD movies but the live action felt dry to me. I wouldn't watch the HTTRD live action again but I would watch Supergirl again.

But that's just me. :)

reviews.author: THETILER24

reviews.title: Not worth watching
reviews.review:
This movie suffers from absolute tonal inconsistency. The film attempts to frame itself as a high stakes emotional space road trip centered around finding an antidote for Kara's dog which is fine in theory, as the dog represents the last remaining connection to her destroyed homeworld. However, any genuine emotional weight the movie tries to build is completely derailed by baffling character logic.

The absolute lowest point of the film comes during the climax. Kara delivers a moral lecture to a kid about how vengeance is a dark, cyclical path that will destroy them. Then, literally moments later, she turns around and brutally stabs the villain to death herself.

It is impossible to take a movie seriously when it completely invalidates its own protagonist's message and character growth within the span of a single scene. Giving her an emotional hook like a sick pet doesn't automatically fix a deeply hypocritical and fundamentally broken script. Any positive review is incredibly generous for a story that doesn't even know what its own moral standpoint is.

reviews.author: Yuvraj-561

reviews.title: The review that matters
reviews.review:
An absolute trainwreck of a cinematic experience. From the opening sequence to the final, merciful credits, this film serves as a masterclass in how not to make a movie.

The plot is a chaotic mess, riddled with glaring logical fallacies and narrative black holes. It behaves as though cohesion is entirely optional. Character motivations shift without rhyme or reason, leaving the audience detached from any semblance of stakes. The pacing is agonizingly sluggish, dragging out a threadbare premise far past its expiration date.

The true failure, however, lies in the performances. The acting isn't merely subpar; it is downright offensive to the craft. The lead actors deliver lines with the emotional range of a concrete block, rendering critical, high-stakes dialogue completely lifeless. Chemistry between characters is completely non-existent. Subtle moments are ruined by aggressive overacting, while scenes requiring genuine gravity feel entirely flat. Every interaction feels stiff, forced, and completely inorganic. It becomes instantly clear that the director surrendered all control over the set.

Technically, the film offers zero redemption. The editing is erratic, cutting mid-scene with jarring transitions that destroy any remaining immersion. The score is equally mismanaged, blaring loud, generic compositions over quiet dialogue, completely missing the intended emotional beats. Production design feels cheap and rushed, mimicking a low-budget student project rather than a professional release.

Do not waste your time, capital, or cognitive energy on this disaster. It lacks depth, structure, and basic competence. It is an unmitigated failure across every single metric of filmmaking. Clear out of the way and avoid this at all costs. An absolute zero out of ten.

reviews.author: wiezeboe

reviews.title: Good character movie, poor superhero movie
reviews.review:
When you go to see a superhero movie, as a ticket-buyer, you have two main expectations - good action and lots of campy humor and fun. Unfortunately, those two things are Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow's (SGWOT) greatest weaknesses, which is why I think this movie is getting panned harder than it should be and people are missing the good in it.

Thinking on all of the action scenes, I think there are two that were actually fun or exciting, and even those largely have the same problems that all of the actions scenes have. For me it was the fight vs the raiders on the space bus with all the teleporting and such, and the fight at the very end with the tanks and bikes making a dust cloud when Kara goes bananas on them.

But all of the action scenes feel like they were shot by someone who wasn't sure how to shoot action scenes. They are often chaotic with the protagonists coming in and out of frame, enemies emerging suddenly from off-frame only to be dispatched immediately. It felt like someone hiding the fact that they didn't really know how to do these things.

The two scenes that worked for me overcame this problem because one involved alot of fun teleporting, and the other worked because of a long shot of Ruthie's face in pure awe of what a Kryptonian not holding back looked like, and it was mostly that emoting that made the occluded action feel more impactful than it really was.

Another problem with the action is the power scaling. In SGWOT, Kara is constantly getting and losing her powers. And yet, sometimes when not powered, she does things that would require superstrength, much less for them to be done by a fairly small woman.

In the comics, one variant of Supergirl has it that she was trained on Krypton as a warrior. I don't like that take on the character, but that seems to be the case here...but is never stated, leaving me to wonder what people thought about her fighting like a ninja if they didn't know that.

One thing I did like about the action is that when Kara was powered, her action beats were far more dynamic than Superman's.

The second expectation failed to me was comedy. This show is VERY light on the comedy, which is very off-brand for a James Gunn movie. And probably half of the best gags were in the trailers, I suspect to give the impression that the movie is funnier than it is. It really feels like someone didn't understand the assignment.

Where I think the movie succeeds (well, mostly) is in the character building/arc. Kara is introduced to us as a young woman in pain, drowning her sorrows who cannot bear to be around her chipper cousin who doesn't really seem to know what pain, fear, anxiety, and doubt are. Kal-El have lived an idyllic life. He is an aspirational character. He's perfect.

Kara is everything Kal is not. She has suffered. She knows constant pain and doubt. Her journey, which is basically the story of True Grit, is to find the purpose she's been missing by helping Ruthie. And I think the show does that reasonably well.

There was just enough origin content to set up Kara's pain. I wouldn't have minded some more. I'd have liked to see more of how she and Kal cannot relate to one another (also, she should NOT call him Clark except in public on Earth...he's Kal-El to her), though some of that was there with the earnest and well-intentioned Superman really not being capable of understanding what she's going through, and her not being able be around his relentless optimism given her emotional state.

But with such a light touch on that relationship, I fear Kara comes off poorly. How many audience members will read between the lines and recognize that these are just two people in very different places in life.

One of the things that I think hurt this show is that it feels like there's a major pacing and editing problem throughout. Someone I heard mentioned that it kind of FEELS like the pacing of a comic or an episodic TV show, and they're not wrong. Each setpiece feels like it only barely connects tot he next.

And there are moments where it feels like moments come out of nowhere. Two quotes I loved from the trailer that I think encapsulate the differences between Kara and Kal are the 'Krypton didnt die in a day' line and the 'Superman sees the good in everyone, and I see the truth'.

But in the movie, these lines lack the pregnant pause and gravitas they have in the trailers. And while they are prompted by Ruthie's questions, they feel jarring and out of place along as Kara's only answers. It feels like an opportunity for Kara to expound upon these things was missed or left on the editing room floor.

For a James Gunn adjacent movie, the soundtrack for this movie was remarkably weak. The Blondie needle drop is missing. The slowed down 'The Middle' made an odd choice for an action beat song. It was odd.

Odder still is that the movie opted for a very brown and gray color pallette. This is especially odd given that the comic story this movie is a sort-of adaptation of featured endless striking colors and was very bright. It made the space realm of the DCU seem fantastical and remarkable. This almost felt Snyder-y in it's desire to bore us with bland colors and grit.

There did seem to be some effort to make the main villain more powerful/interesting than the one from the comic, who was really just a dude...and a dude who was remarkably absent for most of the comic. But they failed. This guy is no physical rival for Kara when she's powered up...and yet, for some reaon he does better than he should when she is, and she does better than she should when she's not powered up.

There is a rather major difference from comic to movie in terms of the ending. Kara killing this guy I think is perfect in isolation. For one thing, the movie versions of Batman and Superman have never been shy about killing (at least implied killing). Having Kara take the darkness for herself and stab Krem to me perfectly distinguishes her though from Kal-El. The killing of a helpless enemy is something Superman would never do.

The problem though, is that Kara spends the ENTIRE MOVIE preaching against it. To have her do it, and not comment on the fact that she was taking the darkness on for herself to do what must be done and sparing Ruthie from that, undermined the moment. It especially doesn't work that this is the final act before she returns to Earth and becomes a superhero? As if killing Krem DID releieve her pain? I don't think that's the intended message, but it's kind of what the movie seems to be saying.

I think there's a world where this act works and fits within the larger narrative, but the way it's done here, it really doesn't fit. Her action undermines her words and her character arc. On the other hand, her walking away and leaving him wouldn't have worked either. I think the rest of the movie needed to be altered to match this ending.

Let's talk Lobo. I actually don't know much about Lobo from the comics, so I can't comment on how well/badly Jason Mamoa adapts the chcaracter, but I felt his presence added very little and very much sucked time that could have been spent deepening Kara/Ruthie's connection or linking elements together better.

I kind of wish that if Lobo was going to be part of this that we would have gotten him earlier, and we could have had an arc with him. But failing that, I think I'd rather he not have been there. As it was...he felt like a cameo. He was fan service and little else. He isn't an obstacle nor does he help resolve anything. He's just kind of there. Like a congressman voting 'present' on a criticial bill.

Likewise, the entire Kryptonite Sun thing - what did this do? In the comic, Ruthie spends this time defending Kara, showing her worth and mettle, and nursing her to help keep her alive. This feels like a pointless time waster. Imagine that entire scene being missing. Aside from being the time when Ruthie is captured, which could have happened before or after quite easily, there's nothing to this scene.

So look, at the end of the day, was this a good superhero movie? Definitely not. Was it a good movie? Not really. But is there a nice character arc within? Yeah, I think so. I think this is a decent movie. It's just not the movie you EXPECT when you go to see superhero fare. This movie definitely could have been better. But it wasn't terrible like the internet wants you to believe.

reviews.title: Bad character writing, empty plot, poorly executed

Was looking forward to this movie and ended up highly disappointed.

I found the new Supergirl movie extremely disappointing. Kara felt less like the compassionate, courageous hero she is meant to be, and more like a rebellious, overconfident teenager whose motivation to help others came only after something personal happened to her. For characters like Superman and Supergirl, their strength is not just in their powers, but in their kindness, sense of duty, humility, and deep concern for others.

What disappointed me most was the way "female empowerment" was portrayed. Strength in a female character should not have to mean arrogance, recklessness, dismissiveness, or acting as if she is superior to everyone around her. A truly strong female lead can be confident, smart, independent, and powerful while still being considerate, compassionate, respectful, and morally grounded.

To me, as a woman, this version of Kara felt like a disservice both to the character and to the idea of a female role model. Supergirl should inspire because of her heart as much as her abilities, and this movie missed that completely.

Alcock delivers a punk rock take on the character that's refreshingly different from typical superhero portrayals, though her performance feels somewhat constrained by the material. The film's biggest concern is that neither Supergirl nor the antagonist feel like the most compelling characters in their own story. In fact, the most interesting character was Jason Momoa's Lobo, who dominates every scene he's in. Therein lies the problem when the stars are taking a backseat to the 7th person in the billing order.

While I recommend seeing it, particularly for fans of the new DCU, don't expect greatness. The film suffers from sloppy action sequences, complete predictability and glaring plot holes. It's an adequate vehicle for the character that sets up future appearances.

reviews.title: Milly Alcock Puts the Super in Supergirl but James Gunn's Influence is Starting to Sour...
reviews.review:
You won't find a bigger Superman fan on the planet than me and this includes Supergirl. So, I preface this review saying, I'm critiquing this movie through the eyes of someone who holds the Superman and Supergirl storylines in the highest of regards. I'll start with what works. Milly Alcock is great as Supergirl. Jason Momoa is great as Lobo. The casting is just fine. As an audience member, I care about Kara's story. Milly is able to convey vulnerability but also command a strong screen presence too. Anyone criticizing her and her performance is unfounded in my opinion. She gives a great performance here. I also liked that Kara and Clark keep in touch and that their stories will likely intertwine in future films.

Let's move on to what doesn't work. The script feels rushed. There's just things that don't make sense. Kara is poisoned but she's Kryptonian? Huh? Krypto is poisoned too but Supergirl can't take him to the sun to heal him? How does Krem even know about Kryptonians? Krem knows about them enough to have Kryptonite weapons? This feels like bad script writing because no explanation is given. Lobo doesn't get the payoff that I hoped. The times Lobo is on screen is lackluster and we get virtually no backstory. The character of Lobo is really cool but in the film, Lobo doesn't really hit on how powerful he is and he feels like more of a spectator than a necessary character. This was disappointing as Lobo shouldn't be a background / spectator character. I didn't understand the revenge plotline and then Supergirl trying to talk the little girl out of finally taking revenge only for Supergirl herself to do it. This just didn't make sense. Krem is a boring villain. Krem seems like à lackluster ravager from Guardians of the Galaxy who even Yondu wouldn't accept to be a ravager because he's so lackluster. The final battle scenes in the 3rd act felt rushed with sloppy visual effects. This whole film felt like they were trying to get this film out there quickly rather than actually take the time to fine tune the details. And in losing the small details, the film just doesn't land like it should.

Finally let's address James Gunn. It feels like a love / hate relationship with James Gunn at this point. He's managed to breathe new life into the DC Universe. But, he's adamant to leave his same goofy and weird style and characters in the movies he directs and produces. While he didn't direct this Supergirl movie, he produced it and his finger prints are all over it. He's starting to remind me of Tim Burton caring more about the style rather than the actual story. We don't need weird alien characters in every movie Gunn produces or directs. Supergirl is not Guardians of the Galaxy and if you didn't know any better you'd think Chris Pratt's, Starlord, and the rest of the Guardians are hiding in the background somewhere. That's how similar it is to the style and backgrounds of Guardians of the Galaxy. I see James Gunn not learning from the mistakes Marvel has made in the past which is audiences will appreciate quality of trying to crank out movies too fast. Slow down and take some time to get the script right and fine tune the details.

I had the highest of expectations for Supergirl and it didn't exactly hit my expectations. The film manages to be entertaining nonetheless, even still, it could've been better. There's a lot to like here. Milly Alcock is phenomenal here. Krypto is adorable. Lobo is a cool character even if they didn't quite use him correctly. But, script issues and James Gunn's insistence of making these films too quirky and goofy prevent Supergirl from truly taking off and being an instant classic. I would still recommend to action and superhero film fans but with expectations of knowing the small details will be wrong even though the film is entertaining nonetheless.

reviews.title: Supergirl
reviews.review:
I went in with the bar underground literally.

The online reaction this week had me genuinely confused. People comparing this to Madame Web? Come on. Not even close. Like I get that it's not perfect, far from it actually, but that comparison is just unfair imo.

Here's the thing though. This is an adaptation of a genuinely hard book to adapt. Tom King's run is very specific, very narration heavy, almost literary in how it tells its story. The comic is this episodic odyssey and the movie had to compress that into something that works on a screen. And I actually think in some ways they pulled it off better than the source. The constant narration on every page of the book, I genuinely don't even know how you would put that in a movie without it feeling completely suffocating. So I'm glad they didn't try.

What I do miss though? The space. The actual traveling through space. The book made it feel massive, very pretty when she is traveling on the horse with all the colors and starts, planet to planet to planet, each one with its own whole thing going on. The movie keeps it very general. It's pretty enough but it doesn't hit the same. I wanted something more visually alive out there in the cosmos. The horse as well (i actually did not like what happend to the horse in the book).

Milly Alcock though. She gives Kara this razor-sharp edge and it carries the entire movie, even through the parts where the script isn't doing her any favors. The intro in Superman already sold me on her and she delivers here too. Kara on her birthday, drinking under a red sun specifically so she can actually feel it, that's such a specific character choice. Clark came to Earth as a baby and experienced Krypton's loss second hand. Kara watched it happen at an age where she could actually understand what she was losing. The flashbacks to Argo City are scattered through the film rather than dumped on you all at once, i liked those parts.

Lobo. He was never in King's comic at all, so people who know the book went in already knowing he's outside the book. And honestly? Momoa was good. He's exactly what you'd want Lobo to be.

The ending is the biggest change and actually the most interesting one. In the comic, Kara stops Ruthye from killing Krem and sends him to the Phantom Zone instead, keeping the line between justice and revenge very clear. In the movie, Kara kills him herself. That's a way darker choice. It gives Ruthye clean hands but puts the weight on Kara. More interesting tbh.

That's kind of the whole thing with this movie. Some of what it changes works. Some things were better in the comics. Milly Alcock is going to be very good for this franchise when she gets a story that matches her.

7/10. Same as the book, but for different reasons.

Supergirl hits the big screen, while not smashing a home run out of the park it does deliver a fun and sometimes emotional trip around the galaxy.

The performances are solid throughout, the action sequences were mostly fun and overall the movie flowed pretty well with story progressing at a good pace while also giving some insight into the Gunn universe back story.

There were few major negatives in this movie, the story overall was good but not excellent and there were some questionable character motives and performances.

Overall it was an enjoyable couple of hours and in the end what more do we want from a movie.
